News.title: My brother, 14, was raped & burned alive in ‘cult’ killing – his murderers are still free three years after conviction
News.content:
LUCAS Terra was 14 years old when he was raped and burned alive in the basement of a church – and despite being convicted three years ago, his evil killers remain free.

In an exclusive interview with The Sun, Lucas’ heartbroken brother Carlos Terra reveals the horror of identifying his sibling’s charred remains after they were found inside a crate on a busy street – and the hidden force he says has protected Lucas’ murderers for years.



On March 21, 2001, Lucas left home to attend a religious service led by the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG).

He worked for the UCKG and was going to stamp leaflets at the Temple of the Red River – his regular branch in the Brazilian state of Bahia.

Soon after the boy called his family from a public telephone, saying that he was with Pastor Silvio Roberto Galiza and he was going to sleep at the church because it was late.



But the next day Carlos, who was 25 at the time, received a call from his father who said Lucas had not come home.

Carlos said: “People had seen him leaving with Pastor Silvio Galiza. But when he went to the church, they told him Lucas was not there.

“But 25 years ago, we didn’t have the information we have today. There was a presumption that being with a man of God is safe.”

The family created a search taskforce, scouring the neighbourhood for any signs of the boy.

Carlos said: “I thought he was going to show up at any moment. But then things started to get strange.”



A meeting was held at the church, led by Bishop Fernando Aparecido, who allegedly banned people from helping in the search for Lucas.

And two days later, Lucas’ remains were found inside a crate on Avenida Vasco da Gama, a busy public street in Bahia.

Carlos was called in to identify the body of his younger brother.



He said: “When I saw the body I didn’t think it could be Lucas.

“Then I saw parts of the skin that had not been burnt, hair strands that looked like Lucas’ and patches of fabric that matched his clothes.”

Carlos described the moment forensics confirmed a DNA match as “earth-shattering despair”.

The medical report revealed that there was an attempt to strangle him and he was charred to such an extent that it was impossible to determine the cause of death.

But prosecutors believe “there was certainly an act of sexual violence”.



In 2004, Galiza was sentenced to 18 years for Lucas’ murder – and granted parole after serving seven.

But Galiza’s testimony also implicated UCKG pastors Fernando Aparecido da Silva and Joel Miranda – who were convicted of murder and concealment of a body in 2023.

They were sentenced to 21 years in prison but shockingly, they are both free due to appeal proceedings launched by their defence teams.



Under Brazilian law, a person convicted of any crime – including murder -can remain free while appealing their case.

The country’s constitution states that no one is guilty until a final judicial decision is reached.

Carlos said: “For years people have sent me evidence that Joel is still working as a pastor for the UCKG in Santa Catarina, including treating children and teenagers.

“And Fernando. The last information I received was that he is a tour guide inside the Salomão Temple in São Paulo. This is the most absurd thing.”

According to witnesses, Galiza became “obsessed” with Lucas and he was irritated when the boy grew close to girls at the church.



He would also invite Lucas to sleep in the church with others boys, reports said.

The pastor’s bosses moved Galiza to another institution after discovering that he slept in the same bed with Lucas in church – while the other boys slept in a separate room.

He had already been kicked out of another religious community – where he had the nickname “The Secretary of the Devil”.



But Galiza continued to visit the church where Lucas attended.

Carlos’ father, Jose Carlos Terra, died in 2019 and was buried next to his son after 18 years of unrelenting campaigning.

Carlos said: “I saw my father die fighting for justice, crying out for a state and judicial system to do a simple thing. To comply with the law that puts crime against children as a priority.”

In 2007, the UCKG was ordered to pay damages to Lucas’ family as “the occurrence of this heinous crime was only possible due to a careless attitude of the religious institution in question”.

Founded in Brazil by billionaire banker Edir Macedo in 1977, the church now operates thousands of temples in more than 140 countries.



Since its arrival in the UK 30 years ago, 38 churches have sprung up across the country, including 18 in London.

Former member and founder of Surviving Universal UK, Rachael Reign, told The Sun: “All survivors are traumatised. It is spiritual abuse.”

Rachael spent eight years in the “cult-like” church, which practices miracle healing and promises divine blessings in return for cash.

Aged 13, she was approached by a UCKG member on the street in South London and encouraged to join the youth group.



Within two years she was made assistant. Her roles included fundraising drives and performing what the church coins “strong prayers” – but which Rachael said are “exorcisms”.

Pastors at the church carry out the prayers to rid members of “demons”.

Former gay members reported being given strong prayers to make them straight, the BBC reported.

Rachael said: “There would be a real stillness in the room. But as soon as the person had a reaction it would turn into hysteria. People would be screaming, crying and chanting prayers in unison.



“The UCKG is a danger to the most vulnerable in society.”

The UCKG said it does not “practise exorcism or conversion therapy” in the UK and “any suggestion that we attempt to change a person’s sexual orientation is categorically untrue”.

In Brazil, the church has seven million members – making it the country’s second-largest Protestant denomination.

Davi de Oliveira Vieira, a former pastor in the UCKG, told The Sun: “The pastor follows an order, there is a hierarchy. And he has to do what he is told to do.

“All meetings have financial goals. The pastor is given a text from the Bible, and he has to make that into a fundraising campaign. It’s a new religion disguised as a business.”



In Brazil, where a quarter of the population live in poverty, the church has built a multi-million pound fortune from its “prosperity theology”.

Its membership are asked to donate a minimum of 10 per cent of their income, plus any extra “sacrifices” they can afford in return for blessings.

Davi worked at the church for five years across southern Brazil including Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo.



He said: “It has a national and global project of youth recruitment. I saw children as young as 13 brought in as pastors.”

All pastors, including children, are forced to have vasectomies and cut ties with their families, Davi claimed.

“I witnessed a doctrine of humiliation and brainwashing. Young people were embarrassed and abused,” he added.

Macedo, a former street preacher and lottery worker, has transformed the UCKG into a billion-dollar church-media juggernaut.

He owns a 49 per cent stake in a private Brazilian bank and a growing media empire including Brazil’s number-two television network.



Since 2006, Macedo has travelled by private jet on a Brazilian diplomatic passport. He also owns the $14.6million beachfront Porsche Design Tower in Miami, Florida.

The UCKG rejected the allegations against the church in the UK.

A spokesman said: “[These allegations] are historic, have been previously denied, and form part of a long-running campaign by one former member.

“They do not reflect the experience of our 5,000+ members across 38 branches, where we have operated as a registered charity for more than 30 years.

“Prayer at UCKG is voluntary, offered only with consent, and never a substitute for medical treatment. UCKG welcomes people from all walks of life and treats every individual with dignity and respect, regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.



“Anyone with a concern should raise it through the appropriate channels, which we would fully support.”

The Brazilian branch of the UCKG told The Sun: “Silvio Roberto Galiza was never a pastor of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God; he served only as a volunteer keyboardist in 2001.

“Inquiries regarding Fernando Aparecido and Joel Miranda should be directed to their respective legal counsel.”

Regarding the ex-pastor’s accusations that all meetings “have financial goals” and UCKG is a “new religion disguised as a business”, the Brazilian branch responded calling the claims “outrageous”.

It described it as “the reckless statements of a single source” and added: “Journalism committed to the truth demands rigor and facts, not false accusations or fallacies concerning our liturgy.”

News.title: Inside sprawling abandoned Majorca nightclub that once hosted 10,000 party-goers with naked dancers & its sinister past
News.content:
CREEPING through its surreal grounds, my eyes were swallowed by the sheer monstrosity of the colossal abandoned nightclub – a hulking concrete relic that once throbbed with thousands of revellers and celebrities.

Emblazoned with vivid graffiti, the once-glitzy walls of Majorca’s infamous Es Fogueró club have been transformed into a sprawling canvas across crumbling walls.



The structure now sits mouldering in eerie silence. What was once a glittering temple to Majorca’s nightlife has become a derelict underworld of graffiti, weeds, rats and makeshift shelters.

The desolate concrete beast, perched beside a busy highway, closed its doors in 1992 – and has barely stirred since.



For more than three decades, the enormous shell has deteriorated its once-raucous dancefloors reduced to hollow chambers.

Since then, the decay-ridden estate has been claimed by a population of homeless migrants, drug dealers, skaters and graffiti artists.



People now sleep on bare concrete slabs tucked into the strange recesses and cavities of the building – spaces that once accommodated dancers now repurposed as crude bedrooms.

Its sinister atmosphere was made worse in 2010 when a 61-year-old man was found dead at the foot of a staircase.



Initially, his death was thought to have been an accident after he fell while living at the abandoned site alongside other homeless people.

But an autopsy revealed the man had reportedly suffered a fatal blow to the head from a blunt object.

Yet despite its grim history, the skeletal remains of Es Fogueró continue to lure urban explorers, who venture into its immense interior each year to glimpse what survives of the once-glamorous entertainment colossus.



Inside, rows of concrete pillars line the circular structure, standing inches from the outer walls and creating narrow, shadowy nookes.

These secluded pockets have become sleeping quarters, with mattresses wedged between the concrete.

I found Michael, 32, asleep inside one of the crevices near an entrance – a tiny pocket of concrete he had transformed into a makeshift bedroom.



“There are around 25 people living here,” he said.

The Ghanaian man, who works as a cleaner in hotels, told me he had been living at the site for around a year.

He also recalled a Hungarian man who had previously lived there and died on the grounds from dehydration.

His story offered a glimpse into Majorca’s increasingly bitter housing crisis – an issue that has fuelled mass protests across the island as residents rail against the impact of tourism and soaring housing costs.

More than 25,000 people were reported to have taken to the streets of Palma during one major protest, with campaigners accusing mass tourism of hollowing out local communities and eroding residents’ quality of life.



“Even though some of us work, we still have to sleep on the floor here,” Michael said.

Around me, litter had infiltrated almost every corner of the structure and the air was thick with the acrid reek of urine.

Es Fogueró once hosted around 2,000 revellers a night. Situated on the outskirts of Port d’Alcúdia on the north-east coast of Majorca, the extraordinary venue boasted a revolving, retractable stage, vast terraces and balconies designed to turn a night out into something approaching theatre.

The club opened its doors in the summer of 1989 with world-famous Spanish singer Julio Iglesias headlining its launch.

Horses were brought onto the stage, while flamenco performances, games and elaborate theatrical acts turned the venue into a carnival.



Former attendees have recalled strobe lights slicing through the darkness and speakers supposedly so enormous they were “the size of trucks”.

It was a world away from the desiccated concrete shell that stands here today.

The club’s founder, José Casas, had already successfully established the concept in Palma, but the Alcúdia venture struggled to replicate that success.

Its location was reportedly a major stumbling block, with fewer tourists venturing to this side of the island compared with the bustling resort towns further south including Magaluf.

Its hefty entrance fees and exclusive image are thought to have put off punters, while the cost of running such a huge venue became harder to sustain as takings fell.



Just three years after opening, Es Fogueró Palace finally shut its doors in 1992.

The once-packed party palace was abandoned almost overnight, leaving behind a sprawling relic of Majorca’s wild nightlife era.

Outside, a former shallow pool has since been turned into a makeshift skate park.

News.title: Grandfather who ‘was drunk’ when he crashed his boat that killed his two grandchildren, 7 & 9, is charged
News.content:
BOAT TRAGEDY Grandfather who ‘was drunk’ when he crashed his boat that killed his two grandchildren, 7 & 9, is charged

A GRANDAD who crashed his boat while allegedly drunk, killing his two grandchildren, aged seven and nine, has been charged with homicide.

Stephen Schneider, 64, was arrested after allegedly driving his 30-foot Tidewater 280 into a wood channel marker in Barnegat Bay on July 19.



Mya Bella Golabek, nine, and her brother Sigmund Paul Golabek, seven, were pulled from the water at the Jersey Shore by Schneider and his wife.

The young pair later died in hospital.



New Jersey State Police said Schneider voluntarily surrendered himself at the Berkley Township Police Department in Ocean County, reports say.

He is currently in jail awaiting a court hearing.

READ MORE US NEWS BEACH BLOODSHED Beachgoer pushes pregnant fiancée to safety during ‘bloody’ shark attack



Schneider now faces two counts of reckless vessel homicide – a second-degree charge – as well as operating a vessel under the influence and reckless operation of a vessel.

One of his grandchildren’s obituaries reads: “A sibling bond is a love that lasts forever.



“Mya and Siggy were not only brother and sister, but best friends who shared laughter, adventures, and countless memories.”

“Now they continue their journey together, hand in hand, carrying their love beyond this world and leaving behind a beautiful reminder of the unbreakable bond they shared.”

Mya was described as an athletic and artistic girl who loved sports and swimming at the beach as well as crafting and drawing.

Sigmund, according to his loved ones, enjoyed baseball, basketball, swimming and spending time with family and friends.

The two kids loved playing with their dogs, Tequila and Captain.



Local authorities said the young boy died despite attempts from emergency services to revive him.

Berkeley Councilman James Byrnes said: “The firemen jumped right in.

“The one child had a life jacket next to him. Of course, with CPR being performed, they’re going to remove it.”

He added: “They’re going to be living with this forever in our hearts, and our thoughts go out to the family.

“This is a real tragedy.”

News.title: World-famous tourist ‘town’ scraps popular train attraction this weekend after emergency alert for wildfires
News.content:
HOT RAILS World-famous tourist ‘town’ scraps popular train attraction this weekend after emergency alert for wildfires

A WORLD famous museum has suspended one of its most popular attractions after wildfire alerts were issued across the nation.

Staff said the service would not be running over the weekend, following the Government’s warning to halt any activities that could spark a blaze.



As temperatures remain high, the Beamish Museum has decided to call off its steam train service, an iconic feature of this time-warp town.

The ‘living museum’ covers 300 acres and gives visitors a taste of what life was back in the 1820s through to the 1950s, with replica pubs, shops, homes and businesses.



The museum has asked people to be “mindful” of the hot weather and dry conditions and refrain from smoking on the site.

County Durham firefighters have barely come up for air this week, with over 1,000 emergency call-outs in the space of seven days.





This included a combine harvester blaze in Tudhoe on Wednesday, which sparked a wildfire covering more than 10,000 square metres of farmland.

Elsewhere in Northbridge Park in St Helen Auckland, fire services were called to battle a rapidly spreading blaze on Saturday.

The Government sent out an emergency alert on Friday evening warning millions to avoid lighting anything that could spark a fire, including BBQs and garden incinerators.



Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the alerts should be taken “seriously” given the exceptionally high chance of wildfires.

The warning, which lit up people’s phones with a raucous siren at around 7pm yesterday evening, read: “There is a very high risk of wildfires nationally.

“Residents, landowners and visitors should not undertake any activity that could start a fire, including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators or fireworks.”

It added that “even a small flame” could develop rapidly into a major fire, affecting homes and businesses and putting lives at risk.



Retailers have been asked to remove all disposable barbecues immediately.

The measures will remain in place while the risk of wildfires remains high.

Chief Fire Officer Steve Helps praised firefighters and staff who went “above and beyond”, thanking the public for their support.

He said: “I want to thank all our amazing staff for their dedication to protecting the communities during this incredibly busy time and in such challenging circumstances.



“I also want to thank the public, who have reported incidents and taken on board our safety messages during the hot weather, such as packing a picnic, not a BBQ, to help reduce the risk of a wildfire from starting.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are so grateful for all the kind words and support offered to our crews as they continue to protect County Durham and Darlington. It means so much.”

News.title: Six dead & one critical after gunman opens fire in horror killing spree as child alerts cops to armed maniac
News.content:
DEADLY RAMPAGE Six dead & one critical after gunman opens fire in horror killing spree as child alerts cops to armed maniac

SIX people, including the suspected gunman, have been found dead after a horror shooting spree.

Another victim is in critical condition following the rampage that left bodies sprawled across three different locations in Northern Lower Michigan.



Troopers were called to a home in Lake Township at 11:40am on Friday when an injured child called 911 about a shooting.

Upon arrival they found three bodies and one person in critical condition who was taken to an area hospital.



Cops identified the suspected gunman as Chad Hickman, 39, who fled the scene before they arrived.

During a major manhunt that involved aerial and dog units, a fourth body was found at a second property in Missaukee County.

Michigan State Police then found the suspect’s vehicle in a wooded area near Caldwell Township and in the woods they located the bodies of Hickman and another victim.

It is not immediately clear how Hickman died, cops said.



“The MSP is asking community members to avoid all three areas so investigators can safely and effectively process each scene,” police said in a press release.

“This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved,” said Lt. Ashley Miller.

“We remain committed to conducting a thorough investigation and will provide updates as new information becomes available.”

The details of the victims have not been released at this time as cops contact next of kin.

Hickman’s ex-wife Katie Frye has taken to Facebook to confirm that she and her children are safe.



She filed for divorce from Hickman in 2023 which was finalized last year, per records seen by Detroit News.

Domestic abuse allegations were made on both sides during divorce proceedings and the judge ruled that the relationship “was marked by significant dysfunction and mutual toxicity.”

Katie had told the court that her marriage “was characterized by control, coercion, and fear.”



Hickman denied all allegations made by his ex-wife and continued to launch attacks at her on social media, including in October when he said, “leaving Katie was the best thing I ever did, despite every evil thing she threw at me. I’ve never been happier.”

Meanwhile, his daughter fired back in a post calling him abusive and “psychotic.”

“You are psychotic man that needs help…You are a horrible person for everything that you have done to us,” she wrote.

In 2024, Hickman was convicted of misdemeanor fourth-degree child abuse and sentenced to one year in jail.

So far, investigators have not publicly discussed a motive for the shooting rampage Hickman is accused of carrying out.



“My thoughts are with the victims, their families, and the Missaukee community,” Governor Gretchen Whitmer said.

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 800-422-4453 or live chat at childhelphotline.org.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If a child or other person is in immediate danger, contact 911 immediately.

Help is also available at the 24-hour National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or Text BEGIN to 88788 .

News.title: Body found in search for missing Brit, 18, who vanished in mountains near Dracula’s castle on solo hiking trip
News.content:
A BODY has been found during the search for a Brit teenager who vanished in the snowy mountains around Dracula’s castle in Romania.

Bristol university student George Smyth, 18, went missing while on a solo hiking trip in Valea Gigănesti in November.



The teen was last heard from when he told emergency services he was exhausted and suffering from hypothermia during the 2025 trip.

An initial search for him was called off before a second one was launched in June.



Harsh winter conditions forced authorities to abandon the original search efforts.

Avon and Somerset Police said today: “A body has been found as part of the search for missing 18-year-old George, who went missing while hiking in Romania.

“We have been notified by local authorities in Romania that a body had been found in the Bucegi Mountain region of the European country.”

They added: “While formal identification has not yet taken place, it is believed to be George Smyth, a geology university student from Bristol, who went missing in November 2025.”



The Brit teen’s family have been notified and are being supported, cops added.

George’s loved ones said: “We are all devastated by George’s death.

“He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends.



“We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions.

“They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.”

They also thanked Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol.

His heartbroken family added: “Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye.”

A full autopsy is currently being carried out to determine the exact identity of the body.



During the search, rescuers said some sections of the mountain where George went missing remained buried under snow measuring between six and 10ft deep.

Some accumulations of snow exceeded 10ft, complicating search efforts.

George, from Newport, Shropshire, disappeared while trekking in the Bucegi Mountains on November 23.

The teen had not told his family he was going on the trip.

Rescue teams said he set off from the mountain resort of Poiana Brasov.



He was intending to walk to the village of Bran – famous for Bran Castle, which is rumoured to have been Dracula’s home.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Piecing together his movements, rescuers think he managed to reach the Tiganesti Valley where he then rang the 112 emergency line.

He told the call handler he was exhausted and hypothermic, and pleaded with them to help.

News.title: Man, 40, arrested for ‘attempted kidnap of boy on his bike’
News.content:
KIDNAP PROBE Man, 40, arrested for ‘attempted kidnap of boy on his bike’

COPS have arrested a 40-year-old man for allegedly attempting to abduct a boy.

Police scrambled to the scene after reports a man had tried to grab a child from his bike just before 4pm yesterday in Hartlepool, County Durham.

The youngster managed to get away safely and the man was detained by a member of the public before cops arrived to the incident.

Cleveland Police arrested a 40-year-old white British man on suspicion of attempted kidnap and he remains in their custody.





The force has urged anyone with information that could help their probe to come forward.

Detective Inspector Iain Pearson said: “I understand how concerning this will be for the local community and I want to reassure you that we believe this to be an isolated incident.

“There will be local neighbourhood officers patrolling the area to provide reassurance and I encourage anyone who may have concerns to please speak to them.

“I know there were lots of people around at the time and I want to appeal to you to please come forward if you have information or footage that could help with the investigation.

“You can do this by calling 101 or visiting our website quoting reference number 162346.”

News.title: I brought PC Harper’s killers to justice & comforted his mum – freeing them will drive stake into UK justice system
News.content:
NO JUSTICE I brought PC Harper’s killers to justice & comforted his mum – freeing them will drive stake into UK justice system

A TOP cop who brought PC Andrew Harper’s killers to justice says freeing them will “drive a stake” into the UK’s justice system – and urged Andy Burnham to keep them behind bars.

Former Detective Superintendent Stuart Blaik worked tirelessly for months to ensure then-teenagers Henry Long, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were locked up in 2020.



The trio were fleeing the scene of a quad bike theft near Sulhamstead, Berkshire, on August 15 2019 when PC Harper, 28, became caught in a crane strap attached to the bike resulting in his being dragged for more than a mile.

Veteran Thames Valley Police officer Mr Blaik was bewildered to learn Cole and Bowers – jailed for 13 years – could be released as early as January, just halfway through their sentence, as part of Labour’s soft justice scheme.



As the government looks to reduce the pressure on the overstretched prison system, thousands of lags convicted of manslaughter, sex offences and domestic abuse could be freed from October 1 as part of the landmark Sentencing Act 2026.

Mr Blaik told The Sun he was “appalled”, adding: “I understand the difficulties and the decisions that the government has to make around the growing prison population.



“I just urge the government to do the right thing, which is to make sure that those really serious cases don’t form part of that early release scheme.”

Following a national outcry, new PM Andy Burnham has vowed he will do all in his power to ensure PC Harper’s killers are not among those let out early, having ordered a review into the scheme – with a petition launched by TVP opposing their early release having already surpassed a million signatures.



Mr Blaik, 55, left the force following the conclusion of the Harper case and subsequent Home Office commendations in February 2023 after 31 years.

He said he found out about the potential early release of Cole and Bowers, both 24, from PC Harper’s heartbroken mum Deborah, who’d received a letter from the Ministry of Justice.

“The whole of Andrew’s family are just completely dumbfounded as to how we’ve got into this particular situation,” he explained.



“It just shows incredible disrespect to Andrew and his family, but it also shows disrespect for the criminal justice process… it kind of drives a stake through all of that.”

He said manslaughter charges sit on a broad spectrum – with PC Harper’s killers being on the cusp of meeting the threshold for murder.

“There probably aren’t many cases of manslaughter that are as serious as that… which just makes it even more important that the government make the right decision.”



He added: “It’s just ridiculous.”

The retired cop went on to say: “If Bowers and Cole were to be released early, who’s going to be taking their positions in prison?

“Is it somebody that’s been involved in something as serious as that? I don’t know.”

He added: “They’ve been sentenced by a very senior high court judge who went through a detailed sentencing process. And his words were that they should serve 13 years…



“Nothing has changed in relation to that statement other than the prison population’s growth.”

Mr Blaik said he has remained in contact with PC Harper’s family, including mum Deborah and childhood sweetheart Lissie, who had married the tragic cop four weeks before he was killed.

He said: “I’m just very conscious of the fact that when I speak to them, I’m taking them back to the very lowest point in their lives.

“I do keep in contact with them, but I try to limit it… I don’t want to impose on them.”



Asked about the night PC Harper died, Mr Blaik said: “I remember it very well.”

As a duty senior officer for the whole force that Thursday evening, he said he got a call at 11.42pm – seven minutes after the officer had been confirmed dead.

“I was involved with it pretty much from the very start,” he continued.

“It was hugely complex because of the circumstances surrounding it…

“It’s one of those cases that I’ll never forget for obvious reasons.”



A Government spokesperson said: “The death of PC Andrew Harper was a horrific crime. Our thoughts are with his family and friends, and we understand the depth of public concern about the potential release of those involved.

“We do not believe these offenders should be let out a day before they were due to, and the Prime Minister has asked the Justice Secretary to urgently fast track a plan to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders, including these individuals, locked up.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Thanks to tireless campaigning by Andrew’s family, Harper’s Law means that anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime now gets a mandatory life sentence.

“This Government has gone further by introducing a presumption that anyone convicted of murdering a police, prison or probation officer is handed a whole-life order.”

News.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, described him as "very down" after resigning from Cambridge.

"He was very upset. He felt that there was no way out. He effectively wasn't leaving the house. He had lost a lot of weight," Andrews said.

"There should be a wakeup call to just how bad black academics actually have it in academia."

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy also told the programme "the idea that an academic would be dragged through this amount of media scrutiny is unheard of".

Shadow communities secretary Sir James Cleverly said he was angered by the "tragic" death and said "a number of people at a number of academic institutions have serious questions to answer".

When asked by the BBC on Saturday if the University of Cambridge needs to answer questions over its duty of care, Cleverly said the university should "ask themselves how he got into this position, how he ended up being in the eye of the storm, what could and should have happened to prevent this long before it got to this tragic situation".

Arday had denied plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and said the recent controversy had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

Questions were also raised about parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised Â£5.5m for charity.

He later said the run was actually completed over a 12-day period to allow for rest days - and that the huge sum was raised with the help of others.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation around the circumstances of Arday's appointment.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

In a statement on Saturday, a spokesperson for the university said it was "saddened to hear of the tragic loss of Professor Jason Arday".

News.title: Analysis: Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
News.content:
There was another reason this row had such a high profile. Arday was a celebrity academic known as much for the remarkable life story he told, of an autistic child who didn't speak until 11, or learn to read and write until 18.

Other aspects of his personal narrative came under scrutiny, and he had to clarify that Â£5m raised for charity had been as part of a group effort, and that a 600 mile running challenge had taken twice as long as originally claimed.

Some who had signed a public letter of support quietly removed their names.

By the time he resigned his Cambridge position last week Arday said the "relentless accusations" had taken a "profound toll" on him and his family.

He suggested they had been racially motivated.

There are many unanswered questions which a coroner will no doubt be expected to consider about his circumstances and state of mind in the days before his death.

In the immediate aftermath of his death, his family said Arday had been subjected to a "campaign of misinformation" that was too much for this "gentle man".

Others think that he attracted so much scrutiny because he was a black man in a prominent position.

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us."

There has been deep unease among some academics of colour who feel the ferocity of the debate was due to Arday being a young black academic.

Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, told Newsnight in the wake of his death: "This is not just something that has happened in the past two weeks, we've seen the stories, this goes back three and a half years.

"The very day he got the position at Cambridge he had a Freedom of Information request asking about his credentials. He had all the right-wing people in America and the UK writing in to see if he was credible.

"Some people didn't believe a black man should be in that position at Cambridge.

"It's been a three-and-a-half-year toll which has come its head now."

What is certain is that Arday had sought to defend his reputation, using a high-profile firm of lawyers to send a letter to a journalist from Times Higher Education who first questioned his work.

The University of Cambridge initially robustly defended Arday then announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure amid growing disquiet.

In 2023, as an elite university which had been criticised for a lack of diversity, Cambridge had been keen to make some high-profile non-white appointments. It had already made a huge effort to ensure admission of students was more diverse.

Whoever was appointed into such a high profile post would have faced scrutiny and Arday had a slighter research track record than some others in the field.

Dr Jo Grady, general secretary of the University and College Union, described Jason Arday's death as "devastating".

"There are so many questions that need to be answered. The level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to, has been sickening. It must be investigated."

For the University of Cambridge now there will be the difficult task of holding together an academic community divided and shocked by the controversy and now the death of Jason Arday.

It had announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure at the university and a review of how senior staff are chosen.

Now all of that has been overtaken by his sudden and shocking death.

News.title: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets as coffin taken to Swansea home
News.content:
Legendary singer Bonnie Tyler has made her final journey to her Mumbles home, with thousands of emotional fans lining the streets to pay their respects.

The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in Portugal.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Despite Tyler's career taking her all over the world, she has been described by those living in the coastal suburb of Mumbles as a "Swansea girl through and through", and someone who "never forgot where she came from".

People were invited to "pay their respects" by lining roads, as her coffin was driven through.

News.title: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 people who say they were sexually abused by the late Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Scotland Yard confirmed to the BBC it copied in all those who had signed up to receive a monthly email update for victims instead of blind copying them.

The update revealed a further three suspects in their 70s and 80s had been interviewed under caution, bringing the total number interviewed to seven.

The force said it had referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). It is considering providing further support to the victims along with additional safeguards.

A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC a monthly update sent to victims on 11 August regarding Operation Cornpoppy had contained details of progress in the investigation.

Operation Cornpoppy is the Metropolitan Police investigation into people who may have facilitated or enabled sexual offending by Al Fayed.

The spokesperson said: "Due to human error, recipients' email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken.

"We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident.

"The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."

The force said the breach affected victims who had opted in to receive updates from the investigation team, but recipients had been split into smaller groups, meaning email addresses were only visible within those groups rather than across the entire cohort.

The BBC understands around 140 people have signed up to the updates.

The force has previously said 154 victims have reported allegations connected to Al Fayed and that supporting survivors remains at the heart of the investigation.

It said the incident had been formally recorded within the investigation records and they would continue to monitor the circumstances and impact of the breach, including reviewing alternative methods of updating victims that would reduce the risk of human error.

The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.

News.title: Sellers puzzled by bulk orders suspect secondhand books being destroyed to train AI
News.content:
Something mysterious has been happening in the world of secondhand books.

Over the last few months independent booksellers have been observing a strange pattern of purchases which have seen scores of their novels being shipped to far-off warehouses.

In a typical week, Stuart Manley, from Barter Books, in Northumberland, would sell two or three thousand books. But one recent single bulk order from a Canadian company equalled what he would expect to move in seven days.

He says he has "never seen the like of this after 30 years in the second-hand book trade".

Mr Manley is not alone. Booksellers from around the world have been reporting similarly unusual mega orders.

They aren't sure what the final destination for their books is.

But the suspicion is that they are not being bought for avid overseas readers but instead something else with a voracious appetite for new information: AI.

News.title: When my dog died, my grief was overwhelming and complicated
News.content:
Gemma Champ, a writer from north London, rescued her cat Frankie as a kitten 17 years ago, when she lived in Abu Dhabi. Frankie died at home in January, and at first she felt "ridiculous for making such a fuss".

"I sent out a WhatsApp to all who'd known and loved him - and it turned out everyone had amazing memories of him. He wasn't just a cat. One friend said it was like 'a legendary beast from the great plains has left us.'

"We can see from social media that there's a whole community of people out there who have gone through the same experience and the same pain, so you don't feel like you're just being a drama queen - I think that's definitely how it would have been seen years ago."

After Greg James' dog died, the presenter said he wouldn't be on his show the next day. But getting employers to agree to this isn't always easy.

In 2019, Emma McNulty's 14-year-old terrier Millie died suddenly. Feeling sick with grief, McNulty, from Glasgow, said she was too upset to go into work. Unable to find someone to cover her shift, she said her part-time job in a sandwich shop was terminated. She then launched an online petition asking for employers to recognise pet bereavement.

No country mandates that employers offer paid time off after the death of a pet. Kara Stott, head of in-house legal and general counsel at law firm Peninsula, said more UK employers were starting to show flexibility with workers whose pets had died, even if a change to the law does not appear imminent.

But introducing formal pet bereavement policies has its challenges, Stott tells the BBC.

"Points to consider include how do you define a pet - does the policy just cover cats and dogs or would hamsters, rabbits, goldfish, horses, snakes, or other animals be included?"

Gemma, who is freelance, took a few days off work after Frankie's death, with the support of her "incredibly kind" client. "I doubt I could have done that if I'd been employed," she says, "and I think I'd have been weeping in the toilets at the office."

The reaction from friends and family to Frankie's passing confirmed that her sense of grief was real, she says, and she appreciated that people took it seriously.

"I do think, or hope, that people are learning not to dismiss this very profound and long-lasting relationship so easily."

News.title: Many Canadians are boycotting the US - here's where they're travelling instead
News.content:
Prior to US President Donald Trump's re-election, Kent Truscott and his family, from London, Ontario, had taken multiple trips south of the border, including to California and most recently New York in 2023.

But since late 2024, "my family and I have completely decided to boycott the United States", he told BBC.

That meant cancelling a trip last spring to Texas to watch the SpaceX Starship launch with his brother. The two had planned to fly down from Toronto, rent a car and stay a week to watch the launch, likely spending "thousands of dollars".

Truscott and his wife decided to spend that money in Canada instead â the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to be exact.

Their decision is a response to US tariffs and the president's comments about annexing their country. More than a year after Trump's return to the White House, many Canadians like Truscott are still holding firm on their boycott on travel to the US.

News.title: I wish I had been a more rebellious teenager, says Bella Ramsey
News.content:
Bella Ramsey spent many teenage years working with adults so never really went through the moody, rebellious phase often associated with being a teenager.

The British actor, who debuted in Game of Thrones aged 11 and uses they/them pronouns, says they had consciously decided not to behave like a stereotypical teenager after hearing criticisms from adults.

"I was like, I'm not going to be that."

So when Sunny Dancer, a film about a summer camp for young people affected by cancer, gave Ramsey seven weeks to experience teenage freedom, it was an opportunity to dive straight in.

"I got to be a teenager aged 21, which was brilliant," Ramsey tells BBC News. "It was really nice - and liberating."

Looking back, Ramsey says the experience made them wonder whether they had missed out by being quite so sensible the first time around.

"I kind of wish that I had made the most of being a teenager and getting away with things and being a bit rebellious."

In Sunny Dancer, Ramsey plays Ivy, a young female cancer survivor in remission who reluctantly heads to a "chemo camp" where she finds an unexpected group of friends and has a summer that changes her.

News.title: Weekend to bring significant drop in temperatures as heatwave ends
News.content:
Temperatures are set to tumble this weekend as the fifth heatwave to scorch the UK this year comes to an end.

After Thursday marked the hottest day of 2026 so far, conditions will be noticeably cooler on Saturday and Sunday.

Temperatures will fall by 10-15 degrees Celsius by the end of the weekend, bringing them much closer to the seasonal average.

The change in weather pattern that is bringing this cooler air will also result in an increased chance of rain, including in areas currently in drought.

News.title: Woman allegedly tasered, raped and beaten by ex-partner, court hears
News.content:
A woman was allegedly tasered, raped and beaten in her home by her ex-partner, a court has heard.

In a special court sitting at Lisburn Magistrates' Court, a man aged in his 40s was charged with two counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, threats to kill, non-fatal strangulation, entering as a trespasser to commit rape and assaults including causing actual bodily harm.

He cannot be identified to protect the identity of the woman.

The court heard the man had turned up at the woman's house on two previous occasions, once with a baseball bat, but it was "marked as a domestic".

Warning: This article contains details of sexual assault that some readers may find distressing.

A detective constable told the court on 14 August staff at the Ulster Hospital contacted police to report the woman had presented with significant injuries which she disclosed had been caused by her ex-partner who was also at the hospital.

Officers attended and the woman said she was asleep in bed when she woke to find the defendant was in the room having broken in and was holding a taser.

He physically assaulted the victim and attacked her with the taser.

She described him threatening to kill her and covering her mouth with his hand before raping her twice.

When he agreed to take her to hospital he stopped on a road and discarded the taser, which has also been recovered by police.

The woman sustained a broken nose and bruising to her face and neck.

The defendant was arrested at the hospital and provided a pre-prepared statement accepting that he let himself into the house but denying the offences insisting everything was consensual.

However, he could not account for the injuries.

News.title: Six people arrested after man abducted in Edinburgh
News.content:
Six people have been arrested in East Lothian after a man was abducted in Edinburgh.

Police Scotland said it received a report that a man had been abducted in the Canonmills area of the capital at about 22:30 on Thursday.

A 22-year-old man was later traced in Longniddry on Friday and taken to hospital as a precaution.

Five men - aged 21, 21, 22, 23 and 45 - and a 40-year-old woman have been arrested and police say inquiries are ongoing.

A section of the A198, which runs through the village of Longniddry, has been shut by police and a diversion is in place.

Officers believe this was a targeted incident and there is no risk to the wider public.

Det Insp Robbie Wallace said: "We understand an incident of this nature will be concerning but please be assured our inquiries are ongoing.

"Police will remain in the Longniddry area while this investigation continues and anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers."

One report on social media said armed officers had been seen removing someone from a car.

Lothian Buses posted that some services were unable to serve the village and its routes had been diverted due to the road closure.

Longniddry is a coastal village about 15 miles (24km) from Canonmills.

News.title: Public urged to avoid 'surrounded' New Forest fire site
News.content:
The public has been urged to avoid an area where crews are working to dampen down a wildfire.

The blaze in the New Forest began when a van caught fire on the A31 last Sunday. The road will remain closed until at least Thursday, National Highways has said.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said it has received reports of members of the public accessing the site where its crews are working.

It comes after an earlier update from the fire service on Saturday, saying the fire was now "fully surrounded" after firefighters worked through the night. HIWFRS added: "We will still be on scene for a number of days as we damp down and extinguish hotspots."

The service added: "Accessing an active fire ground puts people at risk, impacts our firefighting operations, risks damage to the critical equipment we have on site, and could therefore cause further delays to this lengthy incident."

News.title: Heathrow Airport roads reopen after mains burst
News.content:
All roads to Heathrow Airport have reopened after earlier disruption caused by flooding from a burst water main on a ring road.

The flooding along Inner Ring Road West prevented access to the central terminal area (CTA), which includes Terminals 2 and 3, a number of other buildings and the road network.

Heathrow Airport has confirmed the airport is now operating as normal and has apologised for the inconvenience after the road closures were made just before 06:00 BST.

Passengers are still being advised to use public transport where possible due to heavy congestion on the roads.

The travel disruption left some passengers struggling to get to their planes on time.

George Smyrniadis, 79, missed his flight to Frankfurt where he was headed for a school reunion on Saturday afternoon.

Smyrniadis, who got in touch via BBC's Your Voice, said: "I was upset. It's the first reunion I've missed since 1987.

"I was so downhearted I just wanted to get home.

"The whole airport seemed completely chaotic, but I got the impression the airlines just carried on as though nothing was wrong - and if you missed your flight you just missed it."

Smyrniadis said his trip from Portsmouth went well until he left the M4, at which point he was sat in traffic for 90 minutes travelling a distance which usually takes him about 10 minutes.

"By the time I got to security it was too late - it was already 09:30BST so they wouldn't let me go through any further."

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

News.title: Derailed Essex train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

News.title: Man United v AC Milan LIVE: Amorim’s side level again in pre-season friendly after Dorgu goal
News.content:
Manchester United face a reunion with former manager Ruben Amorim as they take on AC Milan in their final pre-season friendly before the start of the new Premier League season.

Amorim was sacked at the start of the year after a wretched spell at Old Trafford having arrived with considerable fanfare. The Portuguese coach is settling into Milan after being appointed by the Serie A club, though is already facing familiar issues as he looks to embed his favoured three-at-the-back formation.

Michael Carrick has done strong work since replacing Amorim as Manchester United manager, and will hope his squad can build more confidence and cohesion before the campaign proper begins. Carrick is eager to do more business in the transfer market but his selection here may be instructive with just a week to go until United’s opening game against Hull.

Follow all of the latest from the pre-season friendly in Wroclaw with our live blog below

Heavy rain and strong winds are hammering Hawaii’s Big Island as Tropical Storm Lala approaches, and the storm could strengthen into a hurricane upon nearing land.

A rare hurricane warning was issued by the National Hurricane Center for the island, which has not experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years.

Forecasters warned that higher elevations could receive up to 25 inches (63.5 centimeters) of rain. This could trigger dangerous mudslides in steep areas where residents live off-grid in makeshift housing, prompting officials to urge fast evacuation to safe shelters.

"This is an enormous storm," Gov. Josh Green said. Winds of tropical storm force reached outward as far as 220 miles (350 km), and were projected to hit the islands of Oahu and Kauai by Sunday morning.

open image in gallery Tropical Storm Lala over the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii on Saturday ( NOAA via AP )

Dangerous flooding and potential wildfires whipped up by fierce winds are among the serious threats across the islands.

A hurricane warning has been issued for the Big Island and a tropical storm warning remains in effect for Maui County, encompassing Maui, Molokai, Lanai, and Kahoolawe. A tropical storm warning was also in place for Oahu and Kauai County, including Kauai and Niihau islands.

Even if the system stays just below hurricane intensity near land, forecasters noted mountain winds and slope gusts "are often up to 30 percent stronger than the near-surface winds" listed in advisories, pointing to near-hurricane conditions in higher elevations.

A Category 3 hurricane hit the island's northeast corner in 1871, according to a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist. Current tracks show Lala passing "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," weather service meteorologist Vanessa Almanza said.

Authorities and local residents were preparing for impact regardless of whether the island takes a direct hit. Public shelters were scheduled to open and events were canceled.

open image in gallery Residents pack sandbags in preparation for Tropical Storm Lala ( San Francisco Chronicle )

"It doesn’t take landfall to create destruction," Almanza noted, highlighting that severe weather effects frequently extend beyond the storm's center.

Rainfall predictions from the hurricane center range from 8 to 12 inches (20.3 to 30.5 centimeters) on Maui and lower areas of the Big Island, with 4 to 6 inches (10.2 to 15.2 centimeters) expected state-wide.

The center cautioned that the storm could cause "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," along with dangerous storm surges and ocean conditions "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."

As of 5 a.m. local time, Tropical Storm Lala was positioned roughly 110 miles (175 kilometers) southeast of South Point, Hawaii, carrying maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kph) and moving west-northwest at 13 mph (20 kph), forecasters said.

Officials urge public to stay alert

State Rep. Jeanné Kapela traveled from Honolulu to her Big Island district to assist constituents, urging everyone to stay vigilant.

The southern region of the island is remote and rural, dominated by coffee farms and cattle ranches, but its population is expanding due to housing affordability. Kapela voiced deep concern for people living off-grid in unpermitted structures.

"If you feel now that your house doesn’t have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first you go to a family or friend’s house and you kind of hunker down there," she texted to The Associated Press as her flight took off Friday.

"We're hopeful the storm moves through quickly, but we're preparing for whatever comes."

open image in gallery Dangerous flooding and potential wildfires whipped up by fierce winds are among the serious threats across the islands ( San Francisco Chronicle )

Numerous areas in Hawaii are still dealing with severe flooding from March, Kapela noted. "We know how quickly heavy rain and flooding can impact our rural communities."

Farmers still recovering from those spring floods, including growers on Oahu’s North Shore, worried about further damage, according to Hawaii Farm Bureau executive director Brian Miyamoto.

Coffee grower Bruce Corker noted weather was "sunny and beautiful" Friday in Holualoa, on the west side of the Big Island, with local stores operating normally, though the threat of "streams overflowing and high winds" caused concern.

Wildfire risks increase during windy weather

As wind speeds picked up across the state, Almanza warned that dry, breezy outer conditions could elevate fire danger.

In 2023, high winds pushed by a distant offshore hurricane fueled a destructive fire in Lahaina, Maui.

"Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa of Lahaina, who is well known for his watermanship and has been monitoring the approaching system closely.

Further northwest up the chain, Kauai was hit by Category 4 Hurricane Iniki in 1992. That storm occurred during an El Nino year—like the current season—when elevated ocean temperatures near the equator boost Pacific storm activity and shift global weather patterns.

"It did $3 billion worth of damage. It destroyed thousands of homes, and it did kill six people," stated Steven Businger, the University of Hawaii professor who researched the 1871 storm.

"We just can never know if a storm is going to turn."

A body has been found in the search for a missing British teenager who went missing while hiking in Romania.

George Smyth, a geology university student from Bristol, went missing in November last year trying to hike to Bran, the village known for its castle suggested to be the home of Dracula.

Avon and Somerset Police said a body has been found in the Bucegi Mountain region of the country, which is believed to be that of Mr Smyth, although formal identification has yet to take place.

Officers have informed Mr Smyth’s family of the development and are being supported by a family liaison officer. They shared a statement expressing gratitude to those who have supported the search for Mr Smyth and asked for privacy and time to grieve and process what has happened.

Mr Smyth’s family said: “We are all devastated by George’s death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends.

open image in gallery The operation was hindered by adverse weather ( Salvamont Brașov )

“We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.

“We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family.

“Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss.”

The teenager went missing on a hike near Bran Castle last year after he set off from the Poiana Brasov neighbourhood last November, rescuers said.

The teenager reached Tiganesti Valley, where he made the call to rescue teams. Mountain rescuers, thermal imaging cameras, sniffer dogs, and a Black Hawk helicopter were mobilised as part of the operation, which was hindered by adverse weather with snow reaching more than 2m deep.

Forensic enquiries are set to take place in order to confirm the identity of the body before the deceased will return to Bristol.

Hundreds of fans lined the streets of a seaside Welsh village on Saturday to bid farewell to late singer Bonnie Tyler as her coffin was brought home.

The Grammy-nominated Welsh pop star, beloved worldwide for her 1983 chart-topping power ballad “Total Eclipse of the Heart," died last month in a hospital in Portugal. She was 75.

Tyler was hospitalized in May in Faro, where she had a home, for emergency intestinal surgery.

Locals and fans from around the United Kingdom and beyond took to the streets of Mumbles, near the city of Swansea, to see the hearse, which carried her coffin, draped in a Welsh flag. Dozens waited outside the singer's former home or left floral tributes there.

“She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans in Wales," said Carys Edwards, 18. “Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales; we loved her a lot."

Tyler was born Gaynor Hopkins, a coal miner’s daughter in public housing with an outside toilet in Skewen, Wales, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) outside Swansea. She grew up with three sisters and two brothers.

The singer earned three Grammy nods and in 2013 represented Britain at the Eurovision Song Contest, where she came in 19th. She was honored as a Member of the Order of the British Empire in 2022 for her services to music by Queen Elizabeth II, thanks mainly to “Total Eclipse of the Heart."

The ballad shot to the top of the charts in Britain and the United States and has had more than 1 billion streams, boosted by real eclipses in 2017, 2024 — and most recently during this week's solar eclipse.

She was also known for other hits including “It's a Heartache” and “Holding Out For a Hero," from the soundtrack of the film “Footloose.”

A celebration of Tyler’s life for family and friends will take place at a church in Swansea on Monday, before the singer makes a final journey through her hometown of Skewen.

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal ‘lead race’ to sign £50m target, Tottenham reach Gakpo ‘agreement’, Fernandez latest
News.content:
Cristian Romero bids emotional farewell to Spurs after moving to Atletico Madrid

Arsenal could turn their attention to Brighton’s £51m-rated midfielder Jack Hinshelwood as they continue talks with Bayer Leverkusen over signing England international Jarell Quansah. The Premier League champions have been keen to sign a defender following the injury to William Saliba and the 23-year-old Quansah, formerly of Liverpool, would be able to cover both centre-back and right back positions.

Meanwhile, Barcelona are set to make a third bid of around £60m for Rodri, but are still set to fall £10m short of Manchester City’s valuation of the Ballon d’Or winner. The deal could yet influence the speed of any move for Enzo Fernandez, with his former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca pushing for the midfielder's signature. Chelsea’s deadline of 5pm on Friday passed without City submitting their £120m bid, and the club expect Fernandez – who was booed by Chelsea fans on his return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday – to now stay for the upcoming season.

Tottenham have agreed personal terms with Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, according to reports in the Netherlands, while Spurs are also close to signing Manchester City winger Savinho and have joined Manchester United and Arsenal in expressing interest in Galatasaray forward Victor Osimhen. Arsenal’s Gabriel Martinelli has rejected the chance to join the Turkish club as part of a deal.

In other news, Tottenham captain Cristian Romero has completed his transfer to Atletico Madrid, while Paris Saint-Germain have confirmed the signing of Ferran Torres, the scorer of the winning goal in the World Cup final, from Barcelona. Crystal Palace have completed the signing of right-sided player Anan Khalaili on a five-year contract.

During this Hall of Fame weekend, nearly everyone would like the attention to be on basketball, but it's difficult to ignore the conversations that are swirling around the WNBA — especially with some of the league's greatest icons being enshrined.

The ongoing vitriol centered around race, gender and sexuality makes for daily headlines. They are part of an undertone to fouls and physicality that have come with the evolution of women's skills, all of which overshadow the impressive play that can be seen during the WNBA’s 30th year.

Hall of Famer Dawn Staley, who is getting inducted again Saturday with the 1996 Olympic women’s basketball team, sees a positive side to the negativity. Staley said there are similar parallels between what the WNBA is going through and what the NBA went through in the early stages of its growth.

“All the big pieces and all the things that are happening from a racial standpoint, from an officiating standpoint are great. They’re great because the NBA went through it — the NBA went through all of it,” she said. “So this is just badges of honor. Will we get through it? We will get through it.”

What the NBA had to deal with was who could play in the league. It was an all-white league when it was launched and there was resistance to integration. The WNBA has been hit lately with a narrative on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to play in the league. There has never been one.

There have been players in the league who were assigned female at birth and later came out as transgender or nonbinary.

Polarizing views have become a major topic of conversation.

WNBA players’ union president Nneka Ogwumike said she feels awful for the transgender fans who have supported the league for so many years.

“It really breaks my heart to think about how these conversations may be affecting people who have supported us for so long,” she said.

Using women's sports to make a point

WNBA players have used their platform to engage in social and political discussions, but Ogwumike believes there is an underlying agenda to the off-court questions players are constantly being asked about.

“It’s super unfortunate because we’re now in a time where I think there’s a lot of different agendas that are being used for something perhaps bigger and broader that people can’t see now that they’re using women’s sports for,” Ogwumike said. “It’s very concerning, but what I really do hate is that we are using a very nuanced conversation — and evolving conversation — to continue to marginalize these groups that we advocate for.”

Ogwumike understands the tough balance that’s going on with the news media and on social media.

"Even something as simple as you guys asking actual basketball questions. I think it’s very helpful,” she said. “I think it’s a very delicate line for me because it’s like, OK, you know, we want to act like your job is to cover this game, you know, and our job as athletes is to play it and to also give you what we can. But then it’s also like do I want to seem insensitive by not talking about the things that are going on?”

Staley agrees that it's unfortunate that all the great things happening on the court are put on the backburner in discussions.

“It’s an incredible product that we’re missing out on because we got distractions every time,” she said. “There’s something great happening, there are always distractions placed in your life, but you got to be able to handle them.”

Vitriol not new and now can't be ignored

There are so many more eyeballs on the WNBA now, with viewership 17% higher than last season’s record-setting year. Attendance is also strong again this season. Not all attention is good, though.

As the league continues to grow in popularity, social media attacks directed at players have skyrocketed and betting on the sport also has increased.

“I think it was more swept under the rug in the past, but now it’s not because you can’t,” Hall of Fame inductee Candace Parker said of the personal and threatening comments directed at players. “We can’t tell every player to just deal with it. That’s not how it works. I know I’m proud that some people think that they’re anonymous when they make comments online and they’re finding out that they’re not. There are going to be repercussions.

“Unfortunately, that’s the climate in our country right now, to be honest with you. And I think women always feel it more and it’s always been that way, from top to bottom.”

Chamique Holdsclaw said she had disagreements with teammates during her WNBA days from 1999-2010, but those were kept in the locker room and not brought out on social media, which was in its infancy.

“I’ve had teammates that I may not agree with their politics or beliefs," Holdsclaw said, "but we all know that as long as the locker room is good, we’re good.”

There isn't much kept in the locker room in today's WNBA, or any sports league, and leagues are coping with the repercussions of those public discussions.
