World.title: Rejection of Flávio Bolsonaro exceeds Lula's despite his gains in voting intention
World.content:
Rejection of Flávio Bolsonaro exceeds Lula's despite his gains in voting intention

15th Saturday, August 2026 - 05:01 UTC Full article

The figure coincides with an improvement for the Liberal Party candidate in voting intention. In a potential runoff he would take 40% against the president's 43%

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro registers a 54% rejection rate among Brazilian voters, two points above the 52% recorded by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, according to the Quaest poll released on Friday, two days before campaigning officially opens for the October 4 elections.

The figure coincides with an improvement for the Liberal Party candidate in voting intention. In a potential runoff he would take 40% against the president's 43%. It is the third consecutive measurement in which the gap has narrowed: in July Quaest recorded eight points of difference, in early August five, and now three. With a margin of error of two points, the current gap sits at the edge of statistical significance.

Measurements differ markedly depending on the pollster. The CNT/MDA survey, with fieldwork from August 5 to 9, gave Lula 48% against the senator's 39.1%, a gap of almost nine points, against the three points Quaest returns with fieldwork from August 10 to 13.

In the first round, the president takes 38% and Flávio Bolsonaro 31%. They are followed by Renan Santos and former Goiás governor Ronaldo Caiado, both on 4%. Lula will be the only one of the thirteen contenders running at the head of a formal multiparty coalition.

The survey was carried out after the senator confirmed as his running mate Alfredo Gaspar, a federal deputy for Alagoas, former prosecutor and former rapporteur of the parliamentary inquiry into the social security institute. On Thursday he presented his government programme, centered on combating organized crime, judicial reform, adjusting public spending and a foreign policy oriented towards the United States, Argentina and Israel. Lula released his the previous week, focused on defending sovereignty, reducing inequality and also tackling organized crime.

The opposition candidate's improvement coincides with reduced media attention on revelations about his links to businessman Daniel Vorcaro. In May, The Intercept published recordings and documents indicating the senator negotiated with him some 134 million reais to finance a biographical film about his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. Vorcaro, owner of Banco Master, has been in detention since November 2025 in connection with a fraud investigation; the bank was wound up by the central bank days after his arrest. Flávio Bolsonaro has not been charged or convicted in the case and maintains it was private sponsorship for a private project, with no public funds involved.

Quaest interviewed 2,004 people between August 10 and 13, with a 95% confidence level.

World.title: Colombia: De la Espriella calls the situation in Pereira "apocalyptic" after touring the city
World.content:
Colombia: De la Espriella calls the situation in Pereira “apocalyptic” after touring the city

15th Saturday, August 2026 - 01:08 UTC Full article

De la Espriella said 90 tonnes of humanitarian aid had reached Pereira through the office of the first lady

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella on Friday described the situation in Pereira, capital of Risaralda department and one of the places worst hit by Monday's magnitude 7.4 earthquake in the west and center of the country, as “apocalyptic.”

“Walking through the center of Pereira, walking through the city, wrenches your heart. But Colombians are used to rising to the occasion in the face of adversity, and it is fair to say we have never had it easy. And believe me, this situation will not get the better of us,” he said after meeting local authorities.

The president said Pereira has recorded 94 dead, 259 injured and 260 missing, and put the number of people affected at 140,000, from 41,600 families. That last figure does not match the records of the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, which in its 6:30am update put the number affected across the whole country at 102,262 and in its afternoon revision raised it to 145,601, spread across 448 municipalities in fifteen departments.

According to that latest assessment, current as of 4:30pm on Friday, the earthquake has left 288 dead, 4,018 injured, 202 missing and 354 people rescued. The number of missing fell from the 379 reported in the morning, an adjustment authorities did not explain and which typically reflects progress in identifying bodies and the reappearance of people located since. Of the dead, 250 bodies had reached the forensic service, 227 had been identified and 189 had been returned to their families.

Infrastructure records have also shifted in both directions as engineering teams complete on-site assessment of each building: damaged homes went from 73,455 to 80,744, destroyed homes stood at 12,504 and collapsed buildings were revised from 121 to 66. Cali, Pereira, Quibdó, Manizales and Armenia remain on red alert.

De la Espriella said 90 tonnes of humanitarian aid had reached Pereira through the office of the first lady, Ana Lucía Pineda, and announced that the department's reconstruction needs would be included in the economic emergency he will present next week. “This situation in Pereira and in the department requires special action,” he said.

The president declared an economic emergency on Wednesday, a constitutional mechanism that empowers the executive to issue decrees with the force of law and which will be subject to review by the Constitutional Court. The quake's epicenter was located near San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, one of those with the highest poverty rates in the country.

World.title: Peru rehearses its response to a magnitude 8.8 quake off Lima and Callao
World.content:
Peru rehearses its response to a magnitude 8.8 quake off Lima and Callao

14th Friday, August 2026 - 22:34 UTC Full article

Peru held the year's second national multi-hazard drill on Friday, an exercise testing evacuation protocols and the response capacity of the public and the authorities to a possible magnitude 8.8 earthquake centered off the central coast of Lima and Callao.

At 3pm local time (20:00 GMT), sirens, horns and whistles sounded in public and private buildings, alongside alerts issued by the Peruvian Seismic Alert System and messages sent to mobile phones through SISMATE. Thousands of people left homes, workplaces and schools for safe areas. President Keiko Fujimori led the protocol evacuation in Lima's Plaza de Armas, accompanied by Prime Minister Luis Galarreta, the capital's mayor, Renzo Reggiardo, and the head of the National Civil Defense Institute, Luis Enrique Vásquez Guerrero.

The exercise ran in three stages: activation of alerts and movement to internal safe zones, evacuation along established routes to outdoor areas, and remaining under the guidance of emergency volunteers until the drill closed. Scenarios varied by region. On the coast, an earthquake followed by a tsunami was recreated; in the highlands, landslides and mudflows; and in the jungle, heavy rainfall and river flooding, as explained by the president of Peru's Geophysical Institute, Hernando Tavera.

In the assessment of simulated damage, Reggiardo said an earthquake above magnitude 8 in the capital would leave 8,181 dead and 139,434 injured. In the coastal district of La Punta, in Callao, one of the areas most exposed to a tsunami-generating event, residents rehearsed moving to vertical safe zones after the alert.

The date was chosen to mark 19 years since the magnitude 7.9 earthquake of August 15, 2007, which struck the southern region of Ica and was followed by a tsunami at the port of Pisco. It was the most destructive quake recorded in the country in recent decades, with around five hundred dead according to figures released by the authorities, and extensive material losses.

Peruvian territory sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where around 80% of the world's seismic activity is concentrated. In July, the Andean region of Junín recorded several earthquakes that killed five people and destroyed homes.

The National Civil Defense Institute recalled the importance of every household keeping an emergency backpack with non-perishable food, a first aid kit, warm clothing, hygiene items, cash and specific supplies for infants or older adults.

The exercise took place four days after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia, leaving more than 265 dead.

World.title: Peña says the Milei-Lula crisis has not affected how Mercosur functions
World.content:
Peña says the Milei-Lula crisis has not affected how Mercosur functions

14th Friday, August 2026 - 22:20 UTC Full article

Peña said Lula and Milei now hold “irreconcilable differences,” though he argued both understand that the relationship between their countries is greater than the relationship between them.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña said on Friday that the differences between his Argentine and Brazilian counterparts, Javier Milei and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have had no consequences for Mercosur, despite the diplomatic crisis between the two countries.

“We are always trying to intercede so that differences between heads of state do not reach a point where they affect the bloc,” Peña said in an interview with Paraguayan channel Unicanal, on the eve of completing three years in office. He said Lula and Milei now hold “irreconcilable differences,” though he argued both understand that the relationship between their countries is greater than the relationship between them.

The tension began on July 25, when Milei took part in São Paulo in the Liberal Party convention that proclaimed Senator Flávio Bolsonaro as its presidential candidate. In his speech, the Argentine president called Lula a “thief” and a “convict,” accused him of squandering public funds and directed insults at Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. He also described Jair Bolsonaro, sentenced to more than 27 years for attempting a coup and under house arrest, as a friend unjustly imprisoned.

Brasília recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, for consultations on July 26. After Milei repeated the insults in a television interview on August 2, the Brazilian government decided on August 4 to downgrade relations to chargé d'affaires level and requested the return of the Argentine ambassador, Daniel Raimondi, who left Brasília the following weekend. There was no declaration of persona non grata and no withdrawal of credentials: both diplomats retain their titles, which would allow them to resume their posts if ties are restored. It is the first time since democracy returned to both countries that the relationship has fallen to that level.

Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira described the episode as an unprecedented provocation in more than two centuries of bilateral relations and said the remarks amounted to interference in internal affairs. Argentina's foreign ministry regretted Brazil's “unilateral” decision and said the country “continues to isolate itself from the rest of the region over purely ideological questions.” Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno ruled out a rupture and framed the episode as political and ideological differences between the two presidents.

The matter has caused concern within the bloc. Uruguayan Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin warned the situation “does not help anyone.” Sources in both governments have indicated they expect no change until after Brazil's elections on October 4, in which Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term.

Mercosur comprises Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, with Bolivia in the process of full accession.

World.title: The Falklands Legislative Assembly marks 434 years since the first recorded sighting
World.content:
The Falklands Legislative Assembly marks 434 years since the first recorded sighting

14th Friday, August 2026 - 21:43 UTC Full article

The ship appears on the territory's coat of arms and gives rise to its motto, “Desire the Right.”

The Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly marked Falklands Day on Friday, the anniversary of the first recorded sighting of the archipelago, on August 14, 1592. The day was marked by raising the Falkland Islands flag and the Union flag side by side on Victory Green, in Stanley.

The sighting is credited to English navigator John Davis, who commanded the Desire, a 120-ton vessel, and came upon the then-uninhabited islands after being blown off course while attempting to round Cape Horn through the Straits of Magellan. His account was published in London in 1600 by Richard Hakluyt. The ship appears on the territory's coat of arms and gives rise to its motto, “Desire the Right.”

Davis's voyage was followed by sightings by the Englishman Richard Hawkins in 1594 and the Dutch explorer Sebald de Weert in January 1600. The first recorded landing did not take place until 1690, when English sea captain John Strong came ashore at Bold Cove, near present-day Port Howard.

In its statement, the Assembly described the date as an occasion to reflect on the territory's history and future and on Falkland Islanders “as a people.” The text places immigration at the center of that identity: it holds that today's residents are families and individuals from across the world who put down roots in the Islands, and describes that process as “a thread that runs unbroken through our history,” from the earliest settlers to those who arrive and settle today. The community, it adds, is “diverse, resilient, and proud of its home.”

The statement closes by defining the day as a moment to reflect on “our heritage and our identity as a people with our own culture, way of life, and the right to determine our own future.”

Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the archipelago, which has been administered by the United Kingdom since 1833. In the referendum held in March 2013, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory. The population stands at around 3,660, according to the 2021 census.

Falklands Day was once the territory's national day, but ceased to be a public holiday in 2002, when the Executive Council moved the day off to reinstate Peat Cutting Monday, on the first Monday of October. As the date of greatest symbolic weight it has largely been displaced by Liberation Day on June 14, which commemorates the end of the 1982 conflict.

World.title: A year from the presidential vote, Argentina's parties begin to define alliances
World.content:
A year from the presidential vote, Argentina's parties begin to define alliances

14th Friday, August 2026 - 10:43 UTC Full article

With little more than a year to go before Argentina's presidential elections of October 2027, the governing party and the main opposition force began this week to realign their positions. La Libertad Avanza, the party of President Javier Milei, resumed talks with former president Mauricio Macri's PRO, while the various currents of Peronism agreed a truce aimed at blocking the electoral reform the government is promoting.

Macri and the general secretary of the presidency, Karina Milei, held a telephone conversation of around thirty minutes on Monday, their first in more than nine months. On Thursday, delegates from both forces met for two hours at the Casa Rosada: Cristian Ritondo and Fernando de Andreis for PRO, and Cabinet Chief Diego Santilli together with lawmakers Martín and Eduardo Menem for the government.

The outcome was the creation of a joint political table that will meet every two weeks, and a statement in which both sides said they shared “the conviction that Argentina cannot fall back into the hands of populism.” There is as yet no national electoral alliance. Macri has said PRO will field its own candidate in 2027 and is already promoting former economy minister Hernán Lacunza. Convergence appears strongest in Buenos Aires province.

Karina Milei has a hand in drawing up electoral lists, which gives weight to her role in the negotiations. The governing party is also holding talks with governors in around ten provinces. La Libertad Avanza won the presidency in 2023 without a single provincial governorship, an unprecedented situation in Argentine history.

The main territorial contest of 2027 will be Buenos Aires province, the country's most populous, governed by the Peronist Axel Kicillof. La Libertad Avanza opened on Thursday the premises that will serve as the base for its provincial campaign, and one of its provincial figures, Sebastián Pareja, pointed to Santilli as the likely candidate to face Kicillof.

On the opposition side, Kicillof, lawmaker Máximo Kirchner and former presidential candidate Sergio Massa met for three hours on Wednesday. They agreed to defend the open, simultaneous and compulsory primaries known as PASO, which the government seeks to scrap alongside changes to party financing. The mechanism allows all parties to settle their candidacies on the same polling day; without it, Peronism would lose the tool it uses to resolve internal divisions, and building an opposition alliance would become harder.

Participants in the meeting warned, according to the newspaper Página 12, that those backing the removal of the primaries would have to answer for making Milei's continuity easier. The message was aimed at Peronist governors of northern provinces who tend to side with the government in Congress.

According to the latest Opinaia survey, 55% of Argentines would vote for Milei or would consider doing so, seventeen points above those who would lean towards a Kirchnerist candidate.

World.title: Argentina restricts access to an Andean plain after damage caused by a pickup truck
World.content:
Argentina restricts access to an Andean plain after damage caused by a pickup truck

14th Friday, August 2026 - 08:40 UTC Full article

Authorities in the Argentine province of San Juan will keep access to Pampa del Leoncito restricted until the end of the month, after a vehicle drove across the white clay plain, located at 1,500 meters above sea level at the foot of the Andes, despite a ban on traffic, leaving ruts up to 25 centimeters deep.

The episode took place on Saturday night. According to the authorities' reconstruction, a 46-year-old physician from the neighboring province of Mendoza travelled around a kilometer and a half before the pickup became stuck in the mud. He tried to reverse between 200 and 300 meters, used a ladder in an attempt to free it and, failing to do so, abandoned the vehicle and left on a motorcycle he was carrying in the truck bed, leaving fresh marks on the ground.

Traffic had already been limited before the incident because of rainfall in the area. The surface, made up of silts and clays of saline origin, loses consistency when saturated with water and deforms under the weight of vehicles and people. Once the ground hardens again, the ruts become part of the landscape and cannot be erased with machinery without causing greater damage.

The mayor of Calingasta, Sebastián Carbajal, estimated the deepest marks could take close to a century to disappear, a projection based on earlier damage rather than a technical report on this case. San Juan's director of cultural heritage, Gladys González, called the events “very regrettable” and agreed the deterioration exceeds that caused by previous breaches involving quad bikes.

The driver came forward voluntarily to give his account, provided an address and was released. He said he had not seen the signage in the dark and maintained he was unaware of the restrictions. The justice of the peace handling the case, Andrés Troche, said the man knows the area and crossed it at around 8pm on Saturday. No formal charges have been brought and there has been no conviction. The vehicle remains in place under National Gendarmerie custody, with no attempt to remove it until water levels fall.

Provincial law provides for a fine of up to 1.5 million pesos, around a thousand dollars, an amount Carbajal considers insufficient. The mayor said he would seek to refer the complaint to the criminal courts and to submit a bill to the provincial legislature to strengthen protection of the area. At least three other breaches have been recorded in recent years.

Pampa del Leoncito, also known as Barreal Blanco, is around 12 kilometers long and occupies the bed of a lagoon that dried up some 10,000 years ago. Since 2002 it has formed part of El Leoncito National Park, the first in Argentina whose official mission includes protecting the night sky. Its more than 300 clear nights a year prompted the installation of two internationally significant astronomical observation centers.

World.title: Argentina's largest investment project aims to export Vaca Muerta gas
World.content:
Argentina's largest investment project aims to export Vaca Muerta gas

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 22:46 UTC Full article

The project seeks to turn gas from the Vaca Muerta formation, in Neuquén province, into liquefied natural gas exports

Argentina's majority state-owned oil company YPF confirmed on Thursday that it has filed an application for the Argentina LNG project to join the Large Investment Incentive Regime (RIGI). The venture, developed alongside Italy's Eni and the Emirati company XRG, contemplates an estimated outlay of 51 billion dollars over its full life, the largest figure submitted so far under the scheme.

The project seeks to turn gas from the Vaca Muerta formation, in Neuquén province, into liquefied natural gas exports. Its design includes gas production in Neuquén, dedicated transport infrastructure, processing plants, liquids fractionation trains and two floating liquefaction units with a combined capacity of 12 million tonnes a year, which will operate off the coast of Río Negro, in the San Matías Gulf, from 2031. The consortium plans to scale up to 18 million tonnes.

“We are talking about a growth platform that will generate employment, technological development, local suppliers and an unprecedented international position for our country,” said Horacio Marín, YPF's chairman and chief executive, in the company's statement, which described joining the scheme as “a fundamental step.”

The RIGI, created under the Ley Bases, grants long-term legal, tax, customs and foreign exchange stability, conditions the company considers essential to attract international financing. The largest project filed under the scheme until now was LLL Oil, at 25 billion dollars, in May.

The investment plan foresees some 5 billion dollars for the initial exploration and drilling phase, and 29 billion over the next five years to bring the two floating units into operation, of which 24 billion corresponds to infrastructure: industrial complexes, dedicated pipelines and port facilities. The company estimates export revenues of close to 10 billion dollars a year over twenty years.

A substantial portion of the financing will be structured through project finance backed by long-term export contracts with investment-grade buyers. JP Morgan is acting as arranger. The first stage amounts to 15.5 billion dollars and, according to Marín, 47 banks submitted offers worth 2.4 times the amount sought.

The company holding the blocks was set up with YPF holding 36% of the capital and Eni and XRG 32% each. XRG is the international investment arm of ADNOC, Abu Dhabi's state oil company. Eni, which leads engineering on the development, placed the final investment decision towards the end of 2026 and described the project as a global leader in liquefied natural gas.

During the construction stage, planned between 2026 and 2030, YPF calculates some 20,000 annual jobs including direct, indirect and induced positions, peaking at up to 40,000 in the third year, and around 8,000 during the operational phase. Contracting of domestic suppliers is estimated at 15 billion dollars.

World.title: How Múcara became one of Mexico’s best restaurants
World.content:
If you flip through the Guía México Gastronómico — an annual 200-page book that maps a flavorful constellation of Mexico’s most delicious restaurants, from the northernmost corner of Baja California to the southernmost point of Chiapas — you’ll find it: Múcara.

Off the page, the restaurant is located on a steep, narrow road in the historic center of Xalapa, Veracruz, tucked away — somewhat inconspicuously — between a comic shop, a tamalería, apartments, cafés and bars crammed with college students. It’s easy to miss. In fact, if you were to pass by for the first time, you’d likely skip right past it.

And yet, the intimate fonda, which seats a maximum of 20 diners at seven tables, has quietly risen to become among the most notable restaurants in the country — and is the first in Xalapa’s history to garner such prestigious national recognition, as designated by an editorial board of influential food critics, journalists, sommeliers and hospitality experts in Mexico.

How Múcara became a destination eatery

That is, Múcara is one of Mexico’s best places to eat. And they’ve earned it, despite not being in a buzzy or touristic hub of the nation.

Múcara’s objective is clear. Their menu is about retaining and expanding the overlooked culinary lineage of Veracruz through a delicious balance of elevated-yet-homely dishes — highlighting seasonal ingredients, refined cooking techniques and hyper-regional recipes. Strangely, it’s a radical concept in Veracruz’s capital city, where the dominant foods seem to be burgers, wings, pizza and pasta, and where if you were to ask a local where to find the best traditional Xalapeño bites, the list would be brief. That glaring absence is what inspired Múcara to open in 2016, when Lesterloon Sánchez Trinidad, a lifetime Xalapeño and the founding chef behind Múcara, first launched his vision.

“I wanted people to discover the regional foods from this area; Veracruz food is one of the oldest in the world,” says Sánchez Trinidad. “Veracruz includes the Olmec, and this region has been a historical crossing for Europeans, Asians, Arabs and the world. It’s the cradle of Mexican food. But at the national level, Veracruz is very forgotten. Modernity has caused us to spend our time differently and change our techniques in the kitchen. The previous generation is turning off their ovens, and things are rapidly changing. The history is being lost.”

A life-changing dining experience

At Múcara, that history is potent, and edible. And most of it is life-changingly delicious.

For lunch, that might taste like a courtesy apéritif of tepache de limón (a bold, citrusy shot of fermented lime juice) to go along with a glass of agua de acuyo (a refreshingly sweet and herbal dose of pepperleaf extract), anchored by a round of enchiladas encacahuatadas (a rich portion of four enchiladas, made with in-house tortillas that are rolled up and with filled shredded chicken, then bathed in a very mildly spiced peanut mole and blanched peanuts sprinkled atop).

There’s also envueltos de plátano (rolled tortillas, stuffed with mashed bananas and drenched in sweet, chocolatey mole); enmoladas de tlatonile (tortillas with chicken and regional tlatonile sauce, brought over from the nearby mountain town of Huasteco, and accompanied with epazote, a tea plant, and chile compeño, a rare pepper that is cultivated in Comapa, Veracruz).

Salads include a rich fig variety or a native peach criollo option. Another standout is the pasta with huitlacoche (house-made pappardelle pasta mixed with flavorful corn fungi, nata, garlic, onion, aged cheese and a touch of olive oil). The menu is relatively compact in its offerings, but at Múcara, it’s about quality and perfection, rather than empty spectacle. It’s about savoring the basics, rather than seeking the bombastic.

Mixing and matching the menu

Of course, aspects of the menu are constantly in flux, depending on the time of year and what ingredients are available from producers and local markets, making it an interactive dining experience where you can jigsaw yourself into nirvana with just about any combination of plates at your table.

Having studied the culinary arts in Mexico City with some of Mexico’s most prominent chefs as a young cook, Sánchez Trinidad — who is relatively young — has compiled and combined over a decade of experience in the kitchen through trial and error. Initially, he opened Nao as a café and pambassería (a small shop that only sold pambazos, the small sandwich of Xalapeño fame, of which he says were prominent in his upbringing but are no longer seen as commonly around Xalapa). Unfortunately, Nao closed during the pandemic, though its closure allowed him to shift his full attention to Múcara, the more ambitious of his projects. That focus has paid off, as Múcara has converted into a decade-long fixture in the city’s culinary scene.

If you go to Yucatán, you’ll easily find 20 or 30 places to eat Yucatán food,” Sánchez Trinidad tells Mexico News Daily. “Same in Puebla for Poblana food. Or in Oaxaca. But in Xalapa, there’s nothing like that. It’s an interesting case study. How is it possible that as a state capital we don’t even know our own cuisine that well? What are our dishes?”

Old-school Veracruz cuisine made modern

On a drizzly Xalapeño afternoon, you can discover the answer to Sánchez Trinidad’s rhetorical question. Múcara is a refuge for the state’s fading past — a slow-cooking, old-school type of joint in modern digs, where no one is rushing the process for the sake of instant gratification, but instead cherishing each bite and all that it offers and imparts about Veracruz’s diverse history. In many cases, Sánchez Trinidad has pulled recipes from his childhood memories of preparing food with his mother and grandmother. His restaurant isn’t just a love letter to his state; it’s an entire library’s worth.

Elegant yet elemental

As a result of his careful attention and thoughtful choices, the meals are orchestral: simple, yet highly calibrated and masterfully executed, highlighting the contradictory pleasures of Mexican cuisine as being elegantly refined while, simultaneously, retaining its most elemental essences.

“The origin of the name Múcara comes from a rock (fossilized coral and marine sediments) that was taken out of the sea,” Sánchez Trinidad explains. “They made buildings out of that. The oldest buildings in the Veracruz port are made from it. Churches, forts, everything. Those old buildings remain and haven’t fallen, and that’s what we strive to be for Veracruz cuisine.”

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Thank you, Harry Styles: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A few nights ago, my wife and I watched the movie “Three Amigos” with Steve Martin, Chevy Chase and Martin Short. Even though the movie was first released in 1986 — 40 years ago! — I recently saw a classic clip of them in my social media feed that inspired me to want to watch it again. The clip was of them ordering a beer in a Mexican bar. The bartender says, “We have no beer, only tequila.” They ask, “What is tequila?”, to which the bartender replies, “It’s like beer.” They proceed to do a shot and have a hilarious reaction. Not exactly Emmy award-winning lines and acting, but funny nonetheless.

I understand that the movie is meant to be a parody and not taken too seriously, but I will admit I was surprised at the overt stereotypical imagery used to portray Mexico. Nearly every man shown was dirty, poor and drunk. Nearly every woman shown was poor, sun-burned and disheveled — except, of course, for the few ladies who fell in love with the “three amigos.” The “bad guys” were also drunk and dirty, but also had lots of guns and made a living from robbing people. In addition to the characters, the images of Mexico and Mexican life were about as negatively stereotypical as you could imagine: poor, dusty, lawless, run-down and in the middle of the desert. People hanging around and drinking in the middle of the day, not hesitating to start shooting people. Of course, this is nothing new. Hollywood portrayals of Mexico in this way first began in Western movies in the 1910’s — over 100 years ago!

Again, I know some of you are thinking “lighten up Travis, it’s just a comedy film. I get that, but the decades of stereotypes about Mexico portrayed in movies have had an impact on people’s perceptions about the country and its people. A few months ago, one of our writers wrote an in-depth article about it here: Stereotypes worth 1,000 words: Mexico’s visualization in the media.

And it’s not just Mexico — other countries suffer the same fate at the whims of Hollywood writers and producers.

In the decades after the “Three Amigos” movie, the Hollywood narrative of Mexico changed from the wild west version to the drug lord/narco version. Countless series were made of the cartel leaders, the cartel lifestyle, with “Narcos” from Netflix being the most popular one. In fact, “Narcos” has been one of the most-viewed series ever produced by Netflix. So, for over one hundred years, Hollywood has presented Mexico (not always, but very frequently) as a dirty, lawless location in a Western movie, and more recently as the home of cartels and the drug trade.

Which brings me to the point of my column today: Thankfully, that image is beginning to change. Not by Hollywood, but by musicians (most of them non-American). Over the past two weeks, I couldn’t help but notice in my social media feed all of the images of U.K. mega-star Harry Styles hanging out and enjoying Mexico City. He is in the city to do six concerts over nearly two weeks, and countless videos of him enjoying the city have been popping up. Jogging in Chapultepec Park, going for walks on the tree-lined streets with his girlfriend, eating tacos, standing in line for breakfast pastries — basically, looking and acting like a local and seemingly enjoying every minute of it.

Harry Styles continúa caminando muy relajado por las calles de la CDMX, a un día de su concierto. 🥹 Confiesen, ¿alguien ya se lo encontró? 👀😍 Video por: alexasaeenz pic.twitter.com/NPJqOXrX7r — EstiloDF (@EstiloDF) July 30, 2026

He is the latest artist to do this, but certainly is not the first. Earlier this year, Colombian-born Shakira did a total of 14 concerts (13 in stadiums + 1 free one in the zocalo) in Mexico City. She was seen for weeks hanging out and enjoying the capital city. Also in the past few months, Irish rock band U2 filmed a music video in the city and took time to visit with President Sheinbaum. And Korean mega-K-pop group BTS did a three-day concert series in the city and were seen hanging out and enjoying the sights, as well as visiting with Sheinbaum. Late last year, Dua Lipa — who is Albanian and grew up in the U.K. — spent a week in Mexico City performing three concerts as well. She was seen dancing in nightclubs, eating late-night tacos, and genuinely enjoying the city she calls “one of her favorites in the world.”

What an incredible change this has been in the portrayal of the country. After decades of Hollywood portrayals of Mexico as a lawless, unsafe, dirty place, you now have real stars genuinely hanging out and having a good time in Mexico. The images appear to be real, genuine, authentic and spontaneous — as different from Hollywood as you can get. It would be easy to have a cynical take on these musicians and simply say that what they are doing is good for their own business. Of course it is, but I would prefer someone making money by getting out, walking around, talking to locals and eating local food rather than presenting a stereotypical, outdated and false narrative.

The World Cup was a similar phenomenon. In the months leading up to the games, the media warned us of the dangers of cartel violence and protests. The reality that we saw was of the visiting fans from Colombia, the U.K., Japan, Korea and many other countries having an absolute blast with locals across the country. It truly felt authentic, which is precisely what made it so fascinating to watch.

So let’s hope that we are beginning to see a new trend of how Mexico is being presented to the rest of the world. If so, I think it will have a hugely positive impact on the country and hopefully finally do away with the negative stereotypes that were so common in past decades.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: KIO Data Centers doubles down on Querétaro with a US $1.3B expansion plan
World.content:
The Mexican data center company KIO will pour more than a billion dollars into Querétaro by 2030 as part of an expansion to meet growing U.S. demand for artificial intelligence and data storage.

KIO will spend up to US $1.3 billion to develop the QR03 project, a new data center in the El Marqués Industrial Park in Querétaro city’s eastern outskirts. The latest expansion is expected to create more than 8,000 jobs, direct and indirect.

The move has reinforced the central state’s position as one of Mexico’s leading digital infrastructure hubs. Almost three quarters of all Mexican data centers are in Querétaro.

KIO Data Centers CEO Octavio Camarena Villalvazo announced the decision during an event led by Querétaro Governor Mauricio Kuri González and Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard Casaubón.

Camarena told the gathering that the new infrastructure is part of the company’s growth strategy in a market where data centers are playing a central role in the digital economy.

“Without world-class data centers, there is no cloud, no smart manufacturing, no digitized data, and no artificial intelligence,” Camarena said.

The company’s growth plan has already made some progress with the recent completion of phases two and three of QRO2—the company’s second facility in the state—with a cumulative spend of US $170 million. It has also run its first data center, QRO1, for nearly two decades.

At the same time, KIO plans to invest over US $200 million in 2026 for projects and expansions across Mexico City, Monterrey, Querétaro, and Guatemala, with the objective of meeting regional demand for cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure — two segments that have driven up requirements for power capacity and data processing.

Camarena estimated that the company’s project could generate an economic impact of billions of dollars in Mexico due to additional investments. Companies such as AWS, Microsoft, Google Cloud, Equinix, ODATA, CloudHQ, Ascenty, and Huawei have operations, projects, or infrastructure in the state.

A recent projection by the Mexican Association of Data Centers forecast that, by 2031, around US $20 billion would be directly spent on data centers in the country. In addition, it forecast a further US $64 billion in indirect investment, with much of that spent in Querétaro.

With reports from Cluster Industrial, Mexico Industry and El Economista

World.title: After 60 years abroad, Mexico confirms turquoise-adorned skull is pre-Columbian treasure
World.content:
The National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) has confirmed that a turquoise-adorned skull returned to Mexico from the Netherlands is a pre-Columbian human skeletal remains from Mexican territory.

Although the exact origin of the skull has not yet been determined, its characteristics and the materials used to decorate it indicate it could possibly be from the Late Postclassic period (1200 to 1521 AD).

Ongoing analysis being conducted by INAH specialists suggests it likely came from a region that currently includes parts of the states of Puebla and Oaxaca.

The skull — adorned with a striking mosaic of turquoise, shell, jadeite and rock crystal — was returned to Mexico in May 2025 after spending some 60 years in a museum in the Netherlands.

The piece, acquired on the art market in 1962, had been on display at the World Museum (Wereldmuseum) in Leiden. The process of repatriation began to take shape in late 2023 after the Dutch museum contacted the Mexican Embassy in the Netherlands to address the issue.

A decade earlier, the Wereldmuseum had begun working with the French Center for Research and Restoration of Museums to determine its authenticity, prompting the decision to contact Mexican authorities.

Culture Minister Claudia Curiel de Icaza said that the recovery of the skull “demonstrates that collaboration between authorities and civil society can translate into actions of historical justice.”

Curiel also praised the Nohivi Ñuu Savi collective — an Indigenous grassroots group that focuses on protecting Mixtec rights, history, and culture, and bringing sacred heritage back to Mexico — for their contributions to the repatriation effort.

The Mixtec peoples are a major indigenous Mesoamerican group inhabiting the Mixteca region spanning the states of Oaxaca, Puebla and Guerrero.

In a press statement, INAH described the skull as being “partially covered with tesserae, like a mosaic, forming the schematic design of a snake on the frontal bone.” Tesserae are individual tiles used in creating a mosaic.

INAH analysis has identified the presence of modern adhesive substances, used to fix some areas of the tesserae, which may be due to a decorative rearrangement or reuse of the same by the original owner, before it was acquired by the museum.

Anthropologist Olaf Bello Cardoso hopes that further studies can serve to identify the person behind the turquoise mosaic and to understand if it was part of an offering dedicated to a principal figure.

With reports from El Cronista, El Imparcial, Ancient Origins and Heritage Daily

World.title: Mexico moves past Taiwan as the top AI server exporter to the United States
World.content:
Mexico is quietly becoming a big player in the global AI economy, even surpassing Taiwan as the No. 1 supplier of U.S. AI server imports in the second quarter.

A report by the Economic Studies Department of Grupo Financiero Banamex found that Mexico’s share of U.S. server imports through the first half of 2026 was 34.5%, just behind Taiwan’s 36%.

Mexico and Taiwan have captured the U.S. market for artificial intelligence data center servers, which had previously been dominated by China. In 2017, China accounted for 60.4% of U.S. purchases of computer equipment, while in the first half of 2026 its share fell to 2%, with all that space being taken over by Taiwan and Mexico.

Taiwanese exports of artificial intelligence servers to the United States grew from US $2.8 billion in 2017 to US $72.2 billion in the first half of 2026.

During the first half of the year, Mexico exported more than US $60.4 billion worth of computer servers to artificial intelligence data centers in the United States, first surpassing Taiwan in May sales.

In the second quarter, Mexico was supplying nearly 40% of U.S. server imports — selling more components and servers for artificial intelligence data centers than Taiwan — benefiting by having become an assembly plant for Taiwanese computer equipment manufacturers.

“Mexico has established itself as an assembly platform close to the U.S. market, while design, technological integration and chain coordination activities (for artificial intelligence computing production) remain concentrated in Asia,” Banamex said.

Banamex described the relationship as a regional reorganization led by Taiwanese manufacturers such as Inventec, Wistron and Flex. Earlier this month, Inventec announced plans to invest US $450 million in the border city of Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua.

Furthermore, Taiwanese multinational Foxconn — the world’s largest electronics contract manufacturer — announced in April that it is building one of the world’s largest AI server factories near Guadalajara.

“The recent server boom represents a deepening of Mexico’s manufacturing integration, rather than a displacement of Taiwanese industrial leadership,” Banamex noted.

The recent surge in Mexican exports of servers for artificial intelligence is being interpreted as evidence of Mexico’s success in the most dynamic technology sectors globally.

The shift also creates new exposure to tariffs, while requiring trade-policy changes to address component sourcing and delivery disruptions across the Taiwan-Mexico-U.S. supply chain. The AI boom is reshaping Mexico’s economy, as data servers are going head-to-head with automobiles as the No. 1 export to the U.S.

With reports from Forbes México, AI Weekly, Channel Insider and Deutsche Welle

World.title: Sargassum seaweed levels begin to drop in Quintana Roo after record peak
World.content:
Sargassum is beginning to recede from Quintana Roo beaches after peaking in June and July, but the Mexican Caribbean remains on track for one of its worst years on record.

The decline began this month and should become more pronounced in September and October, Esteban Amaro Mauricio, hydrobiologist and director of the Quintana Roo Sargassum Monitoring Network, said this week.

The arrival of the seaweed has been erratic, however. Tulum and Mahahual still have major accumulations while Playa del Carmen has seen less. Puerto Morelos, recently clear, received a significant influx this week.

At the beginning of this month, 30 beaches in northern Quintana Roo alone were on red alert for excessive sargassum. Amaro said the network’s latest monitoring report put 22 of the state’s northern beaches in red, 17 in orange, 13 in yellow, 45 in green and three free of the algae.

Tonnes on Quintana Roo beaches

Conditions had improved less in the south, where 30 beaches remained on red alert, with two on orange, three a piece on yellow and green, and two free of sargassum entirely.

About 110,000 tonnes of sargassum have been collected statewide this year, Amaro said. He projected a total of roughly 150,000 tonnes by year’s end, well above the 94,000 tonnes collected in 2025.

Amaro said sargassum arrivals should be minimal in November and December but could resume as early as January 2027, as they did this year. In previous years, the season typically began in April or May.

The scale offshore remains enormous. Monitors at one point detected as much as 54 million tonnes of the algae floating between Africa and the Gulf of Mexico, Amaro said, including 4 million to 5 million tonnes off the Mexican Caribbean (coast?) .

Approximately 5% to 10% of the sargassum nearest the coast reaches beaches, Amaro said.

Hurricanes, tropical depressions and tropical storms could disperse the algae, he said, although officials will keep containment barriers and offshore collection vessels in service.

Tourism impact

The influx has compounded pressures on tourism. Quintana Roo Tourism Minister Bernardo Cueto Riestra said Tulum hotel occupancy had fallen to 15%, its lowest level on record, while Playa del Carmen stood at 30%.

He cited the atypical sargassum arrival and reduced airline frequencies linked to fuel costs.

The problem affects about 30 countries, Amaro added. Sargassum is a natural part of Atlantic Ocean ecosystems, but since 2011, extraordinary proliferations have affected the Caribbean region, with impacts on coastal ecosystems, fisheries and tourism.

Mexico and Japan announced last week they are working to establish a joint sargassum-response program that could include Japanese ocean-monitoring technology, specialized equipment, collection vessels, satellite monitoring and technical training. One of its goals would be turning the algae into products such as fertilizer, biofuels and construction materials.

With reports from La Jornada, Prensa IBERO, Peninsular Caribbean and Reportur.us

World.title: Trump administration strips AMLO’s son of his US visa
World.content:
The U.S. government revoked the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán on Thursday, prompting the son of the former Mexican president to publish an aggressively worded letter to President Donald Trump on social media.

In the letter, López Beltrán (often referred to as “Andy” by Mexican media) went on the offensive, calling the decision “politically motivated and propagandistic, in the Hitlerian style.” He also dismissed the impact of the action, saying he has no problem not visiting the U.S. during times of “hate, racism and drug addiction.”

Andy insisted there is “no reason whatsoever” for the “crude and perverse act of villainy” against him, declaring that he is guided by “the ideals, principles and honesty instilled in me by my parents and practiced out of conviction in my political work.”

The letter also speculated that Trump could be unaware of the decision, saying that if the U.S. president were aware then it is an “arrogant” action and “demonstrates, as my father recently wrote, that you are now an apathetic leader, much different from the person he knew and dealt with.”

Andy’s father, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, served as Mexican president from December 2018 through September 2024, overlapping with Trump’s first term which extended from January 2017 through January 2021.

Andy was particularly harsh with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and undersecretary Christopher Landau, referring to the latter as “El Quitavisas” (“The Visa Taker”).

Landau, the U.S. ambassador to Mexico during Trump’s first term, earned his “Quitavisas” moniker — and proudly embraced it — due to his aggressive policy of reviewing and revoking U.S. visas for foreign citizens who in his judgment mocked U.S. figures, glorified violence or participated in political corruption.

In recent months, Landau has orchestrated a sweep that revoked visas for over 50 Mexican politicians, most of them linked to the ruling Morena party for which Andy had been the secretary of organization until resigning in July to prepare a run for office next year.

Members of the opposition National Action Party were quick to demand that the Federal Attorney General’s Office initiate an investigation into Andy’s potential involvement in fuel theft and influence trafficking, while insisting the Financial Intelligence Unit investigate his finances.

For her part, President Claudia Sheinbaum dismissed the revocation of Andy’s visa as “a politically motivated decision aimed at interfering in Mexico’s internal affairs.”

With reports from El País, Animal Político, La Jornada and The Associated Press

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico and Japan to collaborate on new sargassum-themed restaurant chain
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Embassy of Japan announced a revolutionary diplomatic initiative Monday, confirming plans to address the Caribbean sargassum crisis by launching a nationwide chain of high-end, eco-conscious restaurants centered entirely around the invasive macroalgae.

The venture, which will be called Sargassyum!, aims to rebrand the thousands of tons of brown seaweed washing ashore in Quintana Roo into a luxury dining experience. According to official project briefs, Japan will provide state-of-the-art culinary expertise in marine botany (aka phycogastronomy), while Mexico will supply the virtually limitless, self-replenishing inventory directly from the surf.

“For years, tourists have complained that sargassum ruins the iconic turquoise views of the Riviera Maya,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Fernando Morales during a press conference in the capital. “Through this strategic partnership with our Japanese allies, we are changing the narrative. Guests will no longer look at the shore and see an ecological nuisance; they will see an all-you-can-eat raw bar.”

Initial menu concepts, developed by a joint diplomatic culinary task force, feature dishes such as sargassum tempura, tacos de microalgas Ensenada-Style, and a signature tableside guacamole infused with harvest-fresh sea biomass. Project engineers confirmed that specialized Japanese sensors will monitor ocean currents to deliver live, real-time updates to restaurant kitchen monitors, ensuring the morning’s catch goes from tide line to taco plate in under 20 minutes.

Industry analysts expect the business model to achieve unprecedented profit margins due to negligible supply chain overhead. “Most restaurant chains spend millions securing reliable produce,” noted Mexico City economic analyst Sofia Delgado. “This chain features an automated, climate-driven supply chain that literally dumps tons of raw inventory directly onto the property twice a day.”

Diplomatic sources noted that while the initial rollout will focus on the popular Riviera Maya tourist corridor, future expansions may include a drive-thru model situated directly along beachfront boardwalks. Representatives from both nations expressed confidence that with sufficient lime juice and high-end branding, diners will comfortably overlook the texture and taste.

World.content:

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place SPIM’s Big Saturday — Boogarins and More São Paulo Independent Music hits its peak tonight, with four simultaneous bills across the city. The headline is Boogarins — the acclaimed Goiânia psych-rock band — with Pelados at Casa Natura, plus Sugar Kane and Menores Atos at Hangar 110. Buy a ticket for the house you want and dive into the city’s indie scene.

Tonight at a Glance —SPIM peak · Casa Natura & Hangar 110 Boogarins with Pelados, and Sugar Kane with Menores Atos — the festival’s biggest night. Tickets sold per house. —Criolo · SP2B (Ibirapuera) The rapper headlines Saturday with a free show at 6:30 pm — but the free tickets are gone, so you’ll need an SP2B credential to get in. —Luiz Caldas · Sesc Belenzinho The axé pioneer brings Bahia’s dance rhythms to an affordable Sesc stage. —Jazz & forró Derico plays Blue Note; the forró houses in Pinheiros and Vila Madalena run their busiest night. —Clubs at full swing Saturday is the peak — D-Edge and Clash Club in Barra Funda run till dawn.

Tonight, Saturday 15 August 2026, is São Paulo’s biggest night of the week. The SPIM independent-music festival peaks with four simultaneous bills led by Boogarins; Criolo headlines a free show at Ibirapuera (though the free tickets are long gone); axé legend Luiz Caldas plays Sesc Belenzinho; and the Barra Funda clubs are at full throttle. Pick a lane — indie, rap, axé, jazz, forró or the dancefloor.

Saturday is São Paulo’s biggest night of the week. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

SPIM’s peak Saturday — the São Paulo Independent Music festival runs four simultaneous bills tonight, its biggest of the five days. Boogarins, the acclaimed psych-rock band, plays with Pelados at Casa Natura, while Sugar Kane and Menores Atos take Hangar 110, and the Camarones Orquestra Guitarrística meets Zepelim and Sopro do Cão on the “Noite Doido” bill. Tickets are sold per house, so choose your night and go.

Criolo headlines SP2B — free, but not a walk-in — at the outdoor stage by the Auditório Ibirapuera, 6:30 pm, the rapper Criolo shares the stage with Ajulliacosta as the festival’s Saturday headliner (BaianaSystem closes SP2B on Sunday). The show is free, but the free general tickets were released on 3 August and are now long gone; access now depends on an SP2B credential (the free Empower credential covers Saturday, if any remain, and the paid passes include it). Worth knowing about even if you can’t get in.

Luiz Caldas at Sesc Belenzinho — one of the founders of axé music brings Bahia’s carnival rhythms to a Sesc stage, at accessible prices. A joyful, danceable night for a mixed crowd.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (6:30 pm) — Criolo at Ibirapuera if you hold a credential; otherwise an early drink near your chosen SPIM house.

Dinner (8 pm) — Eat in Vila Madalena or Pinheiros, close to the SPIM stages and the forró houses.

Main event (9–10 pm) — Boogarins at Casa Natura, Sugar Kane at Hangar 110, or Luiz Caldas at Sesc Belenzinho.

Dance (10–11 pm) — Forró at Canto da Ema, or hold out for the clubs.

Late (midnight+) — Barra Funda: D-Edge and Clash Club run till dawn. Rideshare in and out.

Scenes & Sounds

Indie and rock — SPIM’s peak night: Boogarins, Pelados, Sugar Kane, Menores Atos and more across the city. Where: Casa Natura, Hangar 110, Bar Alto, La Iglesia and others.

Rap — Criolo with Ajulliacosta headlines SP2B on Saturday (credential needed). Where: Auditório Ibirapuera (outdoor stage).

Axé and MPB — Luiz Caldas at Sesc Belenzinho, with more across the Sesc units. Where: Sesc Belenzinho.

Jazz — Derico plays Blue Note; JazzB continues its weekend programme. Where: Blue Note (Paulista), JazzB (República).

Forró — The Pinheiros and Vila Madalena houses run their busiest night. Where: Canto da Ema and Coringa (Pinheiros / Vila Madalena).

Electronic and clubs — Saturday is the peak. D-Edge and Clash Club run their electronic nights in Barra Funda, with late doors and headliners around 2 am. Where: D-Edge and Clash Club (Barra Funda).

Pick Your Night

Indie explorer: Boogarins at Casa Natura — the pick of SPIM’s peak Saturday.

Dance to Bahia: Luiz Caldas at Sesc Belenzinho — axé, joyful and affordable.

If you have an SP2B pass: Criolo’s free closing show at Ibirapuera.

Forró: Canto da Ema in Pinheiros — its busiest, most danceable night.

Dance till sunrise: D-Edge or Clash Club in Barra Funda.

Where to Go

Casa Natura Musical — Sumaré A well-equipped mid-size music house, one of the ten SPIM venues, hosting the festival’s headline Saturday bill. Tonight: SPIM — Boogarins with Pelados. Check the door and set times on the SPIM site. Best time: By show; doors usually early evening. Cost: SPIM tickets are sold per night; buy ahead online. Card accepted. Address: Check the SPIM listing for the venue address Website: spimfestival.com Getting there: Rideshare, or metro to the nearest line then a short walk. Good to know: A passport ticket covers all SPIM stages, subject to capacity.

SP2B — Parque Ibirapuera The innovation-and-culture festival’s closing weekend, with its two biggest free shows on the outdoor stage by the Auditório. Tonight: Criolo with Ajulliacosta, 6:30 pm. Free, but the free general tickets (released 3 August) are gone; access needs an SP2B credential (Empower is the free option, if any remain). Best time: Arrive well before 6:30 pm — the closing shows are the most crowded of the festival. Cost: Free show; credential required. The park itself remains free to enter. Address: Parque Ibirapuera, Vila Mariana Website: sp2b.com.br Getting there: Rideshare best; buses from Paulista. 18+ for the festival areas. Good to know: Check the Ticketmaster page for any remaining Empower credentials.

Sesc Belenzinho — Belenzinho A large Sesc cultural centre in the east side, with a strong music programme at accessible prices. Tonight: Luiz Caldas — axé and Bahian rhythms. Check the set time on the Sesc site. Best time: By show; the complex is worth arriving early for. Cost: R$18 (US$3.50) to R$60 (US$11.50), with the lowest rate for Sesc cardholders. Address: Rua Padre Adelino 1000, Belenzinho Website: www.sescsp.org.br Getting there: Metro Belém (red line), short walk. Good to know: Buy ahead on the Sesc site — popular shows sell out.

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York jazz club, polished and central, overlooking Avenida Paulista. Tonight: Derico — the saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist, in a swinging set. Check set times. Best time: Wednesday to Sunday. Arrive 30 minutes early — seating is first-come. Cost: Couvert from R$40 (US$8) to R$80 (US$16) depending on the act. Address: Av. Paulista 2073, 2º andar (Conjunto Nacional), Consolação Website: bluenotesp.com Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), 200 m from the door. Good to know: Show seating is first-come; arrive early.

Canto da Ema — Pinheiros One of São Paulo’s classic forró houses, going since 2000, with live bands and a floor that fills with dancers — busiest on a Saturday. Tonight: Live forró, doors around 10 pm. Check the line-up. Best time: Friday and Saturday for the fullest floor. Dance classes some nights before the show. Cost: Cover typically R$20 (US$4) to R$40 (US$8), plus drinks. Card accepted. Address: Av. Brigadeiro Faria Lima 364, Pinheiros Getting there: Metro Fradique Coutinho (yellow line), short walk. Good to know: No dance experience needed — the crowd is friendly and mixed.

D-Edge — Barra Funda São Paulo’s design-icon electronic club with a Funktion-One sound system — a global top-100 club, at its peak on a Saturday. Tonight: Saturday electronic night. Doors around 11 pm, headliner around 2 am. Check the line-up online. Best time: Friday and Saturday, late. Cost: Entry R$40 (US$8) to R$120 (US$24) depending on the night. Comanda card — don’t lose it. Address: Al. Olga 170, Barra Funda Website: www.d-edge.com.br Getting there: Metro Marechal Deodoro, 15-minute walk. Better to rideshare — the street is industrial and dark. Good to know: Buy tickets online. No flip-flops.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Barra Funda: The big-venue and club district — Hangar 110, D-Edge and Clash Club. Industrial by day, packed on a Saturday night.

Pinheiros / Vila Madalena / Sumaré: Bohemian and bar-heavy, with several SPIM stages and the forró houses. Busy and walkable.

Paulista / Consolação: Blue Note and JazzB, safe and well-lit, central to everything.

Ibirapuera / Vila Mariana: The park hosts SP2B’s closing weekend. Leafy and upscale.

Belenzinho / east side: Sesc Belenzinho anchors the culture; more residential, rideshare in and out.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

The big night — Saturday is the peak for São Paulo’s queer scene, with major parties around Barra Funda, Augusta and Frei Caneca. Check listings for tonight’s line-up.

Everyday-friendly spaces — The Augusta corridor and Frei Caneca are broadly mixed and welcoming, and tonight’s music rooms are all easy, inclusive options.

Money & How Paying Works Festival tickets: SPIM sells per night, with limited all-access passports. Buy ahead online; capacity applies at each house. Comanda card: Clubs like D-Edge give you a card on entry; settle the total at the exit. Losing it means a steep fixed fee — guard it. Cash, card and Pix: Cards and Pix are widely accepted, but carry R$100 (US$20) to R$200 (US$40) in cash for smaller bars and kiosks. Tipping: 10% is standard and often added as ‘serviço’. Check before you double-tip.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: The last trains leave between midnight and 12:30 am, depending on the line. On a Saturday you’ll likely be out later — plan a rideshare home.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and widely used. After midnight, expect surge pricing of 1.5x to 2.5x in busy areas. Wait in a lit spot.

Barra Funda clubs: The security team will often help you into your car. Wait inside until the app says the car is arriving; the streets are industrial and dark.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Ibirapuera crowds: The Criolo show will draw a big crowd — expect heavy rideshare demand around the park at closing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I just show up to the free Criolo show?

No. The show is free, but the free general tickets (released on 3 August) are long gone. Access now needs an SP2B credential — the free Empower credential covers Saturday (if any remain on Ticketmaster), and the paid passes include it. Without one, you can’t enter the show area.

I’ve just landed at GRU tonight. Can I still go out?

Yes — it’s Saturday, the city’s biggest night. The SPIM houses, Sesc Belenzinho and the Barra Funda clubs all run late; most are about a 40-minute rideshare from the airport.

What is SPIM?

São Paulo Independent Music — the city’s first independent-music festival, which peaks tonight (its last full night is tomorrow) across ten venues, with tickets sold per night.

What’s the dress code?

Casual for the shows; jeans are fine. Clubs like D-Edge skew darker and edgier but have no strict door — just avoid beach flip-flops.

Sources: spimfestival.com, Rolling Stone Brasil (Criolo/SP2B), Ao Vivo (agenda), sescsp.org.br

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Mart’nália at Circo Voador Lapa’s most emblematic venue hosts the Saturday night of the Festival Medio y Medio — Mart’nália, Moreno Veloso, the Roda de Samba do Mosquito and DJ Orkidia, from 8 pm. Samba, MPB and a surprise guest under the famous open-sided tent, steps from the Arcos. About R$75 (US$15) half.

Tonight at a Glance —Mart’nália · Circo Voador Festival Medio y Medio, from 8 pm, with Moreno Veloso and more. About R$75 (US$15) half. —Rio Scenarium · Centro/Lapa Three floors of samba, gafieira and choro at Saturday capacity — the fullest night of the week. —Carioca da Gema · Lapa The reliable samba house, open 9 pm to 4 am on a Saturday. —Free in Cinelândia · Festa Tribos A free open-air party at the Passeio Público, from 8 pm (voluntary contribution after 10 pm). —Not tonight: Pedra do Sal’s street roda runs Monday and Friday, not Saturday. It’s back on Monday.

Tonight, Saturday 15 August 2026, Rio is at full volume. Lapa is at its weekly peak — Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema packed, Circo Voador hosting the Saturday night of the Festival Medio y Medio with Mart’nália and Moreno Veloso, and free parties spilling into Cinelândia. There’s no arena show tonight, so the neighbourhood itself is the event: pick a house and dive in.

Saturday is Lapa’s biggest night of the week. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Mart’nália at Circo Voador — Rua dos Arcos, Lapa. The Festival Medio y Medio’s Saturday bill brings samba-MPB singer Mart’nália together with Moreno Veloso, the Roda de Samba do Mosquito, a surprise guest and DJ Orkidia, from 8 pm, under Lapa’s beloved open-sided tent. Tickets around R$75 (US$15) half. A warm, danceable night in the heart of the nightlife district.

Rio Scenarium at Saturday capacity — Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro. The grandest of Lapa’s houses runs its three floors and seven spaces at full weekend strength — samba de raiz, gafieira and choro, from 7 pm into the early hours. Buy online to skip the queue; it’s the busiest night of the week.

Carioca da Gema — Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Lapa. The city’s most consistent samba room runs its Saturday show from 9 pm to 4 am, a five-minute walk from Rio Scenarium and Circo Voador — the three make an easy Lapa circuit.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (7 pm) — Rio Scenarium opens; kiosks along Avenida Mem de Sá sell cold beer under the Arcos.

Concert (8 pm) — Mart’nália and Moreno Veloso at Circo Voador, or the free Festa Tribos in Cinelândia.

Main event (9 pm–late) — Carioca da Gema and Rio Scenarium fill; Lapa is at its loudest. All three venues are within a few blocks.

Jazz alternative — TribOz in Lapa runs two sets; the late one is around 9 pm.

Getting home — Book a car rather than hunting for a late bus. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Scenes & Sounds

Big concerts — Mart’nália and Moreno Veloso headline the Festival Medio y Medio at Circo Voador. Where: Circo Voador (Rua dos Arcos, Lapa).

Samba houses — Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema carry Lapa at full weekend strength; Bip Bip carries Copacabana. Where: Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio 20), Carioca da Gema (Av. Mem de Sá 79), Bip Bip (Copacabana).

Street samba — but not tonight. Pedra do Sal’s free roda runs Mondays and Fridays; on a Saturday the largo is quiet. Where: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde (Mon and Fri).

Jazz — TribOz runs its Saturday sets; Blue Note Rio programmes jazz and MPB in Copacabana. Where: TribOz (Rua Conde de Lages 19, Lapa), Blue Note Rio (Av. Atlântica 1910, Copacabana).

Free and alternative — Festa Tribos throws a free open-air party at the Passeio Público in Cinelândia. Where: Passeio Público (Cinelândia).

Clubs — Lapa’s clubs and the port-district nights are at full weekend swing. Where: Lapa and Gamboa.

Pick Your Night

A proper concert: Mart’nália and Moreno Veloso at Circo Voador — the pick of the night.

The full house: Rio Scenarium — three floors at Saturday capacity.

The safe bet: Carioca da Gema — reliable, intimate live samba, a few blocks away.

Free: Festa Tribos at the Passeio Público in Cinelândia.

Something quieter: Jazz at TribOz, or Bip Bip’s roda in Copacabana.

Where to Go

Circo Voador — Lapa Rio’s beloved open-sided concert tent beside the Arcos da Lapa — a launchpad for Brazilian music since 1982, from Criolo to Gilberto Gil. Tonight: Festival Medio y Medio with Mart’nália, Moreno Veloso, Roda de Samba do Mosquito, a surprise guest and DJ Orkidia, from 8 pm. Best time: Enter between 8 and 9 pm to beat the box-office queue. Cost: Around R$75 (US$15) half; official tickets via Eventim or the box office (Wed–Sat, 2–8 pm). Address: Rua dos Arcos, s/n, Lapa Website: circovoador.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, about a 7-minute walk. Good to know: Buying online usually needs a CPF; the box office takes walk-ups.

Rio Scenarium — Centro/Lapa A magical three-floor 19th-century mansion packed with antiques and seven distinct spaces — one of Rio’s great samba-and-gafieira houses, at its Saturday peak. Tonight: Live samba, gafieira and choro across the floors, from 7 pm into the early hours. Check the site for tonight’s line-up. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday; Saturday is the fullest. Cost: Tickets via the venue’s site; price moves with the line-up (roughly R$40–R$80, US$8–US$16). Card and cash. Address: Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro Website: rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk to Rua do Lavradio. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Buy online to skip the queue on a busy Saturday.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa Lapa’s most awarded samba house, going since 2000. Live samba, chorinho and MPB in an intimate, air-conditioned room. Tonight: Saturday samba from 9 pm. Check the site for tonight’s act. Best time: Saturday 9 pm–4 am; it fills up, so go early or reserve. Cost: Weekend cover is higher than the R$30 (US$6) weeknight rate. Card and cash. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Lapa/Centro Website: barcariocadagema.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door at night. Good to know: A five-minute walk from Rio Scenarium and Circo Voador — an easy circuit.

TribOz — Lapa A tiny, Australian-run jazz room and the city’s dedicated home for the genre. Intimate and serious about the music. Tonight: Two jazz sets (typically around 8 pm and 9 pm on a Saturday). Confirm tonight’s act. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday. Two sets a night. Cost: Couvert roughly R$15 (US$3) to R$30 (US$6). Card and cash. Address: Rua Conde de Lages 19, Lapa Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door. Good to know: Small room — reserve ahead.

Bip Bip — Copacabana A hole-in-the-wall Copacabana legend where the music is sacred. A different genre most nights, players in a circle, crowd on the pavement. Tonight: A nightly roda; check tonight’s genre before heading over. Best time: From about 8–9 pm. Get there early for a plastic chair. Cost: No cover; drinks on an honesty-style tab. Cash. Bring small notes. Address: Rua Almirante Gonçalves 50, Loja D, Copacabana Getting there: Metro Cardeal Arcoverde or Siqueira Campos, then a short walk or ride. Good to know: The house rule is silence while the musicians play — respect it.

Festa Tribos — Passeio Público (Cinelândia) A free open-air party in the historic Passeio Público gardens, with live sound-system acts and DJs — an easy, low-cost start or end to the night. Tonight: Ministério Público SSA, Baixa Santo Sound System and DJs, from 8 pm. Best time: Early — free entry until 10 pm. Cost: Free until 10 pm; a suggested voluntary contribution of R$7.50 (US$1.50) after. Address: Passeio Público, Rua do Passeio, Cinelândia Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk. A few minutes from Lapa. Good to know: An easy pairing with the Lapa houses next door.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: Rio’s nightlife heart under the Arcos, at its Saturday peak — Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Circo Voador and TribOz within a few blocks. Rideshare door-to-door late.

Cinelândia / Centro: The Passeio Público free party sits right between Lapa and the centre. Busy tonight; travel by car late.

Copacabana: Home to Bip Bip and Blue Note Rio, and an easy beachfront base. Walkable and lively.

Botafogo: Buzzy bar and cinema scene that ticks over any night. A relaxed alternative to Lapa.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. Charming and low-key; rideshare up and down.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

The big night — Saturday is the peak for Rio’s queer scene, with major parties in Copacabana, the port district and Lapa. Check listings for tonight’s line-up.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Lapa’s samba houses and the Cinelândia party are broadly mixed and welcoming, and all of tonight’s rooms are easy, inclusive options.

Money & How Paying Works Couvert and cover: Lapa houses charge a per-person music cover, higher on a Saturday. It’s on your bill, separate from food and drinks. Concert tickets: Buy through official channels; Circo Voador’s app usually needs a CPF, but the box office takes walk-ups. Cash for the small places: Bip Bip and street parties are cash-based. Carry about R$150 (US$30) in small notes. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. Check before adding more.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: MetrôRio runs roughly 5 am to midnight Monday to Saturday. On a Saturday you’ll likely be out later — plan a rideshare home.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and the safest way home from Lapa and Cinelândia late at night. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Lapa at night: Busy and fun around the Arcos on a Saturday, but keep your phone and wallet secure and stick to the main, well-lit streets.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Copacabana: Well-lit and busy near the beachfront, but keep the usual awareness on quieter side streets after dark.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Pedra do Sal on tonight?

No — the free street roda runs on Mondays and Fridays, not Saturdays. Tonight, head to Lapa (Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Circo Voador) or Copacabana (Bip Bip). Pedra do Sal is back on Monday.

Rio Scenarium or Circo Voador?

Circo Voador is a ticketed concert (Mart’nália and Moreno Veloso tonight) in a big open-sided tent. Rio Scenarium is a three-floor samba house you can wander, with several rooms and styles. They’re a few minutes apart, so you could do the concert then move to the house.

I’ve just landed at GIG (Galeão) tonight. Where should I go?

Straight to Lapa — Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema run into the early hours and are about a 30–40 minute rideshare from Galeão. Bip Bip in Copacabana is a late, no-cover alternative. Carry some cash.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not at all. The music does the work and the crowds are welcoming. A smile, a cold beer, and cash for the cover or the drinks are all you need.

Sources: circovoador.com.br, rioscenarium.com.br, barcariocadagema.com.br, visitrio.com.br (Pedra do Sal)

World.title: Chile Day 2026: Quiroz Takes His Market Reform to Madrid and London
World.content:
Chile · Economy

Key Facts What: Chile Day, Chile’s annual investor roadshow, heads to Europe.

Chile Day, Chile’s annual investor roadshow, heads to Europe. When: Madrid on September 14, London on September 16, 2026.

Madrid on September 14, London on September 16, 2026. Who: Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz, an economist with a Duke doctorate.

Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz, an economist with a Duke doctorate. The pitch: Chile’s new capital-market reform, making its international debut.

Chile’s new capital-market reform, making its international debut. The tension: Spanish builders are rattled after Chile suspended road concessions in the Biobío region.

Spanish builders are rattled after Chile suspended road concessions in the Biobío region. The stakes: A 2026–2027 concessions pipeline worth about US$8 billion.

A 2026–2027 concessions pipeline worth about US$8 billion. Sacyr’s footprint: The Spanish group has invested more than US$6.5 billion in Chile since 1996.

For a government wrestling with a tight budget and nervous foreign builders, Chile Day is less a victory lap than an audition.

Chile is taking its biggest financial overhaul in years on the road. The first stop is Madrid.

Chile will pitch its capital-market reform to investors in Madrid and London. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
