World.title: US threatens EU over its green reporting rules
World.content:
The dispute centers on two pillars of the EU’s corporate sustainability rulebook: the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, which requires large companies to address human rights and environmental harms linked to their operations and supply chains, and the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, which requires companies to disclose sustainability-related information.

Brussels has scaled back both laws in its drive to cut red tape, but has stopped short of Washington’s demand to shield U.S. companies from their reach.

Last week, Puzder similarly attacked the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism as a tariff on U.S. exporters. On Thursday, the White House also accused the EU and more than 40 countries of enabling Chinese goods to skirt U.S. tariffs by rerouting them through their markets.

A European Commission spokesperson told POLITICO that Brussels had made “considerable efforts” to explain its rules and highlight "its willingness to cooperate with the US to increase trade where possible," but drew a line at changing its regulatory regime in response to U.S. pressure.

“We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation,” said the spokesperson.

This story has been updated.

Koen Verhelst contributed reporting.

World.title: Le Conseil constitutionnel censure la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs
World.content:
“L’interdiction instituée par la loi est susceptible de s’appliquer à des services de communication en ligne dont les risques pour la santé et la sécurité des mineurs ne sont pas établis”, estime encore le Conseil constitutionnel, insistant sur l’imprécision autour du champ d’application de l’article.

Le risque avait été soulevé au moment de l’examen du texte au Sénat, certains élus de la Chambre haute ayant tenté d’imposer l’établissement d’une “liste noire” qui définirait plus précisément les plateformes concernées par cette limitation d’accès aux mois de 15 ans – et éviterait ainsi le risque de censure par le Conseil constitutionnel.

Un élément du texte retiré au moment de son examen en Commission mixte paritaire pour assurer sa conformité avec le droit européen.

Le Conseil constitutionnel estime par ailleurs que le texte ne définit pas les garanties légales propres à assurer le droit au respect de la vie privée des utilisateurs qui seront contraints de faire vérifier leur âge par les plateformes pour prouver leur majorité.

“Le gouvernement n’a pas assez écouté le Sénat et le risque d’inconstitutionnalité que nous pointions depuis des mois. Désormais, le risque, c’est que le texte soit vidé de sa substance”, a réagi, sur ce point, la rapporteure du texte au Sénat, Catherine Morin-Desailly, auprès de POLITICO.

Un constat partagé par le député socialiste Arthur Delaporte, à l’origine de l’une des saisines du Conseil constitutionnel. L'autre émanait du groupe de la France Insoumise (LFI).

World.title: French court blocks social media ban for under 15s
World.content:
The French president has also pushed restrictions to the top of the EU agenda, with an expected announcement of bloc-wide measures by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September.

In a statement late Friday, the French presidential office said the government would not be giving up on the bill. It has set a new target date for spring 2027, which coincides with when Macron will leave office.

The statement said Macron “has instructed the Prime Minister to work, as quickly as possible, on a legally sound draft that takes into account” the court's decision. The ruling hinted at what would make the age restriction align with fundamental rights: giving parents more flexibility.

Peter Craddock, a senior Brussels-based attorney advising social media firms, said the French court decision could have far-reaching implications.

"What they're basically saying here is: 'Listen, government, if you want to get this to succeed, you can't just work on the basis of a general ban. There have to be limitations," said Craddock, a partner at Keller & Heckman. "There have to be ways for people to say, 'well, actually, in my case, my son, my daughter is of a certain degree of maturity and is able to use this properly.'"

The government bill had passed through the French legislative procedure after a lengthy back-and-forth earlier this summer. It was set to bring forward Europe's first social media age restrictions, with Greece and Denmark planning to follow suit.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's military warned that similar incidents may happen again in the future. "While the Russian aggression in Ukraine is ongoing, the recurrence of such cases when a foreign unmanned aircraft enters or approaches Latvian airspace is possible," it said.

An air raid alert was declared in four eastern Latvian municipalities at around 4 a.m. local time. The military urged people to stay indoors and away from exterior walls.

After the drone was downed, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugāji village administration, told the Latvian Information Agency that the incident “caused no casualties,” as the drone wreckage fell in a “wooded area.”

There has been an uptick in similar incidents over recent months in countries close to the war-zone. A week ago, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Ukrainian-made drone crossed Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam.

World.title: Spain and Morocco reinforce border amid fears of fresh Ceuta migrant surge
World.content:
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers.

“We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.”

The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies.

Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

World.title: Lebanon president says Israeli strikes that killed 11 send 'clear message' on negotiations
World.content:
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Saturday that deadly new Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon sent a "clear message" on peace negotiations between the two nations, according to a statement from his office.

 

Lebanese state media had earlier reported that at least 11 people, including three children and two women, had been killed following Israeli strikes on Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani, in one of the deadliest attacks on the nation since a US-led framework agreement aiming to ease hostilities was reached in June.

"President Aoun considered that these violations send a clear message regarding the negotiation process and the US efforts aimed at implementing this agreement," the statement from the president's office reads, adding that "an entire family from the town of Ansar" had been killed in the attacks.

The Israeli military has said the strikes were carried out in response to an attack by the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah on IDF troops "in the Ali al-Taher Ridge, which is located in the security zone."

Lebanon became caught up in the war between Israel, the US, and Iran, which began in late February, after Hezbollah launched rocket attacks on Israel over the killing of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

Israel launched a series of strikes and a ground invasion of southern Lebanon in response, establishing a "security zone" in the region as its forces worked to destroy what it says is "terror infrastructure".

A man checks a destroyed home that was hit by an Israeli airstrike in Ansar village, southern Lebanon, Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

In a statement later on Saturday, Hezbollah warned that the latest Israeli attacks would "be met with an appropriate response."

"The Israeli enemy must clearly understand that its acts of aggression, violations, and attempts to impose a fait accompli cannot continue," the group said, while also calling on Lebanese authorities to "cease chasing after US-led negotiations."

Under the terms of the June framework deal agreed by Israel and Lebanon, Israeli forces were to gradually withdraw from Lebanon "pending the verified disarmament of non-state armed groups and dismantlement of associated infrastructure."

World.title: Wildfires continue to devastate Europe as thousands are forced to flee their homes
World.content:
Europe is continuing to battle a series of devastating wildfires as the continent faces more sweltering conditions and worsening droughts, with thousands forced to flee their homes.

 

In France, authorities said a further 100 residents and holidaymakers evacuated from around the town of Luglon in the southwestern Landes department on Saturday as a fire that broke out on Thursday continued to burn.

In an update on Saturday morning, the Landes Prefecture said the blaze had burned through around 1,580 hectares so far and that it was "particularly active" to the southeast of Luglon, close to the village of Garein.

"In total, 550 firefighters are currently mobilized to fight the spread of the fire. Air resources will resume their rotation," it added.

Fire trucks are engulfed in smoke from a forest fire near the hamlet of Großhau in the municipality of Hürtgenwald, Germany, at a staging area. on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. (Georg Hilgemann/dpa via AP)

In Germany's Eifel region, a major fire has led to the evacuation of at least 1,800 people from Hurtgenwald, where some 1,400 firefighters have been battling flames.

The blaze is believed to be the largest forest fire in the history of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Meanwhile, German firefighting reinforcements have been called in to assist their Belgian counterparts, who are fighting another fire in the Fagnes natural park, close to the border between the two nations.

The blaze began on Friday and has burned through at least 16 square kilometres of forest, authorities said.

Around 1,000 people have also been evacuated in Spain's northeastern Aragon region, where a fire that has ravaged more than 15,000 hectares continues to burn. However, firefighters say they have stopped its spread towards population centres, and weather forecasts in the area suggest temperatures could soon drop, with some light rain also possible.

Greece is also on high alert as severe winds across parts of the nation have raised the risk of fires breaking out.

More than 50 agricultural and forest fires have already erupted in the last 24 hours, although most have been contained, according to the fire service.

The light flows through a charred forest near Ares, during wildfires in southwestern France, Thursday, July 30, 2026. AP Photo /Baz Ratner

Eastern Europe

In Croatia, emergency services are fighting a wildfire on the island of Dugi Otok, where more than 100 firefighters and two water bombing planes are in action.

240 firefighters and three planes were able to bring another fire on the Peljesac peninsula under control on Friday.

Serbian authorities said on Friday evening that they were fighting with 25 forest fires, one of which they said had devastated 25 square kilometres of land in the Deliblatska national park near Belgrade.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Saturday afternoon that Europe was on "high wildfire alert" and that there was increasing pressure on Eastern European nations.

She added that the EU's Copernicus Earth observation satellites were "already supporting mapping operations" in Spain, Albania, Greece, France, Germany, and Serbia, and that the bloc's Civil Protection Mechanism was "there when a country calls."

World.title: Madrid hospital creates first bone metamaterial prosthesis, prevents leg amputation
World.content:
Madrid's Gregorio Marañón Hospital has managed to avoid the amputation of a leg thanks to a pioneering bone implant custom-made for a 38-year-old patient with a sarcoma in his tibia. It is the first personalised metamaterial prosthesis of its kind, a technology originally developed for the aerospace sector that reproduces the mechanical properties of bone through a titanium structure manufactured using 3D printing.

 

Developed together with engineers from the Polytechnic University of Madrid (UPM), the prosthesis is made up of a network of millimetre-scale titanium structures designed to distribute loads in a similar way to bone tissue. The implant has made it possible to preserve both the patient's leg and knee joint and avoid amputation.

A prosthesis that mimics bone

Unlike conventional prostheses, this implant does not replace the bone with a solid piece, but instead recreates its structure and strength through a network of fine titanium rods that distribute loads in a way similar to bone tissue.

Its design helps the patient's bone to grow and integrate the prosthesis, reducing the risk of rejection and complications. In addition, because it is 3D-printed and adapted to each patient, operating time is almost halved.

The implant weighs barely 300 grams, but simulations indicate that it can withstand more than 500 kilos, compared with conventional prostheses, which weigh several kilos and can bear only 100-150 kilos.

An implant designed for each patient

Pierre Chazel, aged 38, had a high-grade bone sarcoma in his tibia. After an infection and severe loss of bone density, his leg could no longer support a conventional prosthesis, so the medical team opted to design an implant tailored to his anatomy.

Using his radiological images, the researchers created a digital twin of his healthy leg and simulated the loads the tibia has to bear when walking, climbing stairs or stumbling. Based on these data, they designed the prosthesis's internal structure and placed the screws in the areas with the best bone quality, which allowed them to plan the procedure with millimetre precision.

A year after the operation, the patient is already able to walk. After almost two years without putting weight on the leg, he says that he has finally begun to regain his mobility. Gregorio Marañón Hospital has already carried out a second similar procedure and is preparing two further personalised implants, one for a wrist and another for a sternum. The aim is to roll out this technology in order to offer hyper-personalised medicine within the public health system.

World.title: Ukraine says it has struck Russian rocket and space centre
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday that Ukrainian forces had struck the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in Russia's Samara region, a facility involved in the manufacturing and operation of space launch vehicles.

 

In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine hit the centre with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, describing it as one of Russian space agency Roscosmos' "key enterprises" and saying it was involved in "electronics production".

Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region - which the Ukrainian leader said housed aircraft used for missile attacks on Ukraine - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, close to the border with Estonia, per Zelenskyy.

He shared video footage on X appearing to show the aftermath of some of the strikes. Large columns of black smoke and flames can be seen at sites in the distance.

"Our plan of long-range sanctions against Russia for this war is being implemented, and it is important that Russia’s war potential be reduced," Zelenskyy wrote.

The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has since shared more details on the operation as well as its intelligence on the targets, confirming hits were recorded at both the Progress centre and the air base and that a fire had broken out on the facilities' grounds.

It added that the launch vehicles produced at the Progress centre were used to "place Russian military, reconnaissance, and communications spacecraft into orbit."

The Savasleyka air base, the General Staff added, is used to operate MiG-31K fighter jets, which it said were used to carry Kh-47M2 Kinzhal ballistic missiles.

Ukraine's 'long-range sanctions' and Russian strikes

Ukraine has repeatedly hit targets deep inside Russia in an effort to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin and the country's military capabilities and to squeeze the Russian economy.

Kyiv has in particular sought to home in on energy facilities across Russia as part of this strategy, striking oil refineries, terminals, and depots across the country. The attacks have led to fuel shortages across parts of Russia and Russian-occupied territories.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press conference with his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vucic at the Serbia Palace, in Belgrade, Serbia. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The Ukrainian air force said on Saturday that Russian forces had launched 152 drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine overnight.

"According to preliminary data, as of 9 am, air defences had shot down or neutralised 124 enemy UAVs," it said, adding that strikes had been recorded in 16 locations.

Russian attacks on the Kherson region in southern Ukraine over the past day injured 28 people, including a child, according to Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration.

A child was also killed and 11 people were injured in a series of strikes on the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, per regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha, while four were injured in Sumy Oblast in the country's north.

A further nine people were injured across the regions of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv, per local authorities.

World.title: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Indonesia, killing at least 40
World.content:
A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake hit the Southeast Asian nation of Indonesia on Saturday, killing at least 40 people.

 

The quake struck to the north of Flores Island in the eastern part of the country in the early hours of the morning, sparking panic as people fled into the streets amid crumbling buildings.

A tsunami warning was issued but was later lifted, with Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) saying it was no longer detecting significant sea level rises that could threaten coastal communities.

Fathur Rahman, a rescue official, said the death toll had risen to 40 on Saturday evening, with 50 people also injured.

According to the National Agency for Disaster Countermeasure (BNPB), 2,000 people in the Nagekeo Regency self-evacuated after the quake.

Nelly Florida Riama, a deputy director for geophysics at BMKG, earlier warned that while the tsunami warning was over, aftershocks were "still occurring."

"We urge the public to remain calm, not to be swayed by irresponsible rumours, and to keep up to date with information from the BMKG’s official channels,” Nelly added.

The BNPB said tremors were reported to have been felt across the regencies of Nagekeo, Sikka, and West Manggarai in the province of East Nusa Tenggara; Bima City and Bima Regency in West Nusa Tenggara; and in the Jeneponto, Selayar Islands, and Maros Regencies in South Sulawesi.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has expressed her condolences to families affected by the quake and said the EU was ready to deploy its Copernicus Earth observation satellites to assist.

"From solidarity to action, Europe stands ready to deploy Copernicus, our eyes in the sky, to support search and rescue efforts," she wrote in a post on X.

A second 6.9-magnitude earthquake later hit Pematangsiantar on the western island of Sumatra, at a depth of around 183 km. The first quake hit at a depth of around 10 km.

Earthquakes that occur at greater depth tend to cause less destruction than those closer to the surface, as the strength of shaking reduces with increasing distance from its source.

Authorities are assessing the impact of the second quake.

World.title: Judo World Tour: A day of firsts at the Lima Grand Prix
World.content:
Welcome to Lima for the opening day of the Judo Grand Prix!

 

In -48kg, Assunta SCUTTO faced Maria Celia LABORDE. The reigning World Champion managed a clever turnover and held LABORDE down for victory, earning her very first Grand Prix gold medal.

IOC Member Dr Paula PARETO awarded the medals.

I am very emotional because this is my first competition after surgery and my first competition of qualification. I’m so happy. Today’s been a very difficult day for me, a lot of emotion but I’m happy for the gold medal. I wished for this, I got it. Assunta SCUTTO (ITA)

In the -60kg, Michel AUGUSTO faced Jonathan YANG. AUGUSTO took the lead with an ashi-waza for yuko and managed to defend the score to take home his first Grand Prix gold medal.

International Judo Federation Education & Coaching Director Mr Mohammed MERIDJA awarded the medals.

This was my first gold medal in a Grand Prix, I'm very very happy. Thank you. Michel AUGUSTO (BRA)

At -52kg, Rafaela RODRIGUES faced Francine ECHEVARRIA. RODRIGUES came back from a yuko down and held ECHEVARRIA for victory. A debut Grand Prix gold for the Brazilian.

Peruvian Judo Federation President Mrs Maria MARTINEZ MURCIEGO awarded the medals.

At -66kg, Radu IZVOREANU faced teammate Denis VIERU. An absolutely huge ippon from IZVOREANU left no doubt that he would stand on the top spot of the podium. A spectacular finish. Gold and silver for Moldova.

Peruvian Olympic Committee President Mr Renzo MANYARI awarded the medals.

At -57kg, Pihla SALONEN faced Adriana RODRIGUEZ SALVADOR. SALONEN took the gold medal with a brilliant ippon, finishing the contest in style after an impressive performance all day to secure Grand Prix glory in Lima.

International Judo Federation Referee Director Mr Raul CAMACHO PEREZ awarded the medals.

Thank you for joining us here in beautiful Lima! We’ll see you tomorrow.

World.title: In Turkey, one of the world's longest conflicts reaches a turning point
World.content:
Turkey stands on the threshold of closing a conflict spanning almost 50 years, after the Turkish parliament this week passed a law allowing exiled Kurdish militants to return home and rejoin society. The legislation aims to end the war with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has battled the Turkish state for independence since 1984.

Advertising

On Monday, legislators voted 468-88 in favour of a law detailing how the PKK will lay down arms, disband and guide most members back into civilian life.

Many see this legislation as a turning point after decades of bloodshed.

“This law in question is going to make a giant contribution,” predicts sociologist Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

“If the PKK militants are convinced that they can be safe in Turkey, it's estimated that some 15,000 people in Europe, in Syria, in Iraq and in the prisons in Turkey are going to be either released or are going to be able to come back home.”

The PKK leadership, based primarily in Iraq, is not covered by the legislation. Nor is the group's founder and leader Abdullah Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999 in a Turkish jail.

He initiated the peace process and last year called for the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK.

People hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Hope, caution

Istanbul, now the city's with the world’s largest Kurdish population, became a sanctuary in the 1990s as hundreds of thousands fled the violence raging in Turkey's southeast. At the conflict’s peak, the Turkish army destroyed villages in relentless scorched-earth campaigns.

In Istanbul's Bagcilar district, home to a vibrant Kurdish community, conversations reveal a fragile mix of hope and caution.

“This law seems good for the honour of the Kurds and to stop bloodshed,” said 31-year-old Ahmet, who only wanted to be identified by his first name. “Mothers should not shed tears anymore.”

But others were more wary. “The state has been delaying our rights for decades; I do not believe this process will be different,” said Kava, who also preferred not to give his full name. “I do not trust an arrangement in which Kurds do not have legal status.”

Kurds make up around a fifth of Turkey’s population, but are not legally recognised as a minority.

Emotions appear equally divided among Turks. “If they’re agreeing to live under the Turkish flag and love our country, that’s fine – let them,” said 51-year-old Mehmet Tas.

But 40-year-old Ertugral Zengin is unconvinced. “They committed a crime – and now they are to be pardoned? Do I want something like that? No, I won’t accept it.”

PKK ends 40-year fight but doubts remain about the next steps

Political momentum

The decades-long conflict has claimed 40,000 lives and forced more than 3 million people from their homes.

While major political parties support the peace process, hardline nationalist groups remain staunchly opposed, insisting it rewards a PKK they see as already defeated.

The process hinges on the laborious task of disarming the PKK and verifying its weapons are gone.

Maintaining the current political momentum is vital, warns Asli Aydintasbas, a Turkey expert at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC.

“If this drags on, political support for the legislation and for the return of former PKK members, seen by many Turks as terrorists, would become politically problematic for the government. Timing and moving fast is very important to achieve reconciliation,” she says.

The government is expected to face growing pressure to address Kurdish rights, including Kurdish-language education in schools and local autonomy, along with broader democratic reforms.

Social media buzzes with questions: how can PKK members walk free while critics of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan remain behind bars?

Kurdish demonstrators in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Peace or politics? Turkey’s fragile path to ending a decades-long conflict

Yegen warns that since the new legislation fails to address Kurdish rights and democratisation reforms, the government needs to move swiftly.

“The fact that these two issues are not touched upon by the law has created many doubts on both Kurdish and Turkish sides about whether disarmament will be the government's only agenda,” he says.

For Erdogan, steering the peace process to success could secure the vital Kurdish vote in the 2028 elections. Yet extending Kurdish cultural rights risks alienating Turkish nationalists, and relaxing pressure on the opposition brings its own perils as their electoral strength grows.

For now, the negotiations present a rare window for reconciliation and lasting peace.

World.title: Lebanon says 11 killed in Israeli airstrikes
World.content:
Lebanon's prime minister denounced the attacks on villages in southern Lebanon for targeting civilians in their homes. Israel said it was firing on Hezbollah infrastructure.

At least 11 people were killed when Israel launched fresh airstrikes in southern Lebanon on Saturday, the deadliest since the Israel-Hezbollah truce nearly two months ago.

The attacks were met with defiance by the Iran-backed Hezbollah, which demanded an end to "humiliating" peace negotiations with Israel.

What do we know?

The Lebanese Health Ministry said one of the strikes, on the edge of the village of Ansar, killed seven people and wounded two.

The dead included three children and two women, according to the ministry.

The strike, which happened at dawn, hit a house and destroyed it, according to NNA, the Lebanese state news agency.

Germany's DPA news agency cited residents as saying the property served as a base for Hezbollah.

The Israeli strike on Ansar, in southern Lebanon, hit a house Image: Marwan Naamani/ZUMA/IMAGO

The second strike hit the village of Deir al-Zahrani, killing four and wounding 17.

NNA reported other strikes around the strategic Ali Taher hill, which overlooks parts of the southern city of Nabatiyeh and key roads to it.

The Israeli military confirmed hitting Hezbollah infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it was retaliation for an attack by the militia on Israeli forces.

Hezbollah vows revenge

Later Saturday, Hezbollah hit back at the latest strikes, saying they would be met with an "appropriate" response.

Israel "must clearly understand that its attacks, violations and attempts to impose a fait accompli cannot continue, and will be met with an appropriate response", the Iran-backed group said in a statement.

Hezbollah warned Lebanese authorities against continuing its "humiliating" negotiations with Israel, which would provide "the enemy with free concessions."

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam denounced the strikes, calling on Israel to "halt this escalation."

"The seven martyrs of the Israeli airstrike on the town of Ansar are not military infrastructure and the children and women killed were not military targets,” he wrote on X.

Hezbollah accused Israel of reigniting the war Image: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ceasefire struggles to stick

The Israel–Hezbollah war reignited in early March around the start of the Iran war, when Hezbollah launched attacks on northern Israel to avenge the killing of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

It rapidly became a full-scale conflict that involved Israeli ground operations in southern Lebanon, mass evacuations of residents and the deaths of over 4,300 people.

Israel claims to have established the so-called security zone in southern Lebanon to prevent Hezbollah attacks on northern Israel.

According to Lebanese media, the Israeli-controlled area covers approximately 620 square kilometres, or about 6% of the country's total area.

Israel and Hezbollah have repeatedly accused each other of ceasefire violations following the announcement of a framework peace agreement in late June,

The deal lays out a plan for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon, in return for Hezbollah laying down arms. It also envisions steps toward eventual peace.

The two sides have held seven rounds of talks; the most recent in Rome earlier this month.

Hezbollah refused direct talks, wasn't party to the deal and has refused to disarm.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: In Germany, record heat meets climate action fatigue
World.content:
Climate action does not seem to be a priority for the German government — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why aren't more people taking to the streets in protest?

When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" climate activist group glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (the 2026 toll, so far), or record temperatures across Western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.

"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner told DW.

"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."

Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This summer, entire villages have been evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are expected to lose about 3 million metric tons of grain and rapeseed to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes are facing an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning.

But so far, the federal government has remained astonishingly quiet. Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," said Werner.

Fridays for Future finds it difficult to motivate people

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

In November 2022, activist Lars Werner glued himself to the street in Munich to protest CO2 emissions Image: Benjamin Rückert

Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they're take to the streets.

Kastrup isn't surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she said.

In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.

"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," said Kastrup.

Focus has shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a political science researcher at the University of Bremen, said it's surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he said. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party — Editor's note] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss pointed out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, he believes a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," said Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics.

"In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront."

A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities.

However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical of the plan and has cited "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, told DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."

For instance, Scheer said, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.

Climate activists try bold new strategies to make an impact To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" said Scheer.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act , Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians have raised doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.

"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recently, a statement that Scheer considered disastrous.

"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Hawaii under state of emergency ahead of historic hurricane
World.content:
A hurricane is forecast to hit the Big Island of Hawaii this weekend, bringing heavy rain and wind. Should it make landfall, Lala would be the first hurricane to hit the island since 1871.

Residents on the Big Island of Hawaii, which gives its name to the volcanic US Pacific archipelago, are preparing for a potentially historic weather situation with a tropical storm gathering hurricane-level strength as it approaches.

The US Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) National Hurricane Center (NHC) on Friday said Lala, a powerful tropical storm at the moment, should be at hurricane strength by the time it approaches the Big Island on Saturday.

Hawaii Governor Josh Green, who called the storm "enormous," declared a state of emergency on Friday in an effort to make sure the state and its counties "have sufficient resources to clear debris, secure infrastructure and take other measures to prepare."

Currently, a hurricane warning is in effect for Hawaii County, which covers the Big Island. The islands of Maui, Molokai and Kahoolawe to its northwest are under a tropical storm warning.

Should the storm make landfall as expected, it would be the first time the Big Island has been hit by a hurricane since 1871.

The storm is expected to bring winds, rainfall and heavy surf, spurring government and residents to prepare for the worst.

Shelters have already been set up and residents encouraged to remain vigilant and get themselves and their families to safe spaces before they become trapped.

What if Lala doesn't make landfall?

Experts say a direct hit is not necessarily the concern here, with meteorologist Vanessa Almanza of the National Weather Service (NWS) in Honolulu cited by the Associated Press as saying: "It doesn't take landfall to create destruction. A lot of the impacts are felt outside of the hurricane."

The National Hurricane Center predicts 8 to 12 inches (20.3 to 30.5 centimeters) of rain across Maui and the Big Island this weekend, with maximum totals as high as 25 inches (63.5 centimeters) in some Big Island locations.

The NHC also warned that the storm could bring "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," as well as dangerous storm surges and ocean swells, "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."

Residents have been told to prepare for high winds and heavy rain when Lala arrives Image: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/AP Photo/picture alliance

Conditions trigger fear of floods and fires

As of Friday afternoon, Lala was located about 275 miles (440 kilometers) east-southeast of South Point, Hawaii, according to the NHC.

Data showed the storm had maximum sustained winds of 65 miles per hour (100 kilometers per hour) and was moving toward the west-northwest at 14 miles per hour. The wind-speed threshold for a Category 1 hurricane is 74 miles per hour.

Beyond fear of flooding, which the island of Oahu experienced in March, dry and windy weather has increased fear of wildfires as the storm picks up pace.

In 2023, the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds caused by a hurricane passing by far to the south.

Maui housing crisis lingers months after Hawaii wildfires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pointing to 1992's Hurricane Iniki as a tale of warning

The last hurricane to make landfall on the archipelago was Iniki, a category 4 storm, in 1992 — also an El Nino year.

On Friday, Governor Green reminded residents that Iniki made landfall after changing its path, "so we just can never know if a storm is going to turn."

While urging vigilance, Green said: "It did $3 billion (€2.6 billion) in damage. It destroyed thousands of homes and it did kill six people."

Green implored residents: "If you feel now that your house doesn't have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first you go to a family or friend's house and you kind of hunker down there."

The southern end of Hawaii is remote and rural but its affordability has attracted a growing population, some of whom live off-grid in unpermitted structures.

'Prepare, don't wait' say authorities

On neighboring Oahu, Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi said Friday: "I am asking everyone to finish your preparations today. Don't wait for the weather to deteriorate. Stay informed, stay away from dangerous areas and make sure your family knows what to do if conditions worsen."

Residents were encouraged to clean gutters and drains, clear any hanging branches or debris from yards and seal their doors, with emergency services adding, "Stay away from beaches and coastal areas where rough surf and rip currents could sweep you away."

This year's Pacific Ocean El Nino has already attained temperatures so high that when it peaks between October and December NOAA says there is a 69% chance of a "historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Nino events dating back to 1950."

The natural climate pattern occurs when ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific become unusually warm. This tends to fuel hurricane activity in the Pacific while retarding it in the Atlantic.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Russians snap up new homes built on Ukraine 'graveyard'
World.content:
Russia is constructing high-rises in the occupied Ukrainian city of Mariupol, on the sites of buildings it destroyed. Who's buying these properties? And what happened to the Ukrainians who used to lived here?

Halyna Artemova, an English teacher, lived in Mariupol for almost 40 years, at Metallurgy Avenue 87.

"It's my beloved city. When I look at the photos, it brings tears to my eyes. I know every crack in the asphalt, every tree," she told DW. Her apartment block in the city on the Sea of Azov was struck by a missile during a Russian attack in March 2022.

Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky and his wife lived in the house next door, Metallurgy Avenue 85, for 20 years. "I did everything myself, all the interior renovations, and the furniture," he said. "We invested a lot in it; we planned to spend our twilight years there, living quietly." His building also caught fire during the missile attack, and residents were driven out by Russian troops. They weren't even allowed to take food or clothing with them.

Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky documented his apartment before and after the Russian attack Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky

Now there's a parking lot where Sosnovsky's apartment block used to be. Next door, where Artemova once lived, stands a new building. The Russian building contractor Su-2007, which operates in the Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, cleared several buildings on Metallurgy Avenue that were destroyed in the war and constructed high-rise apartment blocks in their place. These form part of a residential complex now known as the Leningradsky Kvartal.

"They're building on human bones, and fast, to eradicate the traces of their crimes," said Sosnovsky.

DW is not allowed in to the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, so cannot report directly from city. However, it is possible to get an idea of what life is like in Mariupol today by talking to people who used to live there, studying satellite images, and doing research online.

Newcomers benefit from cheap mortgages

Many people who have moved into the new apartments on Metallurgy Avenue communicate with each other online in neighborhood forums. From these forums, it's clear that the majority bought the apartments either to live in themselves, or to rent out.

In chats, they ask how they can get furniture delivered from Russia, or which kindergarten or school they should choose for their children. People are reminded that the most important thing when submitting documents is that they should be of Russian origin.

Russian building contractor Su-2007 has advertised its new project in Mariupol online Image: жк-ленинградский-квартал.рф

Not everyone has finished remodeling their apartments, and some people with small children take the opportunity to complain: "It's too late! Stop the goddamn renovations! Or maybe you're pro-Ukrainian and oppose Russian laws?"

Economist Vyacheslav Shiryaev said apartments in the new buildings in Mariupol are being bought primarily by incomers: Russian security personnel, officials and people working in military logistics. "In addition, there are some who would just like to live by the sea but can't afford Crimea or Sochi," he said.

In the Russian-occupied regions, people are offered cheap mortgages at an annual interest rate of 2% for the whole period of the mortgage — provided the borrower has Russian citizenship. The maximum they can borrow is 6 million rubles (around €63,000/$72,000), and they must be able to put down a deposit of at least 2%.

Property prices have soared

Dozens of apartment blocks are being built in Mariupol, and many are already occupied. Russian banks report that the port city in the occupied region tops the list for mortgage loans. Property prices have risen by a third in just one year, primarily because of the coastal location.

You won't find a location like this in Russia, said Shiryaev. However, he pointed out that the apartments are of very bad quality. "Construction companies are cutting corners wherever they can, but still demanding exorbitant prices," he said.

The Leningradsky Kvartal residential complex, 15 buildings of 12 to 15 floors each, is near the center of town and just 10 minutes' drive from the sea. One- and two-room apartments cost between 7.5 million and almost 10 million rubles (€104,000). Three-room apartments can be bought for upwards of 10 million rubles. Newcomers to the region are offered discounts of up to 12%.

In the chats, people living in the complex say they have insured their mortgages "against war risks." If their building is destroyed, they won't have to pay back their loan. They will, however, lose their apartment.

Nobody in the forum talks about the fact that there were other people living on the site of Leningradsky Kvartal just a few years ago.

Dead and wounded in Mariupol

According to the United Nations, 90% of the buildings in Mariupol were damaged or destroyed in the 2022 siege. Media outlets estimate that tens of thousands of people were killed. Former residents of Metallurgy Avenue told DW of neighbors who were killed or injured.

Halyna Artemova lived in Mariupol for most of her life, before fleeing to Kyiv Image: Privat

"A man and his son from the building next door were killed when they went out to fetch water," said Artemova. "In house number 89, a woman was buried beneath a concrete slab after a missile strike and died. A missile struck the first floor of house number 91, and a family was killed."

Artemova herself was wounded by shrapnel, but managed to leave Mariupol with her elderly mother and her son. Sosnovsky was hit by a bullet. He too fled the city, with his wife and mother-in-law.

Many of those who lived in buildings that were hit, but whose apartments were not destroyed, have remained in the city. However, DW was told that the occupying authorities demanded they leave their apartments nonetheless. They were promised new apartments in exchange.

Ukrainian POW returns to front line after Russia torture To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But a source told DW that none of the inhabitants of the former blocks on Metallurgy Avenue was allocated an apartment in the new Leningradsky Kvartal buildings. And those who had lost everything in the attacks could not afford a mortgage. Another source told DW that people were put in accommodation on the outskirts of town, or else in hostels.

'We were robbed of our good life'

The majority of those who fled do understand why their former neighbors stayed in the city. Not everyone had the possibility of leaving Mariupol and starting again elsewhere.

"The local population is being pushed out of Mariupol," said Artemova, who now lives in Kyiv with her son. Like others DW spoke with who had left the city, she said Mariupol had started to develop rapidly a few years before the Russian invasion in early 2022. People wanted to live there.

"We were robbed of our ordinary life, which may have been uninteresting for some, but it was a good life. We'd go to market, knew where to buy what; we'd have a coffee, bump into a school friend with her dog and say hello," she remembered.

Thousands are widely believed to have died in Russia's siege on Mariupol in 2022 Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky

Neither Artemova nor Sosnovsky are considering returning to their hometown and re-registering their apartments according to the regulations of the Russian occupying authority. It's not even clear whether or not they would be allowed to enter the zone. But Ukraine is not compensating people for the loss of property there, as its authorities can't assess the situation without access to the occupied region.

"They're building their shiny new houses on what used to be a graveyard. I'd like nothing better than to bomb them, but only when no one's in the buildings. It's enough to drive you to despair," said one former resident of Metallurgy Avenue. He too lived there for decades, and remembers his child's first steps, taken in an apartment that no longer exists.

This is how he describes the city today: "In the center it's still OK, but if you go just a little to the left or right it smells of death."

This article was originally written in Russian.

World.title: Afghan allies still waiting for the safety Germany promised
World.content:
After the Taliban retook power on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring Afghan staff to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

It is hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June 2026, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.

Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."

In August 2026, 5 years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany. He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park, or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable."

Afghan refugees at risk as deportations surge in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter calling for help: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government remains firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Foreign Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2,500 ($,2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.

Afghan migrants stuck in Pakistan reject German cash offer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission programme for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry maintains it is in the right: "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."

According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.

German aid organization continues support

For Javad Niazi, the trepidation about his and his family's future continues. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport 5 years ago, the German non-governmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning to DW: "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people. And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be 4 weeks has now become 5 years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans. With success: They have won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," Beyer said.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was canceled."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Trump's Latin America allies open arms to Israel
World.content:
While ongoing military actions in Gaza and settler attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have largely isolated Israel globally, Latin America's authoritarian right sees an opening for a strategic alliance.

A three-week military offensive in the Gaza Strip in 2009, which killed more than 1,400 people, including an estimated 1,100 civilians, spurred Venezuela's Socialist president at the time, Hugo Chavez, to expel the Israeli ambassador in protest and end diplomatic relations.

Seventeen years later, Venezuela and Israel have agreed to establish a mechanism for the resumption of consular services. It's a limited step, but one that until recently would have been unthinkable.

In Colombia, the nationalist government of new President Abelardo de la Espriella recently reversed the decision by his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, to sever diplomatic relations with Israel in protest of the country's most recent war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 people, nearly one-third of them children.

De la Espriella has even announced that Colombia will relocate its embassy to Jerusalem, and this week declared that Colombia would join the United States as the only two countries that recognize "Israeli sovereignty" over the Golan Heights, which is Syrian territory under international law but has been occupied by Israel since 1967. The vast majority of the international community, including Germany and the UN, does not recognize the annexation of the Golan Heights by Israel.

"There is a trend toward rapprochement with Israel as a response to the surge of the radical right in the region," said Isaac Caro, a professor at Alberto Hurtado University in Chile. Caro said authoritarians in Latin America were linking relations with Israel to "an active alignment with US foreign policy." He said reinforcing ties with Israel had become a characteristic of Latin America's radical right as part of the renewed discourse of region's place in Judeo-Christian Western civilization.

In Argentina, for example, ultraconservative President Javier Milei has made close relations with Israel a defining feature of both his foreign policy and his own political identity.

Daniel Wajner, associate professor of international relations at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said there had been a "surge" in diplomacy between Israel and Latin American governments. Wajner said Jair Bolsonaro, the neoliberal former president of Brazil, and El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the self-described "world's coolest dictator," were early adopters of warmer ties with Israel. They were followed by Milei and others.

Israel has sent more troops to the occupied West Bank as settler attacks continue Image: Mussa Qawasma/REUTERS

Wajner said Latin America's authoritarians were actively "embracing" the national-conservative government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He also said there were ideological, religious and strategic factors in governments' tightening of bonds with the country, such as the desire to signal a like-minded international orientation with the US.

Gilberto Aranda, a political analyst from the University of Chile, said there had been a trend in Latin America of authoritarians' aligning with the US under Donald Trump — and therefore also engaging in rapprochement with Israel.

Colombia's new president triggers 'fundamental shift'

In 2024, under Petro, Colombia broke off relations because of the war in Gaza. In the week since de la Espriella assumed office on August 7, Caro said there has been a "fundamental shift" in Colombia's foreign policy.

In Venezuela, the stated policies of the current government, which took power after US forces abducted the sitting president in early January, remain rooted in the socialist populism of Chavismo. However, the resumption of consular services has proved a symbolic diplomatic success for Israel.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bolivia's Socialist government severed relations with Israel after the bombardment of a camp for displaced people in Gaza in 2023. When the conservative Rodrigo Paz assumed office 2025, he quickly restored ties.

In Chile, the democratic socialist former president, Gabriel Boric, was highly critical of Netanyahu and his government. His successor, the national conservative, Jose Antonio Kast, is seeking, among other things, to revive Chile's defense cooperation with Israel.

Brazil, Mexico maintain 'critical stance' toward Israel

By contrast, the social-democratic government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil has taken a highly critical stance toward Israeli actions in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

"The country with the most influence in the region, which maintains a critical stance toward Israel, is clearly Brazil," said Aranda. Brazil's demographic, economic and political clout are a major counterweight to the shift by other Latin American governments toward warmer relations with Israel.

Then there is Mexico, the other giant of Latin America. Whereas Lula, in Brazil, is particularly critical, Mexico, under President Claudia Sheinbaum, is trying to preserve greater neutrality as well as a diplomatic balance. Sheinbaum has criticized Israel's actions in Gaza, but still maintains diplomatic relations. This shows that criticism of the Netanyahu government does not inevitably signify the breakdown of relations with the state of Israel.

Still, given the recent mass killings in Gaza, the shift in Israel's relations with some governments in Latin America is significant. Israel is not just interested in winning over friendly governments. These bilateral relationships date back to the foundation of the Israeli state in 1948, and cover migration, trade, and security. The support of Latin America in multilateral organizations such as the United Nations has always been key in countering Israel's international isolation.

Wajner said the decision by Latin American governments to improve ties with Israel offered both sides "legitimacy, cooperation and influence." Israel needs international partners, and Latin American goverments also offer opportunities for economic, technological and military cooperation. For its part, Latin America can turn to Israel as a strong partner in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and defense.

Though Israel has managed to forge new bonds in Latin America for now, long-term relations will continue to depend on who is in power, where and when.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: India: Modi promises free exam coaching, AI training for youth after protests
World.content:
Speaking on India's Independence Day, PM Modi announced free online coaching for competitive exams and AI training for 10 million youths, weeks after protests over alleged exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on India's Independence Day announced training in artificial intelligence (AI) skills as well as free online coaching for young people for competitive exams just weeks after youth-led protests over exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.

Speaking at the Red Fort in New Delhi on Saturday, Modi said the coaching initiative would help ease the financial burden on poor and middle-class families.

"The competition surrounding coaching classes has become a huge burden for middle-class families," Modi said, adding that students could stay with their families while preparing for exams.

Modi's promise comes as last month the country was rocked by protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over alleged irregularities in competitive exams.

The protests ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan highlighting widespread concerns over access to education and jobs.

10 million youths to train in AI skills

The Indian prime minister also said 10 million young people would receive training in AI skills over the next year, in a move to appease the nation's youth that forced the Modi government to face its biggest challenge since coming to power in 2014.

Modi also said India will have eight more semiconductor chip plants in the coming years and five nuclear reactors which will generate 100 gigawatts of power by 2047.

In a speech lasting more than an hour, Modi outlined a seven-point growth and reform framework aimed at making India a developed country within 20 years. The plan focuses on manufacturing, agriculture, technology, defense and sectors including tourism and handicrafts.

Modi warns against 'intellectual Naxals'

At the same time, Modi also took aim at the latest enemy of the state — the "intellectual Naxals."

This was a reference to India's Naxal movement, which waged a guerrilla-style insurgency against the government, particularly in central and eastern India, leaving thousands dead and injured over nearly 60 years.

Modi said his government had defeated the armed movement but warned that the fight against the "Naxal mentality" remained, as its adherents looked for "opportunities to create violence and unrest."

Modi said these "intellectual Naxals" had to be identified and isolated to connect young people with the mainstream. Modi did not specify who these "intellectual Naxals" were in his speech.

In the past, Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has labelled rights activists, academics and intellectuals, journalists, political opponents, government critics and others with left-wing views as "urban Naxals."

08/15/2026 August 15, 2026 Heightened security planned at Berlin techno parade

The Techno Parade, some of whose participants are seen here in 2023, is a major spectacle Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

The techno parade Rave the Planet is expected to draw tens of thousands of people in Berlin in Saturday, with police stepping up security at the event after last month's Islamist attack on fringes of the Pride march in the capital.

Participants in the parade will also have to contend with high temperatures of up to 37 C (98.6 F).

Police say they will deploy at least one water cannon to spray a cooling water mist and free drinking water is to be made available along the route of the parade, organizers have said.

The parade is to start in the early afternoon and run until late in the evening.

It is planned to run along the main boulevard through the Tiergarten park, between the Brandenburg Gate and the Victory Column, close to the site of the July 25 attack, in which an Islamist assailant killed a woman and injured at least 31 people, some seriously.

A police spokeswoman said some 1,500 officers would be deployed at the event, with Berlin police supported by colleagues from the states of Brandenburg and Saxony-Anhalt.

The techno parade was first held in Berlin in 2022 to celebrate electronic music culture and has taken place every year since then.

Organizers have registered 300,000 participants, though police have put the number closer to 100,000 at previous parades.
