Serbia faces both energy and transport problems

Serbia’s challenges are somewhat different but are also closely linked to the Danube. Lower water flows have reduced production at major hydropower facilities, while the river’s role as a major transport corridor has created additional difficulties for energy security.

With water levels exceptionally low, cargo vessels are unable to operate at their normal capacity. This complicates the transport of diesel and other strategically important goods, potentially putting additional pressure on domestic supplies.

According to the HIIA analysis, Serbia has responded by releasing fuel reserves and seeking to strengthen alternative electricity-generation capacity.

The situation illustrates why the Danube drought cannot be treated as an isolated problem affecting individual countries. The same river is simultaneously a source of cooling water, hydropower and drinking water, as well as a crucial transport route.

Austria, Slovakia and Bulgaria have proved more resilient

Austria, Slovakia and Bulgaria have also experienced pressure from the drought, but their energy systems have so far been better able to absorb the shock. Austria has been able to compensate for weaker hydropower production partly through solar and wind generation and increased electricity imports.

Slovakia’s nuclear power plants are less directly dependent on Danube water for cooling because they use cooling towers, reducing their vulnerability to low river levels. Bulgaria’s Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant also has dedicated infrastructure designed to cope with exceptionally low river levels, providing greater resilience than facilities that depend more directly on the river’s flow.

These differences show that the impact of the same climate event can vary considerably depending on national energy infrastructure and the availability of alternative sources.

If you missed it: PM Magyar: Hungary begins sinking two huge barges to raise Danube water levels near Paks

Why countries along the Danube need to act together

The bigger lesson of the 2026 drought is that water security is becoming energy security. The same water resources may be needed at the same time for nuclear cooling, hydropower, irrigation, drinking water, shipping and the preservation of natural ecosystems. As climate change increases the likelihood of prolonged heatwaves and droughts, competition between these needs could become more frequent.

The HIIA analysis therefore points to the need for long-term investment in diversified energy systems, improved water retention, more resilient cooling technologies and stronger cross-border cooperation.

Regional coordination could become particularly important during simultaneous crises. Central and Eastern European electricity markets are closely interconnected, meaning that a shortage in one country can quickly affect neighbouring states. At the same time, when drought hits several countries simultaneously, the countries that normally provide emergency electricity imports may also be struggling with reduced generation.

This means the countries along the Danube have a shared interest in preparing for future droughts together. Coordinated water management, information sharing, emergency planning and electricity-market cooperation could help reduce the risk that a local water crisis develops into a regional energy crisis.

The 2026 drought has provided a grave warning: the future resilience of the Danube region will depend not only on how individual countries manage their own water and energy systems, but on how effectively they can respond together.

For Central Europe, the Danube is no longer just a river running through the region but a critical part of the region’s shared energy and security infrastructure.

World.title: Hungary overhauls tourism: Minister Kapitány announces three major appointments
World.content:
Hungary is overhauling the senior leadership of several key organisations within the Hungarian Tourism Agency (MTÜ) group, with changes announced at Visit Hungary, the Kisfaludy Tourism Support Management Company and the organisation overseeing Hungary’s participation in EXPO 2027.

The changes were announced by István Kapitány, Hungary’s Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, who said the overhaul was aimed at putting several areas of tourism management on a new footing. The renewed leadership team is being formed under the direction of Olivér Csendes, who was appointed to lead the MTÜ in July.

Three new leaders appointed

According to Kapitány, Andrea Róna has been appointed to head the Kisfaludy Tourism Support Management Company, Andrea Tóth will lead Hungary’s EXPO 2027 organisation, while Botond Boros has taken over the leadership of Visit Hungary.

Kapitány said the government intends to make tourism support and tourism lending more transparent and efficient in order to support the sector’s development. He also praised Csendes’s professional credibility and the trust he has established with representatives of the tourism industry, saying these provided a strong foundation for achieving better results.

New plans for Hungary’s EXPO 2027 participation

One of the most significant announcements concerns Hungary’s participation in EXPO 2027 in Belgrade. Kapitány said the government would not automatically continue with the concept inherited from the previous administration. Instead, it will develop a new plan based on professional and financial considerations.

The government also plans to launch new public procurement procedures, with the stated aim of creating genuine competition between multiple bidders and securing the strongest professional results.

Closer cooperation with the tourism industry

The minister said the government would maintain close professional dialogue with representatives of Hungary’s tourism sector, as well as with the Ministry of Transport and Investment. The changes come as the new MTÜ leadership seeks to accelerate decision-making and introduce changes across several areas of tourism policy.

Csendes was appointed to lead the Hungarian Tourism Agency on 21 July. He previously served as CEO of Visit Hungary and as director of digital and innovation at the Austrian National Tourist Office.

Kapitány said the first week under Csendes’s leadership had already seen numerous initiatives launched, suggesting further changes could follow as Hungary seeks to reshape the management and support of its tourism industry.

World.title: Fires break out across Szeged in Hungary, railway traffic halted near blazes
World.content:
Several fires broke out in and around Szeged on Saturday, with firefighters battling flames across thousands of square metres and railway traffic temporarily suspended because of one of the incidents.

One of the largest fires was reported near Vértói Road and Merkúr Road, where dry grass and fallen leaves caught fire alongside the railway tracks. Firefighters from Makó, Ruzsa, Hódmezővásárhely and Kiskunmajsa were deployed under the direction of the Csongrád-Csanád County disaster management operations service.

The flames threatened a nearby solar park, but firefighters managed to prevent the fire from spreading to the facility. Railway traffic between Sándorfalvi Road and Vértói Road was also suspended temporarily because of the fire. The flames were surrounded using six water jets.

Hay bales and buildings also catch fire

Firefighters were also called to Erdőszéli Road, where around 60 large round hay bales caught fire. A shed and a trailer also caught fire in the incident. Firefighters from Szeged and Kistelek managed to extinguish the flames and were carrying out follow-up operations.

The fire involving the bales is expected to require additional work as crews separate the piles to deal with the remaining hot spots.

Woodland vegetation catches fire

Another fire broke out along Bordányi Road, where approximately 2,000 square metres of woodland undergrowth, dry grass and fallen leaves caught fire.

The flames posed a threat to an unoccupied farmstead, but firefighters were able to contain the situation. Crews from the Szeged professional fire service continued working at the scene, with firefighting water supplied by a local volunteer association’s water tanker.

Authorities warned that operations at the site could continue for an extended period.

Dry vegetation increases fire risk

The incidents show the heightened fire risk created by dry vegetation during the summer. Firefighters were required to respond to several separate locations around Szeged within a short period, including another vegetation fire along Vértói Road covering roughly 1.5 hectares.

The emergency services deployed crews from several surrounding towns to deal with the outbreaks and prevent the flames from spreading to nearby infrastructure and buildings. Residents in the affected areas are advised to follow instructions from emergency services and avoid approaching active firefighting operations.

World.title: Sinking barges are already raising the Danube at Paks before reaching the riverbed
World.content:
Hungary’s emergency operation to raise the Danube’s water level near the Paks Nuclear Power Plant has produced its first encouraging result, even before the two barges being sunk in the river have reached the bottom.

The two 80-metre barges were positioned across the Danube as part of the emergency intervention designed to slow the river and raise water levels at the power plant’s cold-water intake. According to Gyula Kovács, the local technical coordinator of Hungary’s water management authority, simply positioning the barges across the river has already created a small damming effect.

During the first day, a 4-centimetre difference was measured between the water levels above and below the barges. By Saturday morning, the difference had increased to 7–8 centimetres. At the nuclear plant’s cold-water intake, the arrangement had already raised the water level by around one centimetre.

Engineers hope to restore reactor operations

The early results could prove crucial as the Danube continues to fall. Károly Vigh, operations director of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, said that once the effect of the temporary bottom weir currently being constructed becomes apparent, the reactors will gradually be brought back online.

According to Vigh, Unit 3 will be restarted first, followed by Unit 1. The plant can only return to its nominal maximum output once the water level at the intake has risen by approximately 25 centimetres from its current level.

Emergency intervention aims to prevent further shutdowns

The emergency works are designed to prevent the exceptionally low Danube level from forcing further reductions in the plant’s output. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Saturday that without the intervention, the river could fall to a level at which one of the plant’s two currently operating turbines would have to be shut down. A further decline could eventually lead to a complete shutdown.

The government is therefore combining the controlled sinking of the barges with the construction of a temporary bottom weir to raise the river level around the plant. Magyar said the immediate goal was to keep the two remaining operating turbines running and then gradually restore the others once sufficient water levels had been secured.

If you missed it: Hungary begins sinking barges to save Paks NPP and raise critically low Danube levels, PM Magyar receives good news

Political leaders stay away from Paks operation

During his press conference at the site, Magyar also criticised opposition party leaders for not accepting his invitation to visit the emergency works. He said leaders of Fidesz and other parliamentary parties had not attended the briefing and accused them of failing to offer assistance or call for national cooperation.

The prime minister also criticised what he described as misinformation about the situation online. The immediate focus, however, remains on the engineering operation at Paks, where water-management specialists are working against the clock to raise the Danube enough to protect the nuclear plant’s operations.

World.title: Hungary begins sinking barges to save Paks NPP and raise critically low Danube levels, PM Magyar receives good news
World.content:
Hungary has launched an extraordinary emergency operation on the Danube near Paks as authorities race to prevent critically low water levels from affecting the operation of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

Two 80-metre barges have been positioned in the river between Paks and Dunaszentbenedek and their controlled sinking has begun. The temporary structures are intended to slow the flow of the Danube and raise water levels around the power plant, producing a similar effect to a low-head weir.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Saturday that the first signs were encouraging: water levels had already risen by one centimetre near the plant’s pumping station.

“This is good news,” Magyar said, while stressing that the situation remains serious.

Water levels threaten reactor operations

The emergency intervention comes as the Danube continues to recede. Water levels at Paks were around -122 centimetres on Saturday, according to Magyar. Current forecasts indicate that the level could fall below -132 centimetres early Monday, a point at which one of the two operating turbines would have to be shut down.

In a more severe scenario, the water level could fall below -140 centimetres, potentially forcing the entire plant to shut down. The government therefore considers preventing a further fall in water levels a priority.

Hundreds of workers and tonnes of rock involved

Around 130 people are currently working directly at the site, while another 50 are involved in administrative tasks. More than 100 lorries are transporting rock to the construction area. Around 5,000 tonnes of rock are expected to arrive during Saturday alone.

The barges have initially been lowered by around 20 centimetres. Eight pumps are being used to bring water into the barges as part of the controlled sinking operation. Meanwhile, work has also begun on both banks of the Danube to construct the temporary structure designed to help raise the river level.

Hungarian military helicopters are also taking part in the operation. Two Airbus H225M helicopters have been used to lift two-tonne concrete blocks brought from Dunakiliti and place them in the river.

National effort mobilised to protect Paks

Magyar said the scale of the emergency justified a broad national effort. Several senior government officials and water-management experts were present at Paks, including Economic and Energy Minister István Kapitány, Minister of Defence Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, Minister heading the Prime Minister’s Office Bálint Ruff and national security adviser Péter Tóth.

Pál Kádár, head of the Defence Administration Office, thanked companies and members of the public who had offered assistance. However, he stressed that the most urgent need was for equipment capable of transporting rock.

Up to 100 lorries may be needed simultaneously on the two sides of the Danube, he said. Magyar added that companies were particularly encouraged to make offers of assistance. The authorities have also warned swimmers and small boats not to approach the work sites because of the serious accident risk.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Operation could determine Paks’s next days

The intervention is being carried out under considerable time pressure. If the river continues to fall as forecast, the first operational threshold could be reached in the early hours of Monday.

The emergency project has already attracted around 150 offers of assistance, according to Magyar.

The government hopes the temporary measures will provide enough of a rise in water levels to keep the power plant operating safely while the Danube remains at exceptionally low levels.

For Hungary, the stakes are high: Paks is the country’s largest nuclear power facility and a key source of domestic electricity. The ongoing operation on the Danube is therefore not simply a major engineering challenge, but an urgent effort to protect the stability of Hungary’s power supply.

World.title: Mysterious cult behind Hungarian murder: Man killed his ex-wife after bitter family dispute – tabloid
World.content:
On the morning of 18 August 1995, a visibly distressed man walked into the police station in Jászberény and told officers to arrest him.

He said he had strangled his wife during an argument at their home in the Hungarian town. However, investigators soon established that the killing had been preceded by months of escalating tension within the family.

At the centre of the conflict was the woman’s involvement with a mysterious religious group, which her husband believed had taken her away from her family. The case would eventually result in a 10-year prison sentence for József Sz. for killing his former wife.

How a religious group tore the family apart

According to Blikk’s account, the couple’s relationship had begun to deteriorate around a year before the murder.

Neighbours recalled that the woman had become increasingly involved with a secretive religious community. She reportedly spent more and more of her time with its members, while her family life was pushed into the background.

Blikk identified the group as the Children of God, an American religious movement whose first Hungarian-speaking group reportedly appeared around Novi Sad (Újvidék), in Serbia, in 1994. The movement allegedly reached the Jászság region several months later, where it was known locally as the Jesus Movement.

The community reportedly imposed strict rules on its members. According to the account, relatives were excluded from membership, only one person from a family could join and married couples were not admitted together. Members were also reportedly expected to abstain from sexual relations with partners or spouses outside the group.

These rules had a profound impact on the family. Neighbours claimed that the woman eventually stopped working and that family savings were being spent on the religious community. Her daughters reportedly complained that their mother was rarely at home.

Husband left the family home

By December 1994, József had had enough. He reportedly left the family home with his daughters and decided to seek a divorce. The divorce was finalised in May 1995, but another dispute soon emerged: who would live in the family home on Kárpát Street?

According to evidence obtained by police, the property had originally belonged to József, who had received it from his parents before his marriage. It therefore was not considered part of the couple’s jointly acquired property. His former wife nevertheless refused to leave.

The final confrontation

On the evening of 17 August 1995, József went to the house to discuss the matter. According to the investigation, he gave his former wife an ultimatum: she should move out before the start of the school year because he and their daughters intended to live there.

He reportedly told her to move in with one of the members of the religious group instead. The woman disagreed. She planned to remain in the property and, according to the account, intended to have a man she had met through the group live there with her.

An argument followed. József turned up the music, reportedly so that neighbours would not be able to hear the dispute. During the ensuing struggle, he grabbed his former wife’s neck and did not let go.

She died from strangulation.

The following morning, József went to the police station and confessed. He was subsequently sentenced to 10 years in prison for the killing.

The Jászberény police station:

What happened to the mysterious group?

The Jesus Movement originated in the United States in the 1970s and grew out of the hippie counterculture. Although it was not a single centrally organised sect, some of its more radical branches later became controversial religious groups.

The movement never became established in Hungary in the same form, according to the account. Some of its followers later became involved with other religious communities, while the group that had caused so much controversy in Jászberény eventually disappeared from the area.

More than three decades later, however, residents around Kárpát Street still remember the extraordinary case, not only because of the murder, but also because of the mysterious religious community that neighbours said had played a role in the breakdown of the family.

World.title: Budget flights are getting expensive: How Ryanair and Wizz Air make money from hidden extras
World.content:
Flying with Europe’s biggest low-cost airlines is becoming significantly more expensive, even though carriers such as Ryanair and Wizz Air are still competing fiercely on headline ticket prices.

An analysis by aviation data provider Cirium found that the selected economy fares of Ryanair, easyJet and Wizz Air were 39.2 per cent higher in May 2026 than a year earlier. Compared with early 2024, average fares had more than doubled.

Importantly, these figures cover the airlines’ basic fares before taxes and external charges. They also exclude many of the extras passengers often end up paying for, such as checked luggage, seat selection and priority boarding.

In other words, the final price of a “cheap” flight can be considerably higher than the advertised fare.

Jet fuel is putting airlines under pressure

The biggest driver behind the rising costs is aviation fuel. According to Világgazdaság, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) expects airlines’ global fuel bill to increase from around $252 billion in 2025 to $350 billion in 2026, representing an increase of almost 40 per cent.

Jet fuel prices surged dramatically in the spring, reaching an average of $188 per barrel in April. Although prices have subsequently fallen, they remain significantly higher than before the latest energy shock.

Airlines cannot simply pass all of these additional costs on to passengers, however. European carriers are also facing increased competition. Cirium data shows that more than 5 per cent more seats are available on intra-European flights this summer. With passengers highly sensitive to prices, airlines have limited room to raise basic fares indefinitely.

The financial results of the low-cost giants demonstrate the pressure. Ryanair’s after-tax profit fell by around a third in the April-June quarter, while its average fares were 6 per cent lower than a year earlier. Wizz Air, meanwhile, reported an operating loss of €183.3 million for the same period.

The real money is increasingly in the extras

So if airlines cannot simply keep raising ticket prices, where does the money come from? Increasingly, it comes from everything outside the basic fare. Baggage, seat selection, priority boarding and other optional services have become crucial sources of revenue for low-cost carriers.

Ryanair generated €4.99 billion from ancillary services in the financial year that ended in March. That worked out at around €24 per passenger and accounted for almost a third of its total €15.54 billion revenue.

The proportion is even higher at Wizz Air. Ancillary services accounted for almost half of the airline’s total revenue in its financial year ending in March 2025. This means that the basic fare is becoming an increasingly incomplete measure of how much a low-cost flight actually costs.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Is the low-cost model changing?

The traditional low-cost model is not disappearing, but it is becoming more complicated for passengers. Someone travelling with only a small amount of luggage, accepting an automatically assigned seat and avoiding additional services can still benefit from a genuinely cheap fare.

But once a passenger adds checked baggage, chooses a particular seat, wants priority boarding or requires other extras, the final bill can move considerably closer to the price charged by a traditional full-service airline. For carriers, meanwhile, ancillary revenue provides a way to keep headline fares relatively competitive while recovering some of their rising costs.

If you missed it: Hungarian Wizz Air opens new base in another European city!

Ryanair and Wizz Air face a delicate balancing act

There is little evidence that the low-cost sector itself is in crisis. Ryanair carried a record 208.4 million passengers in its latest financial year, with a load factor of 94 per cent, while its revenue increased by 11 per cent. The bigger question is how much passengers are willing to pay before the low-cost advantage starts to disappear.

As fuel remains expensive and airlines face rising operating costs, carriers such as Ryanair and Wizz Air are being forced to balance two competing priorities: keeping the advertised fare low enough to attract highly price-sensitive travellers, while generating more revenue from the extras passengers increasingly pay for.

For travellers, it’s important to learn the lesson: the cheapest ticket is not necessarily the cheapest flight. When comparing low-cost fares, the total cost — including luggage, seating and other necessities — is becoming more important than ever.

World.title: Budapest has never seen heatwaves like this: 2026 breaks records twice
World.content:
Both of this year’s extreme heatwaves in Budapest were more intense than ever before, according to an analysis published on the specialist portal Másfélfok (One and a Half Degree) – Climate Change Explained.

Péter Szabó, a climate researcher and PhD student at the meteorology faculty at ELTE, said that Budapest had never before experienced heatwaves like the two that occurred this year.

The first began on 20 June and lasted for 12 days; the second began on 30 July and lasted for 9 days. Although the July heatwave was shorter, it was more intense. On both occasions, it was hotter in the capital than in 2007, when the previous all-time heat record was set.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The 1994 heatwave also lasted 12 days, but it was nowhere near as intense as the two this year, Szabó said. Although the heatwave in July 2024 was the longest, lasting 13 days, it was less intense than the one at the start of August this year.

He added that for several decades in the 20th century, moderately intense heatwaves occurred every few years, followed by a longer period during which no heatwaves developed. However, after 1990, the effects of climate change became apparent, and it was really only after 2010 that heatwaves became prolonged and intense. During the hottest summer, in 2024, a total of around 1,300 more people died over the course of three weeks of heatwaves, meaning that excess mortality stood at nearly 20 percent nationwide.

World.title: Romanian swimmer David Popovici claims third European 200m freestyle title after 100m triumph
World.content:
Romanian swimming star David Popovici has won the 200m freestyle race at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris, his third consecutive European title in the event.

The win on August 14, following the August 12 gold in the 100m freestyle race, makes him the only athlete to have won both races at three consecutive editions of the European championships.

The 21-year-old Romanian swimmer finished the race with a time of 1:44.15, 0.40 seconds ahead of runner-up Tomas Navikonis of Lithuania, and 0.72 seconds ahead of Britain's James Guy.

In the 200m freestyle event, Popovici also won the Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, as well as two world titles, in Budapest in 2022 and in Singapore in 2025.

His personal best in the 200m freestyle came at the 2022 European Championships, when he clocked 1:42.97, the third-fastest time in history.

World.title: Romanian executive to submit fifth payment request under Recovery and Resilience Facility
World.content:
The Romanian government is set to submit the fifth payment request under the EU-backed Recovery and Resilience Facility, or PNRR, according to an announcement from European Investments and Projects minister Dragoș Pîslaru.

Payment no. 5 is worth EUR 2.84 billion, and is the penultimate request that Romania will submit within the PNRR. Once approved, the fifth payment will bring Romania’s absorption rate of PNRR-related grants to 78%, from 66% currently.

“One final request remains, request no. 6, worth EUR 2.58 billion in grants and EUR 1.76 billion in loans. From a total of EUR 13.57 billion allocated at the time the PNRR was signed, we will reach EUR 10.56 billion after request no. 5,” Pîslaru said during a press conference.

Initially, the European Commission planned for a single final payment request, reuniting the now separated requests no. 5 and 6, the minister noted.

The final payment request will be submitted at the end of September, and with it “we could reach 97.2% of the PNRR,” he said, referring to the grants component.

“47% was the percentage of the PNRR when I came to the ministry, after four years since the program was launched. The annual average was about 10.4% of the PNRR. In one year and two months, under the Bolojan government, we added 31% of the PNRR,” the minister also said.

Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan is financed through EUR 21.41 billion under the EU mechanism, including EUR 13.57 billion in grants and EUR 7.84 billion in loans. The fourth payment request, worth EUR 2.62 billion, was approved by the European Commission in May of this year.

World.title: Drone crashes in Romania’s Tulcea County
World.content:
A drone crashed on Friday, August 14, in the area of Luncaviţa, a locality in eastern Romania’s Tulcea County, about five kilometers from the border with Ukraine, the Defense Ministry (MApN) announced.

The drone crashed in a wooded area and caused no casualties, according to preliminary information provided by MApN.

The drone was not detected by MApN’s radar surveillance systems as it was flying at a very low altitude, the ministry said.

The crash resulted in an explosion followed by a fire, which has been extinguished, the Emergency Situations Inspectorate of Tulcea announced.

A MApN team, using an IAR 330 PUMA SOCAT helicopter, will investigate the area.

A day earlier, drone remains were discovered in the sea, close to Romania’s Costinești beach, on the Black Sea shore. Five drones were tracked nearing Romanian territory on the night of Wednesday, August 12, to Thursday, August 13, around 1 AM. One drone briefly entered Romanian airspace in Tulcea County but then exited and headed to Ukraine. Another drone was detected in Romanian airspace around 9 AM. Earlier this week, two Gerbera-type drones were destroyed by divers of the Romanian Army in the exclusive economic zone, approximately 165 kilometers from Constanța, in the Neptun Deep exploitation area.

At the end of the August 14 government meeting, prime minister Ilie Bolojan said the country’s military was doing “everything in their power to combat the drones.”

“We have a reality that we cannot deny, namely that the war resulting from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is having an impact, including along our borders, and we can expect drone debris, drones reaching the river areas along Romania’s border, in the vicinity of ports, to stray into Romania,” the PM said.

“It is regrettable that we are facing such situations, but given what has happened in recent months, we are beginning to see that this is becoming something of a constant; it is not just in Romania, we have seen what has happened in other areas as well. It is becoming clear that equipping our Armed Forces as quickly as possible with counter-drone systems is a necessity,” he added.

World.title: Romanian telco Digi reports 10% higher revenues in Q2 2026
World.content:
Romanian telecommunications company Digi (BVB: DIGI) reported consolidated revenues of EUR 608 million in the second quarter of 2026, representing an 11% YoY increase.

Adjusted EBITDA (ex. operating leases) for Q2 2026 increased by 23% compared to the result from Q2 2025, reaching EUR 169 million. Consequently, in the first semester of 2026, the group recorded consolidated revenues of EUR 1.2 billion, a 10% increase versus 6M 2025, and adjusted EBITDA of EUR 398 million, up 17% YoY.

“Spain continues to be our primary growth engine, maintaining strong commercial momentum and progressing in line with our long-term plans, while Romania continued to perform well,” said Serghei Bulgac, CEO of Digi Communications.

Last month, Digi successfully completed an initial public offering for its Spanish subsidiary. The Spanish IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, showing investor appetite for the company’s shares.

In Q2 2026, Digi reached 33.9 million revenue-generating user agreements (RGUs) across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy, a 14% increase compared to Q2 2025.

The mobile segment stands out for generating the most RGUs within the group’s array of services, accounting for 51% of the overall clients across the four markets. In Q2 2026, the mobile segment saw its RGUs climb to 17.3 million, a 19% YoY increase, covering mobile telephony clients across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy.

In Romania, the mobile service segment remained the largest, reaching 8.4 million RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026, a positive evolution of 20% compared to Q2 2025. Broadband services registered an increase of 4% in Q2 2026, compared to Q2 2025, up to 5.2 million RGUs, while the segment of Pay-TV services (cable and satellite) increased by 2% YoY, up to 6.1 million RGUs. Together with fixed-line telephony, the total number of RGUs in the Romanian market amounted to 20.5 million customers as of Q2 2026, a 9% increase versus Q2 2025.

Spanish operations continued the strong performance in Q2 2026, with the number of users of fixed services, internet, and mobile telephony increasing by 23% compared to Q2 2025, to 11.9 million RGUs. Mobile users increased by 19% to 7.8 million RGUs, while broadband users increased by 28% to 2.9 million.

In Portugal, the number of RGUs amounted to 960k, up 22% YoY, of which 545k were mobile, and 186k were broadband users.

In Italy, mobile users increased by 4,5% YoY, reaching 535k RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026.

In the United Kingdom, Digi launched its fiber broadband services and continued expanding its network footprint during the second quarter of 2026, while onboarding its first customers.

World.title: Romania’s Presidential Administration to host summit on animal welfare
World.content:
The Presidential Administration will host the second edition of Animal Summit Romania on September 29 - 30, Diana Pungă, a state adviser for relations with civil society at the institution, announced on Friday, August 14.

The event, organized by the non-profit Sache Vet Association and Bucharest’s Animal Protection Administration ASPA, will take place at Cotroceni Palace.

Over two days, it will gather public administration representatives, veterinarians, legal and education specialists, non-governmental organizations and other experts to discuss animal protection and welfare and solutions to challenges in the field.

“Romania continues to face major challenges in the field of animal protection. Beyond the issue of abandonment and the lack of education about responsible pet ownership, civil society frequently raises concerns about the non-transparent operation of some private shelters, suspected abusive euthanasia practices and difficulties in uniformly enforcing existing legislation. In many communities, volunteers, NGOs and active citizens end up compensating for the lack of coherent institutional mechanisms by becoming directly involved in animal rescue, shelter monitoring and the promotion of responsible sterilization and adoption,” an announcement from the organizers reads.

All of these aspects point to an urgent need for clear standards and consistently implemented public policies protecting both the communities and the animals, the organizers said.

World.title: Central Romania: EBRD extends EUR 120 mln loan for PV plant, battery system near Brașov
World.content:
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Friday, August 14, that it has extended a financing package of up to EUR 120 million for the development, construction, and operation of Econergy’s Părău 2 project in Romania.

The project includes a 342 MW solar photovoltaic plant and a 150 MW/300 MWh battery storage system in Brașov, according to a statement by the lender.

The financing consists of an EBRD A loan of up to EUR 57 million and an EBRD B loan of up to EUR 63 million, which includes a EUR 3.6 million debt service guarantee provided by commercial banks Privredna banka Zagreb and NLB.

According to the EBRD, the Părău 2 project will increase renewable energy production, help improve grid flexibility, and strengthen Romania’s energy security.

The project is co-financed by BSTDB (the Black Sea Trade and Development Bank), OTP Bank, and Exim Banca Românească, as part of a debt financing package of up to EUR 229 million.

“By financing one of the country’s pioneering solar and battery storage investments, the EBRD is helping to increase the generation of renewable energy, strengthen energy security and support a more resilient and flexible electricity system. The support of the European Union through InvestEU demonstrates how public and private partners can work together to mobilize financing for the green transition,” said Georgios Gkiaouris, the EBRD’s Head of Energy Europe.

The project is backed by Romania’s Contract for Difference scheme, which was developed with EBRD technical assistance and aims to unlock 5 GW of solar and onshore wind capacity. The solar plant has secured a 125 MWac allocation in the first auction at a strike price of EUR 49.4/MWh for 15 years, while the remaining capacity will operate on a merchant basis.

The European Union supported the EBRD A/B loan through a first-loss portfolio guarantee provided by the InvestEU programme, which covers up to EUR 115 million and helps mitigate the risks associated with the project’s substantial exposure to merchant revenue.

World.title: Romanian consumer goods distributor AQUILA reports slightly higher revenues amid challenging context
World.content:
AQUILA, one of the largest players in the fast-moving consumer goods distribution sector from Romania and the region, reported revenues of RON 1.6 billion in the first half of 2026, amid an economic environment marked by declining consumption, according to a report submitted to the local stock exchange.

The figure represents a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year.

Revenue from the distribution segment increased by 6% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, driven by the organic growth of this business line. The main contributor to this performance was the traditional retail channel, which grew by 22%, followed by the HoReCa channel with 7% growth, and the gas station channel with 1%, evolutions that offset the 19% decline recorded in the organized retail channel.

Revenue from the logistics segment increased by 6%, driven by higher operating volumes and the expansion of logistics activities across multiple temperature categories, particularly in the frozen products segment. Revenue from the transport segment increased by 13%.

The company's own brands continued to strengthen their contribution to the group’s performance, with revenues of RON 78.5 million in the first half of 2026, up 23% compared to the same period in 2025.

The results for the first half of the year were affected by a more challenging operating environment, marked by weaker consumer spending in Romania, an approximately 30% increase in fuel costs, and unfavorable foreign exchange movements, as well as by the temporary impact of the group’s market share expansion strategy and continued investments in the development of our operating platform.

In this context, EBITDA amounted to approximately RON 61 million, down 33% compared to the same period in 2025, while the net result was negative, at approximately RON 21 million.

During the first six months of the year, the group invested EUR 3 million in the development of its logistics infrastructure, process digitalization, operations automation, and equipment modernization, in line with its growth strategy and commitment to improving operational efficiency.

“Our distribution segment continued to deliver growth, supported by the expansion of the traditional retail and HoReCa channels, the consolidated contribution of our own brands, and the commercial synergies generated through the integration of the acquired companies. At the same time, we chose to prioritize strengthening commercial relationships and increasing market share, which play an essential role in supporting long-term growth and value creation,” said Cătălin Vasile, CEO of AQUILA.

The company head noted that the strategy had a temporary impact on commercial margins and profitability but created “a foundation for capitalizing on the investments made and supporting sustainable performance in the period ahead.”

World.title: Raiffeisen Bank Romania issues a new series of bonds denominated in RON
World.content:
Raiffeisen Bank, one of the largest banks in Romania, issued on August 13, 2026, a senior preferred eligible bond issue maturing in 2033, with a total value of RON 750 million.

The tranche represents the bank’s 0th series of eligible bonds, the financial institution informs through a statement sent to Economica.net.

The bond issue was addressed to institutional investors and was placed at a fixed coupon of 7.538% for the first five years, respectively 0.85% above the yield of the benchmark Romanian government bonds denominated in lei.

The bonds received a Baa1 rating from the rating agency Moody’s, two notches above Romania’s sovereign rating (Baa3).

After obtaining approval from the National Bank of Romania, the bonds are set to be included in the bank’s own funds and eligible liabilities base and listed on the Luxembourg and Bucharest stock exchanges.

In Romania, Raiffeisen Bank serves approximately 2.4 million individual and corporate customers. The bank has been active in Romania for more than 25 years.

Earlier this year, Raiffeisen bought Garanti BBVA's ​Romanian business for EUR 591 million, its ‌first significant acquisition in recent years. The deal marked a turning point for Raiffeisen, which has long been under pressure to withdraw ​from Russia due to its invasion of ​Ukraine and the imposition of Western sanctions on ⁠Moscow.

World.title: Albania Ruling Party Documents Highlight Country’s Ageing Demographic
World.content:
Documents produced by governing Socialist Party experts for a reform of the country’s municipal set-up, seen by BIRN, reveal an ageing population that could have adverse economic consequences for Albania.

The “Administrative-Territorial Reform 2.0” documents, prepared by experts on a special parliamentary committee, also show how emigration and internal migration have emptied out small towns and rural areas while concentrating the population in a few urban centres.

At one end are several urban centres where both population and economic activity are increasingly concentrated. At the other end are peripheral areas, particularly in the northeast, southeast and mountainous regions, which are caught in a vicious cycle of population decline and subsistence economies, with few formal jobs.

In these areas, municipal budgets survive largely on central government transfers, with funds often used mainly to cover the salaries of local administration staff.

The Urban Mass Index, UMI, one of three analytical documents underpinning the proposed new map of 46 municipalities – which would merge 15 local government units with larger municipalities – documents the territorial transformation of Albania since the 1990s, with a few centres continuing to grow as an increasing number of municipalities lose residents.

The “dependency ratio” in the index, which measures the burden that children and elderly people place on the working-age population, shows that in 51 municipalities out of 61 in total, this burden is higher than the national average. In many of them, the number of elderly residents exceeds the number of children.

The data highlights an Albania divided into three distinct realities: a small group of municipalities that continue to attract population and economic activity; a group of municipalities with intermediate potential; and a majority of the country’s territory, which is losing the critical mass of population needed to sustain local economies and public services.

The analysis is based on data from the 2023 census and, as part of the technical report accompanying the reform proposal, suggests that Albania is experiencing a growing concentration of its population in an ever-smaller number of urban centres, while the rest of the country is losing residents, functions and development capacity.

The index results show that only 13 municipalities are classified as having a high level of urban mass and are home to 62.5 per cent of the population.

By contrast, 30 municipalities – covering almost half of the country’s administrative map – are classified as having a low level of urban mass and account for just 14.2 per cent of the population.

Another 18 municipalities fall into the intermediate or medium category.

According to the data, the country’s population is concentrated in the capital, which is home to more than half a million people, followed at a considerable

distance by the municipalities of Durres, Vlora, Elbasan, Shkoder, Fieri, Kamza and Berat.

At the other end of the scale, municipalities such as Pustec, Libohova, Himara, Kelcyra, Memaliaj, Selenica, Dropull, Finiq, Delvina and Kolonja have the smallest populations.

The ruling-party experts did not build the index solely on population size. It also combines other indicators, including population density, the spatial distribution of residents, the demographic dependency ratio and the level of urbanisation.

This means that a municipality may cover a large area, but if its population is concentrated in a small town while the rest of its territory is largely empty, it is considered structurally weak.

One of the most significant findings is that, on average, 57 per cent of Albania’s territory is uninhabited.

The analytical document notes that the country no longer has the same population distribution it had in 2014, when the current administrative-territorial division was introduced with the aim of creating larger and more efficient municipalities.

“Some areas have grown, while others have lost a significant share of their population,” the report says, arguing that some municipalities are struggling to secure sustainable finances, qualified staff and adequate administrative capacity.

The Socialists have submitted a bill to parliament proposing a new administrative-territorial map that would merge several smaller municipalities with larger neighbouring ones – without explaining how the proposed map would address these underlying problems.

The proposal has faced opposition from residents in the affected areas. Some fear mergers will leave them with even more limited access to public services.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Man Suspected of Spying for Serbian Intelligence
World.content:
Fehim Sali, second left, at a court hearing in Pristina on August 14, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court on Friday ordered 30 days of detention for a dual Kosovo and Serbia citizen, Fehim Sali, who is suspected of spying for Serbia’s intelligence agency, the BIA.

It is alleged that he passed the BIA information about Kosovo officials, politicians and Islamist radicals, including potential recruitment targets, and received money in return.

Sali, a resident of Kosovo’s southern Dragash/Dragas municipality, was arrested on Thursday at the Merdare border crossing point while entering from Serbia. He appeared before the Basic Court in Pristina on Friday.

“The court’s assessment took into account the circumstances relating to the risk of absconding, the risk of influencing witnesses and evidence, and the risk of repetition or continuation of the criminal offence,” the court said in a statement.

According to the prosecution file, Sali is suspected of “maintaining contact with BIA officers using four different mobile phones”, which were found during raids at his house on Thursday, alongside around 40,000 euros in cash.

The prosecution file alleges that Sali “worked as a recruited agent for Serbia’s Security Information Agency, BIA, in exchange for material benefits”. The file alleges that he acted on the instructions of a senior BIA officer identified as Zelimir Matovic, nicknamed Zeljko.

It alleges that Sali provided the BIA with information about Kosovo’s political situation and helped it identify officials of Kosovo’s own intelligence agency, the AKI. According to the case file, he photographed some of its officials to facilitate their identification.

Sali is also accused of providing information about members of the radical Islamist Wahhabi movement as well as other people whom he allegedly proposed to the BIA officer as potential targets for contact and recruitment.

According to prosecutors, Sali also “mediated matters and documents connected to Serbian state institutions and maintained contacts with people with political and social influence in Serbia and Kosovo, particularly members of non-majority communities”.

The prosecution stated that he provided some of these people with “guidance on political activity, with the aim of gathering and transmitting information of interest to the BIA”.

Prosecutors argue that these activities were carried out against the state interests of Kosovo and endangered its constitutional order and national security.

The prosecution also alleges that the 40,000 euros found and seized during a search of Sali’s home came from his alleged activities on behalf of the BIA.

According to the case file, the evidence against Sali includes his own statement.

Prosecutors claim he described in detail his alleged activities, including how and where he communicated with BIA officials, exchanged information and provided assistance to the Serbian intelligence service.

Prosecutor Bekim Kodraliu told media that Sali admitted having been recruited and maintained regular contact with BIA officials.

“The suspect himself stated that he had been recruited and had ongoing contacts with BIA officials,” Kodraliu said.

The case comes two months after another Kosovo espionage conviction involving Serbia’s intelligence service.

In June, the Pristina Basic Court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage.

Prosecutors said Selimi had provided the BIA with information about religious radicalisation in Kosovo, former members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and people who had joined Islamic State.

World.title: Week in Review: Between the Absurd and the Unexpected
World.content:
Kosovo’s governance drama is beginning to border on the absurd. Weeks after the June election results were certified, two months after the elections were held, MPs have yet to elect a parliamentary speaker and deputies and, in doing so, constitute the new parliament.

The winning party, Vetevendosje, has the votes to elect a new speaker, and indeed a new government. But it has conditioned the election of a speaker on reaching a wider agreement with the opposition on the election of a new president. With deadlines imposed by the Constitutional Court passing, is Kosovo heading to a fourth parliamentary election in two years?

World.title: Thousands Flee, 14 Hospitalised as Wildfire Menaces Croatian Coastal Town
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said on Friday that 14 people have been hospitalised, with ten in intensive care, after a wildfire that reportedly forced some 2,000 people to evacuate homes around the Dalmatian coastal town of Omis overnight.

“The government and all relevant services are coordinating to protect people and rectify the consequences of the large fire in Omis,” Plenkovic wrote on X.

The fire swept through forested areas to destroy property and vehicles. Chief national fire officer Slavko Tucakovic told media that he had “never experienced anything like this in my career”.

“Unfortunately, many houses were damaged or burned down. A large number of vehicles were also burned up,” he said.

The Croatian coast has seen record high temperatures this summer. The heatwave left dry vegetation as fuel for the fire, and the flames were spread by high winds, Tucakovic explained.

World.title: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN .

The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June.

Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls.

“From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group.

“The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added.

“We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election.

Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency.

“We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said.

“We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added.

Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties.

So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

World.title: Democracy Digest: US Charges Mexican Cartel Members over Czech Weapons Deal
World.content:
Russia on the radar; Slovakia picks a fight with Brussels over same-sex marriage

Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has been forced into an embarrassing retreat over speed cameras with suspected Russian links, a week after dismissing opposition warnings about their origin. The National Security Authority (NBU) confirmed on Tuesday that the two devices in question contain Russian components. The finding vindicates concerns raised by Progressive Slovakia (PS), the country’s strongest opposition party, which had warned that the cameras could pose a security risk. There were red flags from the start. Journalists found that the cameras closely resembled equipment made by the St Petersburg-based company Simicon. More strikingly, the measurement software listed in the Slovak certification had the same digital fingerprint as software used in a Russian CORDON speed camera. The ministry’s story has shifted ever since. It first insisted the cameras were not Russian, then conceded it could not prove their origin, before ordering IT supplier Soitron to remove the test devices. It now says two ministry employees will lose their jobs and cooperation with Soitron will end. Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok, of the governing Hlas party, has resisted calls to take political responsibility. “We were lied to,” he said on Thursday, blaming the Slovak Institute of Metrology, which certified the cameras. The institute says checking cybersecurity risks, supply chains or the origin of components is not its job. Soitron also denies misleading the state. Soitron obtained the devices from a Slovak distributor whose CEO had worked in Russia for many years and had previously imported similar equipment to Slovakia through another company. The ministry will not publish the NBU analysis, and it is unclear why the country’s security services failed to spot the potential problem before opposition politicians and journalists did. The General Prosecutor’s Office has now said it will examine the case.

There was another controversy this week involving the Interior Ministry, and Interior Minister Sutaj Estok in particular. His ministry has refused to register same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad. Several Slovak same-sex couples applied in December to have their foreign marriage certificates entered into Slovakia’s special registry. After waiting eight months, they received an answer not from the registry, but directly from Sutaj Estok. He argued that registering the unions as marriages would conflict with Slovak law and the constitution, which has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 2014. Among those affected are former diplomats Ivan Novotny and his husband Metod Spacek. They argue that the minister intervened in a procedure that should have been handled by the registry and are now preparing an administrative lawsuit. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union involving a Polish-German same-sex couple. The court ruled that an EU country cannot refuse to recognise a same-sex marriage legally concluded in another member state if doing so interferes with rights guaranteed under EU law, particularly freedom of movement and residence. The ruling does not require member states to introduce same-sex marriage into their domestic law. The European Commission has reminded Slovakia that EU law, as interpreted by the EU’s top court, takes precedence over national law and that member states are required to implement its judgments. It told the SME daily that it would continue to monitor the situation and could use the tools at its disposal if needed. The ministry argues that EU law may require Slovakia to recognise same-sex marriages for specific purposes, but does not oblige the country to enter them in its registry as marriages with the same legal status as marriages recognised under Slovak law. Novotny, Spacek and other couples dispute that interpretation. Their planned legal challenge could now put that question before the Slovak courts.

World.title: Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law Won’t Succeed Without More Gynaecologists
World.content:
Imagine a woman called Milica. She is 29, on a fixed-term contract, and every month menstrual pain keeps her from working for several days.

Milica has not seen a gynaecologist in two years. There aren’t enough appointments where she lives and she cannot travel to the capital, Podgorica, because of work.

When she finally gets a diagnosis, she learns a law offering paid leave exists, and she must renew her medical diagnosis certificate every year.

But she wonders whether her employer will extend her contract if he learns why she has been absent.

World.title: BIRN Reality Check: What Has Albania’s AI ‘Minister’ Achieved So Far?
World.content:
According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process.

But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear.

At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage.

“There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement.

According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system.

The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules.

The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties.

Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption.

According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement.

“Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said.

He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.”

Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place.

Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes.

“Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”.

For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems.

“Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said.

Multiple challenges

World.title: Tallinn mulling night-time work for Liivalaia street reconstruction
World.content:
To minimize disruption to daytime traffic, roadworks on Liivalaia tänav in Tallinn will likely be carried out at night this fall.

Tallinn Mayor Peeter Raudsepp (Isamaa) said on social media this week that roadworks must not bring traffic in Tallinn to a standstill and that he had agreed with the city's deputy mayors on steps to prevent this.

"What is happening leaves much to be desired. I have several questions myself and I am hearing them increasingly often from residents as well. One thing is clear: At the start of fall, traffic gets heavier and faster, while roadworks force people to take detours and make them late. For example, work at the Hipodroomi intersection will continue for quite some time, repairs on Sõle tänav have only just begun and work on Liivalaia tänav will start next week. And it makes no difference whether you travel by bus, car or bicycle. Changes are needed," Raudsepp wrote.

Other major streets are also undergoing repairs, with work underway on Peterburi tee and Lauteri tänav in the Kesklinn district, for example. However, the mayor's call does not mean that work planned for this fall will be postponed, Järvan said.

"There is no such plan. Naturally, the city would like to repair even more roads and streets than we are currently able to. But as for these measures [to reduce traffic disruption] — and we are not talking about street reconstruction here, but road surface repairs — the idea is for them to be carried out primarily at night and outside peak hours, so that traffic can flow without obstruction when traffic volumes are at their highest," Järvan said.

This week, Tallinn announced that road surface repairs will also begin next week on Liivalaia tänav, one of Kesklinn's main thoroughfares, and will last two months. The plan is to shift the work there to nighttime hours, Järvan said, although as of this week, the contractor had not yet been issued a permit for nighttime work.

Roadwork will begin on the section of Liivalaia tänav between Juhkentali tänav and Pärnu maantee. Source: Tallinn City Government

"It is standard practice for the Transport Department to issue nighttime work permits for such important arterial roads. Road surface repairs and other work on arterial roads are prohibited during peak hours and temporary traffic management measures cannot be in place during that time. This is one of the main measures for ensuring that traffic disruption caused by road surface repairs, at least, is kept to a minimum," Järvan said.

However, this means that noisier work, such as asphalt milling, will also take place at night and could disturb local residents. According to Järvan, the compromise is necessary.

"The people who live nearby versus the citywide continuity of infrastructure and keeping the city functioning during peak hours — these are always factors that have to be weighed. But the general practice has been to grant construction companies nighttime work permits on arterial roads with such heavy traffic volumes. As things stand today, to my knowledge, the contractor has not yet been issued a nighttime work permit, but the usual practice is for one to be issued, which means less disruption to traffic," Järvan said.

Moving some road repairs to nighttime hours, however, does not mean that roadworks will not affect traffic this fall.

"There will certainly be traffic disruptions, but at the same time, we want our streets to be in good condition. Liivalaia tänav has been waiting for repairs for years, while Pärnu maantee is due to undergo reconstruction in the coming years. It would certainly not make sense to work on a street intersecting with such a major arterial road as Liivalaia tänav at the same time. Unfortunately, the Pärnu maantee end of Liivalaia tänav is already in such a condition that even its base layers need repairs, but unfortunately, we will not be able to do that within the timeframe we are currently working with," Järvan said.

Plans for reconstructing a section of Pärnu maantee in Tallinn's city center. Autor/allikas: K-Projekt

The fact that the road surface on Liivalaia tänav between Juhkentali tänav and Pärnu maantee is now being replaced means that Liivalaia tänav will not undergo a full reconstruction in the next few years, the deputy mayor acknowledged.

"Since Pärnu maantee is due to undergo reconstruction and must be completed by 2029, Liivalaia tänav certainly cannot be reconstructed at the same time," Järvan said.

Ripping up concrete on Peterburi tee still not decided

One of the largest reconstruction projects currently underway in the capital is on the section of Peterburi tee closest to Kesklinn. According to Järvan, the section should be completed by the end of October, although it is not yet possible to say so with complete certainty. The city is currently analyzing how to proceed with the reconstruction of Peterburi tee, as the bulk of the work still lies ahead

Much of the current deliberation centers on whether to remove the concrete base, which has served road users for decades but has now turned into what Järvan described as a "roller coaster." Removing the concrete would mean significantly more work and higher costs, the deputy mayor noted.

There is not much time left to make a decision, however, as work on the next section is scheduled to begin next year.

"If our plans work out and we can go with the lighter option — removing the top layer and repairing the concrete slabs — then we would still like to start next year. But if it does require — and the analyses show that it does require — more extensive reconstruction, then that is something we still need to consider," the deputy mayor said.

According to Järvan, the city also needs to address the longstanding problem of roadworks piling up in the fall, when traffic is significantly heavier than in the summer.

Peterburi tee. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"The reason is that in the past, including last year, contracts and procurements for work to be carried out that same year were not completed in time. That means the procurement process does not begin until spring, contracts are not signed until summer and roadworks only begin after that. This year, we have arranged things so that procurements and contracts will be completed within the current year," he said.

"That means that next year, as soon as the weather permits in spring or early summer, roadworks can get underway. This will spread roadworks out more over the year, which means fewer traffic problems and allows the work to take place primarily in the summer," the deputy mayor added.

World.title: Swiping a few apples may have ended in a beating in 19th century Estonia
World.content:
Nowadays, those caught pilfering peas or apples from someone else's field or garden may justify it as a folk tradition. In the 19th century, however, getting caught meant a trip to court and a sound thrashing as punishment.

The first apple orchards began appearing on farms 150 years ago and establishing one was a very expensive undertaking at the time. That was also why farmers kept a close eye on their apples. While fences kept animals away from the valuable produce, they were no help against people.

"A very common practice was to plant apple trees near the windows so they could be watched from inside the house. There were also dogs in the yard, of course, and some farmers would stand guard themselves," gardening history researcher Anneli Banner said.

Pilfering apples could land someone in court. In 1874, for example, boys aged 13 to 14 were caught stealing apples in Piilsi village near Avinurme — some took eight, others 10 and one 17.

"This was a time when punishment was either a fine or corporal punishment, meaning a birching. The boys' fathers refused to appear in court because they were afraid they themselves might receive corporal punishment," Avinurme local historian Piret Haav said.

That left the mothers with no choice but to go to court themselves and then carry out the punishment, giving their sons 10 strokes with a birch rod. It was quite unusual for parents, rather than the court, to have to administer the punishment. An adult would not have gotten off so lightly.

"The number of strokes varied, as did the fines. They ranged from 50 kopecks to a couple of dozen rubles, or from 10 to 30 strokes with a birch rod," Haav said.

While pea growers are now the ones who mainly have trouble with people helping themselves to their crops, the Estonian term raksus käima originated in apple orchards and comes from the cracking sound made when branches break.

"The word raks is an onomatopoeic word referring to a sudden cracking sound and the expression is presumably based on that comparison. Going out to pilfer or steal is an emotionally charged activity and emotionally charged activities tend to have many synonyms. These are often based on comparisons and one way of forming them is through onomatopoeia," Estonian Language Institute vocabulary researcher Iris Metsmägi said.

But while such pilfering was considered theft in the past, how is it viewed today?

"I suppose nowadays it is, whereas in the past it wasn't really seen that way. When you were a child and took an apple from a neighbor's garden, you didn't feel like much of a thief, although maybe you did feel a little twinge of guilt inside, but..." Ülle said.

"It's like going into a pea field, secretly eating a few peas there and taking a few with you. Or going into your neighbor's garden to eat a few apples — that sort of thing," Liisa said.
