The beginning of a tradition

That is what makes India's first Independence Day so different from the August 15 that Indians know today. There was no established Red Fort ceremony. There was only a country experiencing its first morning of freedom.

Yet, amid all of this, something irreversible had happened.

At midnight, authority had changed hands.

By morning, the Tricolour was flying.

The British Raj was over, and Indians were now responsible for the country they had fought to free.

The first Independence Day was therefore not simply the celebration of an ending. It was the first, uncertain and extraordinary day of the much harder task that followed, building India after freedom had been won.

World.title: Vijayanagara celebrates Independence Day with focus on Constitutional values, development
World.content:
Vijayanagara celebrated the 80th Independence Day on Saturday with a tribute to the freedom fighters and a call to uphold the unity and integrity of the country and the ideals enshrined in the Constitution.

Hoisting the national flag at the District Stadium in Hosapete, Muzrai, Fisheries, Ports and Inland Water Transport Minister and Vijayanagara district in-charge Minister K.S. Basavanthappa said every citizen had a responsibility to protect the country’s unity, integrity and constitutional values.

Recalling the sacrifices of Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bhagat Singh, B.R. Ambedkar, and Sarojini Naidu, among others, Mr. Basavannappa also remembered the contribution of women freedom fighters, including Kittur Rani Chennamma.

“The Constitution, framed under the leadership of Dr. Ambedkar after Independence, had laid the foundation for an inclusive India and enabled every citizen to live with dignity and self-respect… India has made significant progress in science and technology, education, healthcare, agriculture, industry and the economy since Independence. However, challenges such as poverty, unemployment, gender and economic inequality, environmental pollution, climate change, water scarcity and deforestation remained, and they required collective efforts by the government and society,” he said.

Speaking on the district’s development, the Minister said that the Karnataka Mining Environment Restoration Corporation had earmarked ₹4,107 crore for development works in the district, of which 132 proposals involving ₹2,171 crore had been approved.

“A 250-bed hospital, constructed with ₹104 crore from the District Mineral Foundation fund, was ready for inauguration. The construction of a critical care centre at a cost of ₹21.40 crore was in the final stage,” he said.

World.title: Freedom fighters, govt. employees  honoured
World.content:
Honouring of freedom fighters marked the celebration of the 80th Independence Day at the Virudhunagar district on Saturday.

In the presence of Superintendent of Police Gautam Goyal, Virudhunagar District Collector N O Sukhaputra hoisted the national flag and took the salute.

The students from various educational institutions presented a cultural event, which drew applause from the audience. On the occasion, the Collector honoured employees with certificate of merits from various departments. The NGOs and volunteers, who had served during the festivals, were also honoured.

Deputy Director (Srivilliputtur Megamalai Tiger Reserve) Ravi Meena, Sub Collector Mohamed Irfan, DRO Anandhi and among other officers participated on the occasion.

Sivaganga

Sivaganga District Collector P. Akash hoisted the national flag and took the salute in the presence of Superintendent of Police Abishek Gupta. After inspecting a guard of honour, the Collector honoured the freedom fighters and their families.

On the occasion, the Collector also presented welfare schemes to the beneficiaries and certificates of merit was presented to 52 police personnel and other officials from various departments.

The students’ from various schools presented a cultural program. Additional Collector Ayush Venkat Vats, MLAs Kulanthai Rani Nachiar and Illangovan participated.

Ramanathapuram

Ramanathapuram District Collector Sivaguru Prabhakaran hoisted the national flag and gave away welfare assistance to 53 beneficiaries worth ₹32.09 lakh on the occasion.

A total of 831 students presented cultural programmes and the Collector honoured 487 employees and officers from various departments, including 79 police personnel, for their commendable works in the district.

DIG of Police (Ramanathapuram Range) N Manivannan, SP G Chandeesh, Additional Collector (Development) Divyan Shenegan, DRO V Sankara Narayanan and other officers participated.

The Principal District Judge T V Mani hoisted the national flag at the District Court complex where senior judicial officers, including Shanti, Mohanram, Jaya Sudakar, Mumtaz and District Legal Services Authority secretary Baskar, Bar Association president Anbuchezian, secretary Muthu Duraisami and others participated.

In the Ramanathapuram, Government Medical College, Dean R Amudha Rani was the chief guest, who hoisted the flag and took the salute. The students presented the national anthem and Superintendent S A K Noor Ahamed and Vice Principal B Subitha participated.

World.title: Leading countries extend greetings to India on 80th Independence Day
World.content:
India’s global partners, including France, Russia and Australia, on Saturday (August 15, 2026) extended greetings to the country on its 80th Independence Day, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral ties and regional cooperation.

French President Emmanuel Macron, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Maldivian President Mohamed Muizzu were among leaders who hailed ties with India on the occasion.

Mr. Macron took to X to extend his greetings. “Congratulations to the Indian people on your 80th Independence Day!” he said.

Mr. Putin extended greetings to President Droupadi Murmu as well as Prime Minister Narendra Modi, expressing confidence that the constructive bilateral partnership will help enhance international security and stability.

The Russian President said Russia-India relations are developing successfully in the spirit of a “particularly privileged strategic partnership”.

He pointed out that Moscow and New Delhi are engaged in “fruitful cooperation” across a wide range of areas and coordinate closely within the framework of the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), BRICS, and other multilateral institutions.

“I am confident that, through our joint efforts, we will continue to comprehensively strengthen the constructive Russia-India partnership for the benefit of our friendly peoples and in the interests of enhancing international security and stability,” the Russian President said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also conveyed his greetings on the occasion, asserting that India has gone “from strength to strength” in the eight decades since its independence.

In a statement, Mr. Albanese said that India, as the world’s largest democracy and fastest-growing major economy, “fills us with awe at the scale of its achievements and the vastness of its potential”.

He recalled his Mr. Modi’s recent visit to Australia, where he told the Prime Minister, “Our relationship has never been more consequential”.

“We are excited to further deepen Australia and India’s engagement in new and growing areas with the support of the many Australians of Indian heritage who are the living bridge in our valued friendship. I join you in celebrating India’s history and culture, rich diversity and extraordinary achievements - and in celebrating the promise our shared future holds,” he said.

In his greeting, Maldivian leader Mr. Muizzu reiterated the archipelago’s commitment to enhance bilateral ties with India. “Eight decades of Independence reflect the aspirations, resilience and enduring spirit of the Government and people of India.

“On this auspicious occasion, I reaffirm the commitment of the Government of Maldives to further advance our close partnership built upon mutual respect, shared prosperity and enduring friendship between our two peoples,” he said on X.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog also wished India’s top leadership and the “wonderful people” of the country on Independence Day. “May we continue to strengthen the beautiful friendship between Israel and India,” he said in a social media post.

In a letter to President Murmu, her Singaporean counterpart Tharman Shanmugaratnam congratulated her and the people of India on the occasion, asserting that both countries share an “enduring interest in a peaceful, open, and connected region”.

The city-state will continue working closely with India, as one of ASEAN’s oldest Dialogue Partners, to strengthen regional integration and resilience, especially in trade, the digital economy, energy security, and the energy transition, he said.

Calling the Singapore-India ties “multifaceted”, he said the two nations also share a robust and forward-looking Comprehensive Strategic Partnership underpinned by close people-to-people ties.

“By drawing on our complementary strengths, I am confident that our two countries will continue to identify fresh opportunities for the benefit of our peoples,” he said.

On the occasion, Nepal Prime Minister Balendra ‘Balen’ Shah extended “heartfelt greetings” to Prime Minister Modi and the “friendly people” of India.

“May the deep historical ties, close people-to-people relations and cooperation between Nepal and India continue to strengthen in the years ahead,” Mr. Shah said, according to a social media post by his office.

Bhutan’s Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay also wished the government and people of India on Independence Day.

In a social media post, he said, “To my elder brother PM Narendra Modi and the people of India, I extend my warm wishes on the 80th Independence Day.” “May the enduring friendship and close ties between Bhutan and India continue to flourish.”

In his message, former Maldivian President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih called India’s journey since 1947 an “inspiration to developing countries”. “India’s journey since 1947 has been an inspiration to developing countries such as the Maldives on our own path to democracy. May the close ties of cooperation and friendship that exist between Maldives–India grow ever stronger,” he said on X.

Earlier on Friday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also extended his greetings and asserted that the bilateral ties were stronger than ever due to the personal relationship between President Donald Trump and Mr. Modi.

In a statement, Mr. Rubio said the deep ties of friendship and family between the people of the two countries form the foundation of a partnership that is innovative, resilient and forward-looking.

“On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of India on their Independence Day,” Mr. Rubio said, adding that bilateral collaboration is making both nations, and the broader Indian Ocean region, safer, stronger, and more prosperous.

World.title: Memorable Independence Day celebrations for students of govt. school at Kade Nandihalli in Shivamogga
World.content:
For 12 students of the Government Higher Primary School at Kade Nandihalli in Shikaripur taluk of Shivamogga district, this Independence Day will remain a special one — they got to take a helicopter ride over their village as part of the celebrations.

The students experienced the ride courtesy of the Vishwagra Foundation, a private foundation that has been supporting the government school by sponsoring guest teachers and providing study material to students.

Shivakumar A., founder of the Vishwagra Foundation, told The Hindu that as part of the event, 12 students who were toppers in their studies were taken on the ride. “Each ride lasted about six to seven minutes. Six students went up in each batch, with two rounds in all. The students thoroughly enjoyed the experience,” he said.

A committee of alumni of the century-old school has adopted the institution and has been undertaking several initiatives to develop its basic infrastructure with the help of donors. The committee has hired five guest teachers, in addition to the four government teachers, to improve the quality of education, and has introduced pre-primary classes to boost admissions.

Kumar Mattimani, president of the School Development and Management Committee (SDMC), said, “Because of the committee’s efforts, the school’s strength has gone up from 72 to 112 within a year,” he said.

Mr. Mattimani said the villagers had invited the foundation for the Independence Day programme, and the foundation had arranged for a helicopter to give the children the opportunity to enjoy a ride. The SDMC and the villagers had developed a helipad in the village for the occasion.

World.title: Mamallan reservoir project: documentation as advocacy
World.content:
Water moves in two directions across the Nemmeli coastal wetland — freshwater flowing east from inland lakes and tanks, and seawater moving inland through two estuaries. Spread across more than 8,500 acres between Kelambakkam and Mamallapuram, the wetland is a meeting point of these two water systems, shaped by tides, rainfall and the seasons.

That landscape is now being reshaped into a freshwater reservoir. The first phase of Mamallan reservoir project covers 4,375 acres. A second phase is proposed for the remaining wetland.

The proposed reservoir will occupy a landscape marked by marshes, mudflats, shallow waters, salt pans and seasonal grasslands, spanning freshwater and brackish-water habitats. The wetland is also a seasonal stopover along the Central Asian Flyway, drawing migratory birds, while its waters support fish, prawns, crabs and other species that sustain fishing activity in the surrounding villages.

The wetland is also being documented from the ground up. Environmental groups and naturalists are recording its biodiversity through field surveys, documentaries, signature campaigns, rallies and a coffee-table book.

Nemmeli’s Last Tide, a documentary conceptualised by Deepak Venkatachalam of Suzhal Arivom, a grassroot level, volunteer-driven environmental education, research, and conservation group and produced by the Wetland Conservation Network, brings together voices from naturalists, scientists, maritime researchers, educators and fisherfolks to document what the wetland holds and what could be lost.

According to Deepak, making people see the landscape is central to conservation. “We try to break that barrier by bringing in people and increasing the footfall to these places,” he says, describing the need to reconnect people with nature through direct experience and visual storytelling. “The landscape has so much life. It is a very complex, intricate ecosystem. It cannot be recreated at any cost once it is depleted.”

That life is reflected in the numbers. Suzhal Arivom’s documentation records 232 species in the Nemmeli Wetland complex, with nearly 45,000 birds counted during the 2025–26 peak season. A count of 16,000 migratory ducks, spread across half-a-dozen species, was recorded.

The wetland is also an important node in the Central Asian Flyway, with 88 migratory species recorded.

The documentation extends beyond birds. In January 2026, Suzhal Arivom recorded a established colony of Burmann’s Sundew (Drosera burmannii) at five GPS-verified locations. The tiny carnivorous plant survives in acidic, nutrient-poor, seasonally waterlogged soils making its presence an indicator of relatively undisturbed wetland conditions.

A parallel effort has come from the Palluyir Trust, a group for Nature Education and Research, founded in 2021 by naturalists, through its coffee-table book Kovalam–Nemmeli Coastal Wetland: A Biodiversity Montage. Combining photographs with species information, the book records the wetland’s birds, insects, benthic life, mangroves and other flora. Crucially, it was printed and sent to bureaucrats, MLAs and government authorities, accompanied by letters highlighting the wetland’s ecological importance and concerns over the proposed reservoir. A digital version is also available on their official website.

The documentation also places these species within the wider wetland ecosystem, its mudflats, marshes, shallow waters and vegetation which provide feeding and breeding grounds for aquatic life and habitat for migratory birds. It also records the wetland’s links to fishing livelihoods and flood protection.

“The idea is we are trying as many strategies as possible to make people feel for that place and be moved by the life there,” Yuvan says. For him, the question is also whether a freshwater reservoir can ever be considered an “alternative” to this landscape. “A freshwater body does not belong by the beach,” he argues, pointing to the difference between inland reservoirs and tidal wetlands.

Fewer fish, less income

Fisherfolk from more than 16 villages depend on the Kovalam–Nemmeli wetlands, with nearly 7,000 families relying on its shallow waters to collect prawns, crabs, oysters and other species. Unlike mechanised fishers, they work largely by hand and foot, following Iral Thazhuvuthal, the traditional practice of catching prawns and fish by hand. The Paraval, as they locally call the coastal wetland, has 18 distinct habitats, with the Purattasi season (mid-September to mid-October) bringing the highest catch. During this period, a family can earn ₹1 lakh–₹3 lakh, an income that can sustain them through much of the year.

The proposed reservoir threatens this livelihood system. About 5,000 acres of the wetland is proposed to be converted into an impounded freshwater reservoir, with Phase I covering 65% Kazhuveli marshland and 35% Uppangazhi salt pans. Forfisherfolk who have depended on these waters for generations, the loss could mean shrinking incomes and a shift to unfamiliar and precarious work.

For Kovalam R. Narayanan, the impact of the Mamallan Reservoir Project can be measured in the distance between what fishing once earned his family and what it brings in today. A fisherman from Kovalam, Narayanan began fishing at 11 and has continued in the occupation for decades. The earnings have now dwindled considerably. Narayanan links the decline partly to what has happened to fishermen who once worked in the coastal wetlands. As access to the wetland has reduced with the progress of the reservoir project, he said, many of those fishermen have moved to the sea.

That has changed the arithmetic of fishing. “Earlier, there were around 500 fishermen fishing in the sea and another 500 depending on the wetlands. Now all 1,000 are going to the sea,” he said. More boats and more fishers are consequently chasing the same marine catch, he said, leaving each fisher with a smaller share.

“The wetlands earmarked for the project are not an empty expanse waiting to be developed. They are a living ecosystem supporting an intricate network of species and livelihoods” said Narayanan.
